This paper investigates the blocking problem within a channel, a scenario where disks of two distinct sizes are stacked in a specific sequence. The objective is to determine the maximum total weight achievable from these disks. This problem extends the blocked disks problem originally formulated by Gallo et al. (2019), which involved only large disks. The solution presented here relies on a dynamic programming algorithm that operates in $O(n^2)$ time, where $n$ represents the count of disks. Furthermore, the algorithm is capable of constructing a corresponding witness sequence in linear time. We demonstrate that the proposed algorithm is optimal by establishing a lower bound on the maximum weight that matches this complexity. Additionally, we introduce a novel class of disk sequences and propose a conjecture regarding the time complexity of solving the blocking problem for this specific case. Finally, we explore applications of this problem in the context of DNA sequencing. The code for the algorithm is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/edgar-garcia/blocked-disk-problem}. This study examines the distinct impacts of different El Niño flavors on extreme seasonal precipitation levels across the Americas, Africa, and Australia. By analyzing precipitation extremes, we identify that the unique spatial patterns of very low and very high precipitation observed during El Niño years are differentially expressed based on the specific flavor of the event. We achieve this by employing a Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on the Niño 3.4 index to isolate the contributions of canonical El Niño and La Niña flavors, alongside a robust flavor index derived from the NCEP/NCAR reanalysis. Furthermore, we apply a clustering technique to the precipitation data to detect the emergence of distinct spatial patterns. The resulting spatial maps reveal that these patterns are more pronounced during El Niño years compared to La Niña years. Finally, we assess the significance of these findings by comparing them against a synthetic dataset generated from a Gaussian random field. This approach confirms that the observed spatial patterns are statistically significant and not merely artifacts of random noise. Ultimately, our findings suggest that precipitation extremes can serve as valuable indicators for understanding the specific impacts of various El Niño flavors. This insight could enhance our capacity to forecast the effects of future El Niño events, thereby improving water resource management and agricultural planning. Additionally, our methodology offers a framework for investigating the differential impacts of other climate phenomena, such as La Niña, the Southern Oscillation Index, and the Multivariate ENSO Index. We present a theoretical framework for analyzing the growth of non-affine growth instabilities in active suspensions through light scattering. This approach is applicable to systems where instabilities arise from non-reciprocal interactions, such as those driven by non-conservative active stresses or non-reciprocal pair potentials. These findings offer a pathway to understanding how non-reciprocity influences the growth and morphology of instabilities in active suspensions. Hidden Markov Models (HMMs) are a fundamental tool in probabilistic modeling, finding extensive use in fields like speech recognition and bioinformatics. This paper introduces a novel, more abstract variant of HMMs, termed "abstract HMMs," which are defined as the free monad constructed from a specific endofunctor on a category of spaces. This monad encapsulates the core components of HMMs in a highly abstract framework. We demonstrate that these abstract HMMs possess a universal property that allows for the generation of various HMM-like structures. Furthermore, we apply this monadic framework to quantitative information flow, a critical area within computer security. By utilizing abstract HMMs, we derive a general formula for calculating leakage from programs, which can be employed to analyze the leakage properties of arbitrary systems. Additionally, we illustrate how to model the leakage characteristics of real-world systems using this approach. The proposed method for analyzing abstract HMMs is both general and flexible, enabling the application of other mathematical techniques to the study of HMMs. Finally, we provide a Haskell implementation of abstract HMMs, which includes a library for analyzing HMMs and a set of examples demonstrating their utility. This work establishes a new foundation for HMM theory and offers a fresh perspective on the analysis of HMM-based systems.

We introduce a phenomenological framework designed to investigate flexible scattering amplitudes across all kinematic regimes. This approach is grounded in the analytic properties of these amplitudes and their expansion within the soft limit. By applying this formalism to various processes involving quarks, gluons, and electroweak bosons, we derive constraints on the subleading soft functions governing these expanded terms. Furthermore, we demonstrate how this method can be extended to final-state observables, such as jet functions, and to particles with non-zero mass. Finally, we outline the application of this formalism to final-state soft radiation. Our findings are derived using the Berends-Dixon algorithm, though we also provide a brief outline of the adaptation required when employing the next-to-leading logarithmic (NLLx) algorithm. Additionally, we present numerical results for final-state soft radiation, comparing our outcomes with those from parton shower algorithms. This work serves as a precursor to a subsequent study where we develop a numerical implementation of the approach to construct flexible scattering cross sections. This study examines the naming problem within beeping networks, where nodes must assign unique identifiers of a specific length without access to any initial input. We demonstrate that networks with an odd number of nodes can achieve energy-efficient, conflict-free, and self-stabilizing solutions, whereas networks with an even number of nodes are restricted to only achieving conflict-free naming without energy efficiency. Our primary contribution is a novel energy-conserving naming algorithm for odd-sized networks that operates in $O(n)$ rounds and utilizes $O(\log n)$ bits of memory per node. This method leverages a new approach to distributed binary counting, which we believe holds independent significance. We further establish that our algorithm is optimal regarding both round complexity and memory usage. Additionally, we prove that any distributed algorithm attempting to resolve naming in these networks must employ at least $\Omega(\log n)$ bits of memory per node. Finally, we present a simple, conflict-free, and energy-conserving naming algorithm for even-sized networks that runs in $O(n)$ rounds and uses $O(\log n)$ bits of memory per node. We also show that any algorithm for this scenario requires a minimum of $\Omega(\log n)$ memory per node. All proposed algorithms are robust against node failures. Furthermore, we extend these results to networks with a fixed number of faulty nodes, demonstrating that all algorithms remain efficient in terms of rounds and memory under such conditions. We conclude by proving that any algorithm for naming in these faulty networks necessitates $\Omega(\log n)$ memory per node. Finally, we explore the relationship between naming and the leader election problem, showing that any distributed algorithm for leader election in beeping networks requires $\Omega(\log n)$ memory per node. This lower bound is tight, as we provide an algorithm that achieves this exact memory requirement. We also discuss the implications of these findings for the general beeping model. This study investigates the pressure-dependent isotope effect on the critical temperature ($T_c$) for H$_3$S hydride superconductors. By employing the Allen-Dynes modified McMillan equation alongside the Debye approximation, we calculated the isotope effect exponent $\alpha$ across a pressure range of 130 to 260 GPa. Motion planning in dynamic settings is a critical challenge for mobile robotics. While numerous methods exist for motion planning, most fail to account for the spatial constraints imposed by the robot's physical dimensions. This paper introduces a novel approach that generates spatial constraints to represent the robot's dimensionally induced restrictions. These constraints are derived from the robot's configuration space and subsequently utilized to direct motion planning. The proposed method is applicable to both point-based and configuration-based motion planning frameworks. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates the method's effectiveness through a series of simulations. The results indicate that the proposed approach yields promising outcomes, particularly in terms of computational efficiency. Additionally, the method successfully produces feasible trajectories for a two-link manipulator navigating a 2D environment populated with moving obstacles. This paper introduces a visual relocalization technique that leverages a 3D surfel map. By employing a neural network to generate 3D descriptors for each surfel and extracting image descriptors from input images, the method establishes correspondences between them. Additionally, we propose a novel strategy to mitigate the impact of incorrect correspondences on the relocalization outcome. Extensive experiments conducted on the TUM RGB-D and KITTI datasets demonstrate that our approach surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods. This paper introduces a novel joint optimization framework for user selection and precoding within multiuser MIMO systems. The objective is to maximize the sum rate by simultaneously determining the optimal precoder and the optimal subset of active users. To address the combinatorial complexity inherent in user selection, we reformulate the problem by relaxing the binary user choice variables into a simplex-constrained vector. This transformation yields a convex optimization problem that can be efficiently solved using the Cyclic Group LASSO (CGL) algorithm. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method achieves performance comparable to exhaustive search solutions while requiring significantly lower computational complexity. Furthermore, the method outperforms existing joint design approaches in terms of both sum rate and fairness. Finally, the paper extends this formulation to handle practical constraints, including imperfect channel state information and finite alphabet signaling. Numerical evaluations confirm that the proposed method remains robust under these realistic conditions. The proposed results are applicable to infinite-dimensional control problems, including those involving infinite state and/or control spaces. Notably, Example 1 addresses a finite-dimensional linear quadratic regulator problem, while Example 2 considers a parabolic partial differential equation. We introduce a new method for designing self-assembly protocols and particles by utilizing neuroevolutionary learning. This approach enables the autonomous development of strategies and particle types capable of forming specific target structures. To achieve this, we developed a novel particle model that extends the hard-core Yukawa potential, allowing for the creation of multi-component systems. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness by successfully designing self-assembly strategies for various target structures, including crystals, quasicrystals, and square and hexagonal lattices. Furthermore, we show that the resulting strategies can generate multi-component systems where components exhibit distinct behaviors, such as varying degrees of mobility. Our findings indicate that neuroevolutionary learning is a highly effective tool for both particle design and the creation of self-assembly strategies. Additionally, we demonstrate that the same strategy can produce different structures, such as crystals and hexagonal lattices, and that the proposed particle model can form structures with varying numbers of components. These results suggest that neuroevolutionary learning is a versatile tool for designing multi-component systems. Finally, we highlight that the strategy can achieve target structures with lower energy than those obtained through standard optimization methods. Overall, our findings demonstrate that neuroevolutionary learning is a powerful tool for designing self-assembly strategies and particles. The proposed method is expected to be applicable to a wide range of target structures and will be valuable for designing complex self-assembly systems. This paper examines the initial value problem for the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations within essential Besov spaces. We demonstrate that this problem is well-posed in spaces $B^s_{\infty,0}$ where $s \leq 0$, thereby extending previous findings by Fabes, J. G. Shen, and S. Wang (2001) and Shen (2002), which established well-posedness for $-1 < s \leq 0$. Additionally, we prove that the stationary Navier-Stokes equations are ill-posed in these same spaces $B^s_{\infty,0}$ for $s \leq 0$. This finding represents the first instance of ill-posedness for the stationary Navier-Stokes equations in a space where solutions are not necessarily Hölder continuous. Furthermore, we show that the ill-posedness persists even when imposing smallness conditions on the initial data. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the regularity of solutions to the time-dependent Navier-Stokes equations. The methodology employed relies on the Littlewood-Paley decomposition. Our results complement and extend the work of Bahouri, Chemin, and Zhang (2011), who previously addressed well-posedness issues in this context. Additionally, we provide a new proof of the ill-posedness of the stationary Navier-Stokes equations in $L^{\infty}$, a result originally established by Koch and Tataru (2001). The paper concludes with an appendix dedicated to a discussion on the definition of Hölder spaces. Loidreau's code-based cryptosystem relies on the rank metric, utilizing Goppa codes to establish its public key. The system's security hinges on the difficulty of decoding in the rank metric. This paper introduces two modifications to the original scheme: the first adapts the public key by applying a specific transformation to Goppa codes, while the second employs a different approach to key generation. Both variations maintain the same key dimensions as the initial proposal. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the second modification offers enhanced security. Finally, we provide a Python implementation of the second variant and evaluate its performance. The results indicate that the second version is approximately 1.5 times faster than the first, with both achieving performance levels comparable to McEliece implementations. Additionally, we present a rank metric decoder that outperforms the rank syndrome decoder described in the original paper. Finally, we analyze the security of both variants, demonstrating that they are resistant to rank metric attacks. Our findings suggest that the second modification is superior to the first, as it offers greater security against alternative rank metric decoding algorithms. Topological data analysis (TDA) offers a framework for visualizing the topology of point clouds. Given a finite set of points in Euclidean space, one can determine a filtration by calculating the minimal spanning acycles for nested radii. The extremal radii within this filtration correspond to the birth and death points in a persistence diagram. This study examines minimal spanning acycles derived from random point sets, specifically those generated by Poisson processes and uniformly distributed points. We derive the scaling behavior of the minimal spanning acycles at both the maximum and minimum extremal birth points, as well as the death points, across various dimensions. Furthermore, we analyze the fluctuations of the extremal persistence diagram by deriving the mass distribution for minimal spanning acycles at the extreme ends of the filtration. These findings are supported by numerical simulations. The results for the extremal persistence diagram are consistent with recent research by Baryshnikov, Bellettini, and Ghiraldin. Additionally, we demonstrate that the extremal persistence diagram exhibits a phase transition at a specific dimension. Finally, we explore the implications of these findings for the statistical analysis of persistence diagrams. This work is a collaborative effort with J. B. Berman, A. Dembo, and J. B. Peterson. Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) represents a privacy-preserving framework where multiple parties collaborate to train machine learning models by contributing only their local feature data. This paper introduces a novel privacy threat against VFL, termed Vertical Inference Leakage (VIL), which demonstrates that an adversary can deduce a target party's private feature vector from a trained model. We establish that VIL remains effective even when the adversary lacks access to the target party's categorical features. Furthermore, we develop a new algorithm, Vertical Federated Gradient Descent (VFGD), which offers robust protection against VIL. Experimental results indicate that VFGD achieves performance comparable to existing VFL methods while significantly reducing the risk of privacy breaches. Additionally, we release the first open-source VFL library, designed to be both practical and secure against VIL. We investigate the exclusive two-body decay of $B$ mesons into a proton and a dark antibaryon, where the dark antibaryon originates from a hidden sector with a mass scale comparable to $\Lambda_{QCD}$. We derive QCD light-cone sum rules for the relevant hadronic matrix elements, incorporating both twist-3 and twist-4 components of the baryon distribution amplitudes. Utilizing these rules, we establish constraints on the $B$-meson decay constants and the Wilson coefficients governing the $B\to p\bar{\chi}$ process. Furthermore, we analyze the implications of our findings for dark matter direct detection experiments. Our results indicate that the $B$-meson decay constant is approximately $0.19\pm 0.01$ GeV, a value that aligns with the upper limits derived from the XENON1T experiment. Additionally, we demonstrate that the decay amplitude can be enhanced by a factor of 100 through the mixing of $B$ and $B_1$ mesons. Finally, we show that the parameter space compatible with the XENON1T result is also consistent with the bounds established by LUX and PandaX experiments. These findings suggest that dark antibaryons may constitute a significant portion of dark matter. Our findings offer a novel explanation for the excess observed in XENON1T data, which has previously been difficult to reconcile with standard WIMP scenarios. This work underscores the critical role of $B$-meson decays in the search for dark antibaryons. Furthermore, it highlights the necessity of conducting direct dark matter detection experiments at low momentum transfer to effectively probe dark antibaryon candidates. Our findings provide a promising framework for future investigations into dark antibaryon dark matter. Additionally, we demonstrate that the $B$-meson decay constant can be determined with high precision using QCD light-cone sum rules. This determination is crucial for understanding the $B\to p\bar{\chi}$ process and for interpreting the results of direct dark matter detection experiments. Our findings suggest that the dark antibaryon scenario is viable and that further research into dark antibaryon dark matter is warranted. In conclusion, our results provide a new perspective on the search for dark antibaryons and emphasize the importance of direct dark matter detection experiments at low momentum transfer. This paper introduces a new intelligent city framework designed to mitigate damage from socio-cyber-physical attacks. The city is modeled as a graph where nodes represent critical infrastructure and edges signify communication links. The system incorporates a defense mechanism that allocates resources to the most vulnerable nodes to counteract potential threats. We formalize the interaction between attackers and defenders as a two-player, zero-sum, non-cooperative game. The attacker aims to compromise the maximum number of nodes within a fixed timeframe, whereas the defender seeks to optimize the distribution of defense resources to neutralize attacks. We present a novel game-theoretic approach that enables both agents to learn optimal strategies through trial and error. Furthermore, we develop a new graph-based damage assessment metric to quantify the impact of attacks on the city. Finally, simulation results demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed method. To our knowledge, this represents the first application of deep reinforcement learning to the defender in a graph-based city attack scenario. Additionally, this work extends our prior research by shifting from a static to a dynamic attack model, where the attacker can compromise a node only if it remains unconnected to already compromised nodes. This dynamic constraint significantly increases the difficulty for the attacker, necessitating a more robust defense strategy. This study examines the thermodynamics of black holes within a cavity, focusing on the Hawking--Page phase transition. By analyzing the system's free energy, we determine the radius of the canonical horizon, which evolves as the temperature changes. The results indicate that Schwarzschild black holes in a cavity do not undergo Hawking--Page phase transitions, whereas charged black holes and rotating Kerr black holes do. Furthermore, we observe that as the horizon radius increases, the specific heat of Kerr black holes shifts from negative to positive, and the chemical potential of charged black holes drops to zero. These findings offer valuable insights for future research. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results in the context of the AdS/CFT correspondence. This study addresses the challenge of ranking under label noise, where information retrieval (IR) data is prevalent. We introduce a novel algorithm that leverages the inherent group structure of IR datasets. By applying bag sampling to each group, we generate multiple training samples from a single group, enabling the training of several models. These models are then evaluated using group-level loss, which calculates the mean ranking performance across all sampled models for a given group. Our experimental results demonstrate that this approach significantly outperforms existing methods. Furthermore, we show that the proposed method is robust against data distribution shifts, a critical characteristic for IR applications. Finally, we validate the algorithm's effectiveness on both synthetic and real-world datasets. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ahmedhassan1998/labelnoise_ranking. Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have proven highly effective for node classification, yet they often suffer from over-smoothing and require a large volume of labeled nodes to achieve satisfactory results. To address this, pseudo-labeling strategies have been developed to generate additional training labels. However, existing approaches typically rely on pseudo-labels derived from the final output layer, which can be unreliable. Experimental results demonstrate that our method surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques. Additionally, we find that pseudo-labels generated from the most informative hidden layers are more robust to hyperparameter variations. This study addresses the challenge of training decision trees in a distributed environment where data is held locally by multiple parties and privacy is safeguarded through differential privacy. We introduce a practical, provably accurate framework for learning differentially private decision trees in a distributed setting. Our approach is grounded in a novel distributed decision tree learning algorithm that operates in a black-box fashion, allowing it to be paired with any existing single-party private decision tree learning method. We demonstrate that the privacy guarantees and utility of the resulting global algorithm are determined by the characteristics of the local components. Furthermore, we establish that our global algorithm achieves differential privacy and maintains a bounded error relative to the optimal tree that could be learned if the local algorithms were released. Finally, we present experimental results comparing our method against other distributed private decision tree learning techniques. These experiments indicate that our algorithm is competitive with other methods in terms of both privacy guarantees and utility. Additionally, our method is significantly more scalable than existing solutions, capable of handling datasets with hundreds of thousands of samples and features. This scalability is achieved by leveraging a distributed implementation of the local private decision tree learning components. We also show that our approach can be further enhanced by integrating a recent single-party decision tree learning algorithm that utilizes a novel quantile estimation technique. This combination yields a highly scalable and accurate solution for private decision tree learning in distributed contexts. This paper introduces a straightforward yet effective approach for regularizing the cross-entropy divergence between two probability distributions, $p$ and $q$, by minimizing the sum of this divergence and a Bregman divergence relative to a reference distribution $q_0$. We demonstrate that this objective is equivalent to optimizing the $\alpha$-R\'enyi divergence between $p$ and $q_0$ as $\alpha$ approaches 1. Leveraging this equivalence, we develop Bregman proximal gradient algorithms to address the problem, with their convergence properties analyzed under the assumption that the Kullback-Leibler divergence is finite. Finally, we apply these algorithms to a classification task, showing that they yield superior performance compared to standard L2-regularized logistic regression. The study includes numerical experiments that validate the proposed methods and highlight their computational efficiency. Chain Event Graphs (CEGs) extend the capabilities of Discrete Event Models (DEMs) by offering a more interpretable and concise representation. While both frameworks are defined as equivalence classes of Markov chains, a CEG is specifically characterized by regular transitions, meaning the future evolution of a Markov chain depends solely on its current node rather than its specific state. This structural advantage makes CEGs particularly advantageous for model choice within Bayesian Markov random field models. This work demonstrates how to calculate the marginal likelihood for CEGs and applies these findings to determine the most probable CEG structure given observed data. Furthermore, we illustrate the application of these methods using a dataset concerning the treatment of acute myeloid leukaemia. Additionally, the code required to replicate these results is publicly accessible. This study examines a dynamical system featuring damping, inertia, and Tikhonov regularization applied to an $\mathcal{A}$-monotone operator. We demonstrate that, under specific conditions, the asymptotic behavior of this system's trajectories aligns with findings from prior research regarding undamped inertial dynamics. Furthermore, we establish that the trajectory sequence approaches the unique zero of the $\mathcal{A}$-monotone operator $F = \nabla f + g$, where $f$ is strongly convex and $g$ is $\mu$-strongly concave, achieving a convergence rate of $1/t$. Finally, by incorporating a vanishing Tikhonov regularization term, we prove that the trajectory sequence converges strongly to the element with the minimum norm within the set of zeros of $F$. These findings are supported by numerical experiments. Additionally, we derive analogous results for a two-parameter family of dynamical systems, demonstrating that it asymptotically behaves like a system with a single parameter. In this scenario, the trajectory sequence converges weakly to a zero of $F$, while the two Tikhonov regularization parameters converge to the elements of minimum norm in the respective null spaces of the gradient of $f$ and the operator $g$. The numerical examples provided illustrate this convergence behavior. These theoretical and computational results hold significant implications for the analysis and numerical approximation of variational inequalities and optimization problems. Notably, this work extends and complements existing literature by relaxing several technical assumptions, such as the Lipschitz continuity of the operator's gradient, the strong convexity of the objective function, and the compactness of the feasible set. Moreover, our approach offers a novel perspective on the convergence analysis of Tikhonov regularization methods. The results are applicable to a broad spectrum of problems, including saddle point problems, constrained optimization, and the minimization of strongly convex functions over convex sets. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 introduces the dynamical system, its Lagrangian, and establishes existence and uniqueness results for its trajectories. Section 3 presents the main theoretical findings, encompassing convergence rates and the application of Tikhonov regularization. Section 4 addresses saddle point problems, while Section 5 focuses on optimization tasks. Section 6 presents numerical experiments to validate the theoretical results, and Section 7 concludes the paper. Finally, an appendix provides a detailed analysis of the asymptotic behavior of trajectories. This work was partially supported by the ANR project ANR-18

Wall-following robots are engineered to trace a boundary while maintaining a constant distance from it. This study investigates the emergence of disorderly motion in such robots, which stems from discrete bifurcations occurring at every sensing event. The resulting motion is characterized by a sequence of period-doubling bifurcations that lead to period doubling, chaos, and band merging. The sequence of period doublings follows a universal law, whereas the bifurcation scaling exponents are universal but do not adhere to Feigenbaum's law. Furthermore, the distribution of sensing intervals displays a power-law tail, and the system exhibits a universal scaling function that describes the transition from periodic to chaotic behavior. These findings indicate that period-doubling chaos is a common feature in wall-following robots. Additionally, we demonstrate that the universal scaling exponents for bifurcations and the power-law behavior of sensing intervals can be utilized to forecast the onset of chaos. This research underscores the significance of discrete sensing in the dynamics of wall-following robots and offers a framework for analyzing the transition to chaos in discrete dynamical systems. The methodology is applicable to a broad range of systems, including those with variable sensing intervals and those governed by quadratic maps. Finally, we introduce a novel wall-following algorithm that eliminates chaotic motion. The study concludes with a discussion of potential applications for wall-following robots. We investigate the impact of extended impurities on transport properties within kinetic energy-driven conductors. Our findings indicate that impurities with an extent $L$ surpassing the mean free path $l$ result in a doping- and energy-dependent transport mechanism. Specifically, the transport diffusion constant $D_{\rm tr}$ scales as $D_{\rm tr}\propto l/L$, while the quasiparticle lifetime $\tau_{\rm qp}$ follows $\tau_{\rm qp}\propto L$. Consequently, the microwave conductivity is expressed as $\sigma(\omega)\propto \tau_{\rm qp}D_{\rm tr}n(\xi)\propto \tau_{\rm qp}D_{\rm tr}n(\omega/T)$, where $n(\xi)$ represents the Fermi function. This formulation implies that the temperature dependence of microwave conductivity in the clean limit ($L\gg l$) mirrors that of the diffusive limit ($L\ll l$). Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Drude-like description of microwave conductivity in kinetic energy-driven conductors is valid only when $L\ll l$. Finally, we outline the necessary conditions for observing the diffusive regime in experiments. These conclusions are supported by the solution of the kinetic equation governing the impurity-averaged distribution function. Additionally, we derive the quasiparticle lifetime and the energy-dependent phase relaxation time, which is defined as the inverse of the microwave conductivity. Our results align with the solution of the impurity-averaged Boltzmann equation for impurities with $L\ll l$. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the study of cuprates. This paper examines a singular curvature flow where crystals evolve by their crystalline-like average curvature. We provide an overview of the short-time existence, non-existence of boundary oscillations, and the long-time existence and convergence of the flow. Additionally, we investigate the convergence of polyhedra and tetrahedra under this flow. The analysis of polyhedra is restricted to the case where the crystalline-like surface tension function is piecewise quadratic. Finally, we demonstrate that the flow preserves the crystalline nature of the initial geometry. Furthermore, we establish that the flow maintains the face structure of a tetrahedron during evolution, thereby enabling the derivation of asymptotic and convergence results for this specific shape. All proofs are presented in a self-contained manner. Finally, we explore potential applications of these findings to the study of the anisotropic singular mean curvature flow of a torus.

Plants are vital to human survival, yet they are not static; they constantly adapt to their surroundings. This dynamic behavior means plant growth is influenced by environmental factors, offering the potential to accelerate growth by optimizing these conditions. This paper introduces GrowSpace, a reinforcement learning framework designed to identify growth-optimal environments for plants. By utilizing a physics-based simulation, the system learns to control the spatial arrangement of lighting and water sources. Experimental results demonstrate that GrowSpace successfully learns policies to locate an optimal configuration, thereby accelerating plant growth. Furthermore, the approach reveals that growth-optimal environments are often non-intuitive, suggesting that growth can be enhanced through the manipulation of plant morphology. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/andrewgao12/GrowSpace. Our findings indicate that GrowSpace can be applied to various plant species, including moss, snapdragons, and sunflowers. Additionally, the method offers a novel research avenue for investigating how environmental adaptations influence plant growth. We hope GrowSpace will inspire further exploration of the complex relationship between plants and their surroundings. This work was supported by the National Science Foundation (Award No. 1909000). We demonstrate that the collection of conformal immersions of quantum disks, termed "wedges," is closed under the operation of quantum gravity conformal welding. This process involves gluing the boundaries of two wedges using an independent family of boundary loop erasure random walks (BLEWs). The resulting object is a wedge whose quantum area corresponds to the sum of the areas of the original components. Furthermore, we establish that the collection of quantum disks, which emerge as limits of these wedges, is likewise closed under conformal welding with an independent family of boundaries. In this specific instance, the boundaries are glued together using a Bessel process. This framework provides a novel approach to proving the existence of Schramm-Loewner evolution (SLE) on quantum surfaces, thereby generating a quantum surface on which the SLE curve can be defined. Additionally, we derive a formula for computing the law of the resulting wedge from the laws of the initial wedges and the welding data. This formula serves as a quantum analogue to the change of variables formula in classical change of variables theory. Finally, we offer a new characterization of the laws of Liouville quantum gravity surfaces. Specifically, we show that any such surface can be decomposed into a collection of quantum disks and quantum intervals, where the intervals are connected via Bessel processes and the disks via Bessel excursions. This decomposition serves as a quantum counterpart to the classical decomposition of Riemann surfaces into pairs of pants. The primary technical instrument for these findings is a new coupling between Bessel processes and loop erasure random walks, which we term "loop erasure Bessel coupling." This coupling is derived from the quantum gravity conformal welding theorem and enables the construction of a coupling between Bessel processes and loop erasure random walks on any quantum surface. We anticipate that this "loop erasure Bessel coupling" will serve as a valuable tool for future research. This proof relies on a new characterization of the quantum Liouville space, which we term the "quantum universal covering space." The normalization of radiomic biomarkers is essential for ensuring their reproducibility. However, the absence of standardized protocols has led to inconsistent findings across various studies. This paper introduces the Image Biomarker Standardization Initiative (IBSI), a global collaborative effort dedicated to developing guidelines for the calculation and reporting of radiomic features. The initiative involves researchers from academia, government, and industry who have created a comprehensive taxonomy of features and established a rigorous testing framework to evaluate their robustness. This document serves as a foundational resource for the robust calculation and reporting of radiomic features, and it is intended to be updated regularly as the initiative evolves. The IBSI offers a robust framework for feature extraction and definition, and its scope extends to three-dimensional features, including those derived from temporal data. Furthermore, the initiative provides a framework for feature selection that can be applied to both retrospective and prospective studies. The $K\Lambda$ and $K\Sigma$ photoproduction reactions on a nucleon target are investigated using a relativistic quark model. This model incorporates the couplings of the $K\Lambda$ and $K\Sigma$ channels to the $N\Delta$, $\epsilon N$, and $\rho N$ final states. The resulting predictions for the cross sections align well with experimental data. Furthermore, the relative contributions of the $N\Delta$, $\epsilon N$, and $\rho N$ final states to the production of $K\Lambda$ and $K\Sigma$ are quantified. The study concludes that the $N\Delta$ and $\epsilon N$ contributions are significant, whereas the $\rho N$ contribution is negligible. Additionally, the influence of the $N\Delta$ and $\epsilon N$ contributions on the photodisintegration of the $\Lambda N$ and $\Sigma N$ bound states is examined. Finally, the implications of these findings for the $K\Lambda$ and $K\Sigma$ photoproduction processes are discussed. These results suggest that the $K\Lambda$ and $K\Sigma$ photoproduction amplitudes are primarily driven by the $N\Delta$ and $\epsilon N$ contributions, respectively. Consequently, the $K\Lambda$ and $K\Sigma$ photodisintegration of the $\Lambda N$ and $\Sigma N$ bound states is expected to be dominated by the $N\Delta$ and $\epsilon N$ contributions, respectively. This conclusion is consistent with the observed experimental asymmetry in the $K\Lambda$ and $K\Sigma$ photoproduction processes. The dominance of the $N\Delta$ and $\epsilon N$ contributions in the $K\Lambda$ and $K\Sigma$ photodisintegration of the $\Lambda N$ and $\Sigma N$ bound states, respectively, is also supported by the $K\Lambda$ and $K\Sigma$ photodisintegration of the $\Lambda n$ and $\Sigma n$ bound states. The primary objective of this research is to automatically detect and extract frontal faces from images in the MORPH-II database using the OpenCV framework. This process involves detecting faces within the dataset and applying pre-processing techniques, specifically contrast enhancement via the histogram equalization algorithm and noise reduction through the median filter algorithm. The study evaluates various face detection methods, including Haar Cascade, OpenCV, and Dlib, to identify the most effective approach for the given database. Ultimately, the findings indicate that the OpenCV framework yields superior results compared to the alternatives. Furthermore, the research demonstrates that both histogram equalization and median filter algorithms are highly effective for the proposed pre-processing pipeline. Finally, the study addresses the challenge of detecting faces in images with low contrast and noise, presenting a solution that enhances image quality for improved detection accuracy. The proposed framework is expected to facilitate face recognition and other related applications. Additionally, the code is made available for future researchers to utilize in their own face detection and recognition projects. The source code can be accessed at: https://github.com/AbdulazizAlshammari1/face-detection-and-preprocessing. The corresponding paper is available at: https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.00070. We propose a mechanism to generate primordial black holes (PBHs) with a mass of approximately $10^{15}$ GeV, utilizing a minimum of two curvaton fields. This scenario arises when the decay of the first curvaton field produces a PBH mass near $10^{15}$ GeV, while the second curvaton subsequently decays into dark matter. We demonstrate that this framework can account for the observed dark matter density and establish a lower limit for the PBH mass of roughly $10^{15}$ GeV. Furthermore, we show that PBHs with a mass of approximately $10^{15}$ GeV can alleviate the tension regarding the muon g-2 anomaly. We also examine the implications of this model for the reheating temperature of the universe and the production of gravitational waves. Finally, we explore the potential for detecting these PBHs through gravitational wave observations. Our findings indicate that PBHs with a mass of approximately $10^{15}$ GeV could be detected by LISA, DECIGO, and BBO. Additionally, we demonstrate that the BBN constraint on the PBH mass can be evaded if the decay of the curvaton field occurs before the decay of neutrons. This model offers a viable explanation for the muon g-2 anomaly and provides a novel method for generating PBHs. Furthermore, it suggests a specific mass range for PBHs that can be investigated using gravitational wave observatories. This work highlights the significance of PBHs in cosmology and underscores the need for further research into their properties and detection methods. Detecting misinformation is a critical challenge in natural language processing, particularly within news domains where fabricated headlines often accompany accurate content. While previous research has primarily focused on identifying fake news articles, this study shifts the focus to automatically generated headlines. Although these headlines are shorter and more concise, they are often more deceptive and harder to distinguish from genuine content. To address this, we introduce a dataset of fake headlines, constructed by translating real headlines and then modifying them to violate semantic and grammatical rules. We evaluate various machine learning models, finding that pre-trained transformer architectures outperform both other pre-trained models and traditional machine learning approaches. Furthermore, we analyze the performance of different transformer variants and investigate the impact of input length on detection accuracy. Finally, we explore the role of human intuition in recognizing fake headlines. Our findings demonstrate that transformer-based models can effectively identify fabricated headlines, achieving state-of-the-art results with an F1 score of 86.42%. The dataset and associated code are available at https://github.com/rohitkumar2001/fake-headline-detection. We present a novel method for generating chiral spin liquids in both two- and three-dimensional amorphous and polycrystalline systems. This approach involves applying a weak, in-plane magnetic field to a spin-1/2 Heisenberg antiferromagnet that is intrinsically frustrated by a next-nearest-neighbor interaction. We demonstrate that this procedure yields a unique ground state characterized by a non-zero local chirality. Furthermore, we show that the resulting phase is stabilized by a first-order phase transition originating from a first-order quantum critical point. Our findings indicate that this phase can be realized in both amorphous and polycrystalline materials, including the quantum magnets $\kappa$-(BEDT-TTF)$_2$Cu$_2$(CN)$_3$ and the frustrated spin-1/2 system Li$_2$CuO$_2$. Additionally, we identify a first-order quantum critical point that separates a unique ground state with non-zero local chirality from a degenerate ground state where local chirality vanishes. This critical point is detectable in both single crystals and polycrystals, though it remains inaccessible in amorphous samples. Finally, we discuss the experimental signatures of this critical point and the chiral spin liquid phase within the context of the quantum magnets $\kappa$-(BEDT-TTF)$_2$Cu$_2$(CN)$_3$ and Li$_2$CuO$_2$. Our results suggest that the chiral spin liquid phase and the associated first-order quantum critical point could be present in these materials. This conclusion is supported by the observation of a first-order quantum phase transition in $\kappa$-(BEDT-TTF)$_2$Cu$_2$(CN)$_3$ and the existence of a finite-temperature phase transition in polycrystalline Li$_2$CuO$_2$. Similarly, the finite-temperature phase transition observed in polycrystalline Li$_2$CuO$_2$ could indicate the presence of a chiral spin liquid phase. This paper introduces a new calibration method designed to efficiently handle the data volumes generated by future radio interferometers. The proposed algorithm operates with $\mathcal{O}(N\log{N})$ complexity, where $N$ represents the number of baselines, by utilizing the Fast Fourier Transform (FFT). This efficiency is achieved through a specific data organization strategy that maps baseline coordinates to FFT indices, enabling the FFT to interpolate the visibility array. The approach is particularly well-suited for interferometers arranged on regular grids, such as the Square Kilometer Array (SKA). We demonstrate the algorithm's functionality using a small array of ten antennas and evaluate its computational performance against a standard correlation algorithm. Our results indicate that the proposed method is approximately 10 times faster than the conventional approach. Additionally, we successfully applied the algorithm to a real-world dataset from the Murchison Widefield Array (MWA) to further validate its effectiveness. We conclude that this technique offers a highly efficient solution for correlating visibility arrays in future radio interferometers. Finally, we outline potential extensions of this work, including the development of an FFT-based imaging algorithm. These enhancements would enable the imaging process to run roughly 10 times faster than current methods, thereby significantly reducing the time required to generate sky maps. This advancement would substantially accelerate the data analysis pipeline, allowing scientists to more rapidly identify and investigate transient events. Ultimately, this improvement would facilitate the real-time monitoring of the sky for transient phenomena. We anticipate that these capabilities will be essential for future real-time transient surveys. Furthermore, we suggest that this approach could be adapted for use in other fields, such as optical interferometry. By applying this method, optical interferometers could achieve real-time imaging, a capability that would greatly enhance their ability to monitor and study transient astronomical events. We believe that this work paves the way for further research into the application of FFT-based algorithms to various interferometric systems. The source code for the algorithms presented in this paper is available at: https://github.com/abhishekkumar1999/fft-correlation. This code can serve as a foundation for future research and development in this area. We hope that this work will inspire other researchers to explore the potential of FFT-based algorithms in radio interferometry and related fields. By continuing to build upon this research, we can unlock new possibilities for real-time transient monitoring and data analysis in the coming years. The source code for the algorithms presented in this paper can be found at: https://github.com/abhishekkumar

We introduce a novel autoencoding conditional Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) designed to create diversified portfolios. This approach leverages the inherent generative capabilities of conditional GANs to produce synthetic data that captures the underlying structure of the input. By utilizing a time-series of synthetic data, the model enables investors to construct diversified portfolios based on this generated input. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the proposed framework outperforms a baseline model relying on Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods in terms of out-of-sample performance. Additionally, the framework exhibits robustness against various market conditions, including periods of high and low volatility. Empirical results indicate that the method is particularly effective during economic downturns, such as the 2008 financial crisis. Finally, we highlight the framework's potential for broader applications in finance, such as risk management and asset allocation. This study presents the application of a Bayesian neural network (BNN) to classify blazar subtypes using data from the Fermi Large Area Telescope (LAT). The model was trained on a sample comprising 1,000 blazars, including 500 Fanaroff-Riley type I (FR I), 250 FR II, and 250 BL Lacertae (BL Lac) objects. The dataset was constructed by selecting sources with redshifts below 0.1 and a significance exceeding 9 sigma. To mitigate class imbalance, the BL Lac population was expanded to match the counts of the other two types. The network was evaluated on a test set of 100 sources, achieving an accuracy of 85% and an F1 score of 86%. The results indicate that the BNN performs comparably to other classification methods, such as support vector machines and decision trees. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that BNNs are effective for classifying astronomical sources and can be utilized to identify new blazar candidates. The trained model is accessible via a web interface at https://blazar-bnn.herokuapp.com/. This tool allows users to input source coordinates to receive classification probabilities for the three blazar types, as well as to input a source name to view its classification history. The source code is available at https://github.com/abhishekkumar1999/blazar-bnn. This paper introduces a tensor merge operation for hypergraphs that encompasses both the tensor product and the direct sum as specific instances. We demonstrate that the spectral properties of a hypergraph under this operation can be derived from those of its constituent hypergraphs. Specifically, we establish that the rank of the tensor merge of two hypergraphs is bounded above by the minimum of their individual ranks. Furthermore, we provide an exact formula for the number of eigenvalues associated with the tensor merge of two hypergraphs. These findings are supported by illustrative examples. Additionally, we explore the connection between the tensor merge of hypergraphs and the tensor merge of their corresponding adjacency tensors. Finally, we examine the merge operation on linear maps defined on hypergraph spaces and outline several related open problems. The terminology and notation employed herein are consistent with those used in our previous work. Keywords: Hypergraph, Hypergraph adjacency tensor, Tensor merge, Eigenvalues, Rank. This study investigates natural cubic splines for analyzing Alzheimer's disease clinical trials. We propose a regression model where the natural cubic spline serves as the link function for a Poisson regression, with the spline's coefficients representing the treatment effects. To address the selection of the optimal number of knots, we employ a Bayesian information criterion (BIC) that incorporates a penalty term for the complexity of the treatment effect. This penalty term is derived from the expected number of changes in the treatment effect's sign across various knot locations. Additionally, we examine a model selection procedure that integrates this knot selection method with a model averaging approach. This process is modeled using a path action functional, where the dominant routes correspond to minimizers of the action in the limit of infinite noise suppression. Our method employs a novel objective function that quantifies the distance between a trajectory and a collection of candidate paths, weighted by their respective action values. We demonstrate that as noise reduction becomes extreme, the collection of global minimizers of this objective function converges to the set of dominant transition routes. The approach is illustrated through an example involving a two-dimensional particle system. Furthermore, we present a numerical algorithm based on the method's formulation as a multi-objective optimization problem, which is subsequently applied to the same two-dimensional particle system example. Finally, the method is tested on a more complex scenario: a two-dimensional particle system subject to a time-dependent driving force. In this case, the transition set comprises two dominant paths, and our results indicate that the transition is not merely a superposition of these two paths but involves a more intricate mechanism. This finding is supported by numerical evidence showing that the transition set includes paths that deviate from the two dominant paths at specific time points. This paper establishes new $L^{\infty}$ estimates for solutions to specific classes of parabolic complex Monge-Ampère and Gaussian equations. The derived estimates rely on the initial data, the right-hand side terms, the dimension, and the parabolic distance within the domain, while deliberately excluding time derivatives. These findings extend the parabolic counterpart of the famous Cheng-Yau gradient estimate for the static complex Monge-Ampère equation on compact Kähler manifolds. Furthermore, the methodology employed is streamlined compared to the original Cheng-Yau approach. The study also incorporates several related applications. Additionally, we derive novel $L^{\infty}$ estimates for parabolic equations of second order that do not necessitate the convexity of the Hessian. Finally, we offer a concise proof of the Cheng-Lin theorem regarding the parabolic Monge-Ampère system. This proof utilizes a novel technique that circumvents the need for the maximum principle, which was previously required in the original proof. Consequently, this approach enables the extension of certain results to non-compact settings. The paper concludes with a discussion of various open problems. The primary technique utilized is a refined version of the Cheng-Lin method, which involves a specific type of weighted trace term. This technique is versatile and can be applied to other problems involving complex Monge-Ampère equations. We anticipate that this refined approach will prove valuable for addressing other challenges in the field. Our work is motivated by the recent findings of Tosatti and Weingrill concerning the parabolic Kähler-Ricci soliton flow. Additionally, we demonstrate that our results offer a streamlined proof of the parabolic version of the Chow-Teicher theorem. In this framework, a function from a superclass is represented by a lambda-term that may utilize these special operations. We demonstrate that, under appropriate conditions, our calculi possess the fundamental properties of normalization and (quasi-)strong normalization. Furthermore, we establish that these properties are preserved when adding type systems with dependent types. Finally, we illustrate the practical utility of this approach by constructing a calculus capable of representing functions that are not definable in the binary tree lambda-calculus, such as the function that counts the number of $\beta$-reductions in a normal form. This construction relies on a specific operation that modifies lambda-terms by inserting a node into their syntax tree. This study examines Itô integrals where the stochastic integrand relies on a conditional measure flow. It is demonstrated that, under specific conditions, these integrals possess path-wise definitions, thereby clarifying the relationship between Itô and Stratonovich integrals within this context. Furthermore, the covariation process associated with such Itô integrals is explicitly calculated. The findings are applied to a specific class of conditional measure flows, which includes solutions to stochastic differential equations with additive noise. Finally, an application to the renormalization of Burgers' equation is presented. The results rely on the existence of weak derivatives of the conditional measure flow with respect to the driving noise and the application of the conditional Fokker-Planck equation. Additionally, the concept of generalized conditional densities is introduced to facilitate the computation of these derivatives. The analysis is conducted using both probability theory and distribution theory. The primary objective is to derive a formula for the Itô correction term in this setting, which extends the classical Itô formula to accommodate functionals of conditional measure flows. This work serves as a sequel to a previous study by the same authors, which addressed the renormalization of Burgers' equation without utilizing conditional measure flows. In that prior study, the Itô correction term was derived via direct computation, whereas the current approach employs a more elegant method based on the aforementioned formula. Consequently, this paper also provides an alternative derivation of the renormalization result for Burgers' equation. The primary innovation of this work is the derivation of an explicit formula for the Itô correction term when dealing with functionals of conditional measure flows. This achievement is achieved by integrating the theory of measure flows with the theory of forward-backward stochastic differential equations. The methodology is applicable to a broad class of measure flows, including those arising from stochastic differential equations with multiplicative noise. The work is structured into two sections. The first section focuses on establishing the formula for the Itô correction term, while the second section applies this formula to the renormalization of Burgers' equation. This paper introduces the concepts of standard quasi-zoomability and standard pre-quasi-zoomability for groups, concepts that generalize quasi-zoomability as defined in [10]. The study examines the class of groups possessing these properties and establishes a connection to the class of groups with a pre-Z-adic topology. Furthermore, we define the standard structure spaces of groups and demonstrate that, for any group $G$, these spaces are homeomorphic to the structure spaces of the corresponding pre-Z-groups. Finally, we outline several topological characteristics of these newly defined spaces. In a subsequent paper, we will extend the notion of the standard structure space to all groups and investigate the topological properties of these spaces. Additionally, we will explore the relationship between structure spaces and the coarse geometry of groups.

This paper introduces a data-driven, risk-aware Model Predictive Control (MPC) framework designed for safe navigation in multi-robot environments. The proposed approach utilizes a Gaussian process regression model to estimate the probability density function of robot poses from a collection of historical trajectories. Leveraging this model, the system calculates the risk of collision between the current robot and others, subsequently solving a cost function optimization problem to generate a control input that minimizes this collision risk. The method's effectiveness is validated through simulations involving multiple robots navigating complex scenarios with dynamic obstacles. Results demonstrate that the proposed approach successfully reduces collision risk while ensuring efficient path planning. Furthermore, the framework exhibits robustness against noise in historical trajectory data and remains effective even when the number of available trajectories is limited. These findings indicate that the method holds significant potential for practical deployment in real-world multi-robot applications. Additionally, the paper outlines several promising avenues for future research, including extending the method to heterogeneous robot teams, enhancing computational efficiency for real-time implementation, and investigating its application in collaborative tasks such as object manipulation and transportation. By integrating historical trajectory data with risk-aware optimization, this method offers a novel and effective solution for safe navigation challenges in multi-robot systems. We report the discovery of Andromeda XXV (And XXV), a new dwarf galaxy within the Andromeda group, based on data from the Gaia Data Release 2 (Gaia DR2). This galaxy exhibits a distance of 770 ± 10 kpc and a heliocentric radial velocity of 270 ± 0.1 km/s. Its proper motions indicate an Andromeda-centric velocity of 100 ± 1 km/s, suggesting it is gravitationally bound to the Andromeda galaxy. We estimate its stellar mass to be 1.1 × 10^4 solar masses, with a stellar mass-to-light ratio of 1.1 ± 0.1. The galaxy's metallicity is determined to be [Fe/H] = -1.1 ± 0.2, and its age is 10.5 ± 0.2 Gyr. Furthermore, we derive a dark matter mass of 1.1 × 10^6 solar masses within 100 kpc, yielding a concentration of 1.1 × 10^-6 M☙/kpc^3. This concentration is significantly lower than the typical values observed in other Andromeda group dwarfs. Additionally, we find that And XXV is not a member of the Andromeda group. We propose that And XXV is a member of the Sagittarius dwarf galaxy, which is currently being tidally disrupted by the Milky Way. The low concentration of And XXV may be attributed to its recent accretion by the Milky Way. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the study of And XXV. This study introduces a two-stage genetic algorithm to generate a set of non-orthogonal sequences that minimize both correlation and auto-correlation values. The algorithm operates in two phases: the first stage employs a genetic approach to design a population of sequences with low correlation, while the second stage utilizes a genetic method to select a subset of these sequences that further reduces cross-correlation. Additionally, the algorithm is engineered to maintain sequence balance, ensuring an equal representation of all possible chip values. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques in terms of correlation properties. Furthermore, the algorithm's computational complexity is analyzed, revealing that it is highly efficient for practical implementation. In a simulated grant-free uplink scenario, the proposed method surpasses other state-of-the-art solutions by achieving superior bit error rate performance. This study examines various approximations employed in modelling moist air, assessing their thermodynamic coherence and the thermodynamic errors they introduce. The analysis evaluates several equations of state alongside multiple formulations for internal energy, enthalpy, and specific heats. Furthermore, it compares different definitions of temperature, along with their corresponding moist adiabats and moist lapse rates. The findings indicate that equations of state based on the virial expansion offer superior thermodynamic consistency compared to those derived from the van der Waals law. Additionally, the specific heat at constant pressure is identified as the thermodynamic potential most frequently approximated, yet it proves to be the least accurate. Finally, the moist adiabatic lapse rate is shown to be highly sensitive to the definition of temperature used in its derivation. These results are intended to assist researchers in selecting appropriate approximations for their specific applications. A Python-based thermodynamic error estimator, developed to facilitate this selection process, is also provided. The error calculations were performed using the TILT thermodynamic library. This study examines the characteristics of a specific mode type, known as the "Palm Tree Mode" (PTM), observed in the JET tokamak. The analysis begins by reviewing the conditions under which PTMs arise, followed by an investigation into their properties using a dataset collected during a deuterium discharge. This data was gathered via a comprehensive diagnostic setup, including the JET Electron Cyclotron Emission Radiometer (JECCER), the JET Electron Cyclotron Emission Imaging System (JECEIS), and the JET Electron Cyclotron Emission Spectrometer (JECEIS). The results indicate that PTMs are driven by a narrow, localized source of free energy situated at the plasma edge. Furthermore, the study explores the relationship between PTMs and Edge-Localized Modes (ELMs), concluding that PTMs can be interpreted as a manifestation of the same underlying physics as ELMs. Finally, the paper outlines the potential for utilizing PTMs as a diagnostic tool to investigate edge plasma behavior. This research was conducted within the framework of the EUROfusion project, which aims to advance the knowledge and capabilities of the European Fusion Programme. Specifically, it addresses the development of diagnostic techniques to support the D-T phase at the JET Advanced Tokamak (JETA) and to prepare for the operation of the next-generation European Fusion Device, the ITER. The findings are relevant to the broader fields of plasma physics and nuclear fusion. Additionally, the study examines the origins and nature of Palm Tree Modes in JET tokamaks, a topic of significant interest to the JET and EUROfusion communities. The work also touches upon plasma stability and control, as well as the study of Edge-Localized Modes (ELMs), all of which are key areas of focus for JET and EUROfusion. Finally, the potential for using PTMs as a diagnostic tool to study edge plasma behavior is discussed, a topic of particular relevance to JET and EUROfusion. The paper concludes by summarizing the findings and suggesting directions for future research. Pretraining has emerged as a highly effective strategy for addressing Continual Learning (CL), yet it often necessitates storing a separate model for each task, resulting in substantial memory overhead. This paper introduces a straightforward baseline that rivals state-of-the-art CL methods while utilizing only a single model. Our approach leverages the pretraining memory bank concept, which we term "L2-contrastive loss," to minimize the impact of task forgetting. We evaluate this method across various CL scenarios, including Incremental, Random, and Joint Learning, as well as more demanding settings like Hierarchical CL and Domain Generalization. Our findings demonstrate that this simple baseline can effectively mitigate catastrophic forgetting. The implementation is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYiYi/CL-Pretraining-Memory-Bank. Furthermore, we have established a new benchmark for CL, known as HCL, which can be accessed at https://github.com/ChenYiYi/HCL. The HCL code and dataset are also available at the same location. Finally, our results indicate that L2-contrastive loss performs robustly across different pretraining methods, including MoCo, SimCLR, and Swin-Transformer. Detecting abuse in online speech is critical for maintaining healthy digital communities, yet it remains difficult due to the diverse nature of abusive content and the scarcity of large, high-quality datasets. While recent studies have attempted to address this using single-modal data, these approaches often fail to capture the full complexity of human communication. This paper introduces a novel multi-modal deep learning framework designed to identify abuse across three distinct speech modalities: spoken language, singing, and chanting. Our results demonstrate that this comprehensive multi-modal strategy significantly surpasses previous single-modal methods. Furthermore, we developed a multi-task learning model that concurrently identifies abuse in all three modalities and extracts specific subtypes, such as hate speech and bullying. To enhance interpretability, we employed three techniques: attention mechanisms, SHAP values, and feature ablation studies. Our findings indicate that the model effectively leverages both content and form features across all modalities to detect abuse. Finally, we conducted a human-in-the-loop study to validate our results and offer recommendations for future research. The code and datasets are accessible at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/IMM-Abuse. This study examines how degree distribution heterogeneity influences the synchronization of type-I neurons connected via random synapses. We begin by deriving the mean-field equations governing the evolution of the order parameter, which characterizes synchronization, for both networks with homogeneous degrees and those featuring heterogeneous degrees. These equations are subsequently solved numerically. Our results indicate that networks with power-law degree distributions are more prone to synchronization than those with exponential degree distributions. Furthermore, we observe that the presence of hubs in networks with power-law degree distributions can induce synchronization even when the coupling strength is below the threshold required for synchronization in networks with homogeneous degrees. Finally, we demonstrate that the coexistence of multiple attractors is more likely to occur in networks with heterogeneous degrees than in those with homogeneous degrees. These findings are validated through numerical simulations of the FitzHugh-Nagumo model. Additionally, we show that these conclusions extend to networks of theta neurons, which also exhibit type-I dynamics. This research underscores the critical role of network structure in the synchronization of type-I neurons. These findings are particularly relevant for understanding the dynamics of heterogeneous neural populations, such as those found in the cerebral cortex. Moreover, they may offer insights into the mechanisms underlying the emergence of epileptic seizures. Finally, our results could contribute to a deeper understanding of the dynamics of coupled oscillators with heterogeneous frequencies. This is especially pertinent for investigating the dynamics of Josephson junctions, which are essential components in quantum computing. In this context, our findings may aid in the design of qubits and the development of quantum algorithms. To achieve this, it is crucial to understand how the heterogeneity of Josephson frequencies affects the dynamics of the system. Our results provide valuable insights into this issue. In conclusion, this work highlights the importance of network structure in the synchronization of type-I neurons and offers a foundation for further research into the dynamics of complex networks. This includes the study of other neuronal models, such as those exhibiting type-II dynamics, as well as the investigation of the effects of other factors, such as the presence of inhibitory neurons, on the dynamics of the system. This research could lead to a better understanding of the mechanisms underlying brain function and the development of new treatments for neurological disorders. In summary, this work provides a comprehensive understanding of the effects of network structure on the synchronization of type-I neurons and paves the way for future research in this area. This includes the study of other neuronal models, the effects of network structure on the dynamics of type-II neurons, and the role of network structure in the emergence of complex brain dynamics.

Automatic Program Repair (APR) has garnered significant research interest recently, with many approaches relying on heuristics to guide the repair process. However, these heuristics are often domain-specific and fail to generalize across different repositories. This paper introduces a novel method that utilizes adversarial mask generation to direct APR. By employing adversarial training, the method learns a mask generator capable of producing masks that isolate the most probable faulty code segments. We evaluated this approach on two datasets: the original and an extended version of the BugsInJava repository. The results demonstrate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art APR techniques, achieving a higher success rate across both the original and extended datasets. Furthermore, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of the adversarial training process and its impact on the generated masks. Finally, we released the extended BugsInJava dataset to support future research. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/AMG4APR. This study establishes the capacity region for a Gaussian interference channel with decode-and-forward (GIFC) relaying using an information spectrum approach. Leveraging the duality between maximizing and minimizing generalized mutual information, we derive a characterization of the capacity region based on minimizing generalized mutual information. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this achieved region corresponds precisely to the capacity region of the GIFC. To our knowledge, this represents the first such result in the field. Additionally, we examine the special case of a Gaussian interference channel with decode-and-forward (GSIFC) relaying, deriving its capacity region by minimizing a specific form of generalized mutual information. We also establish that the GSIFC capacity region can be equivalently defined through the maximization of a particular generalized mutual information. Finally, we illustrate that the derived GSIFC capacity region aligns with the findings of previous studies. These findings offer a novel perspective on the problem and may prove valuable for future research. The paper is structured as follows: Section II introduces the system model and outlines the solution methodology; Section III presents the main results; Section IV provides an illustrative example; and Section V concludes the work. The investigation of the collision geometry and space-time evolution in heavy-ion collisions is crucial for determining the equation of state (EoS) of the quark-gluon plasma. This study examines the impact of initial geometry fluctuations on the development of the EoS. We introduce a novel analysis method that examines the 3-dimensional flow structure in terms of flow coefficients, Fourier harmonics, and flow angle. This 3-dimensional flow analysis is applied to the UrQMD model, which incorporates a realistic EoS. The results demonstrate that 3-dimensional flow analysis offers a more comprehensive and detailed characterization of the initial collision geometry and the EoS. Furthermore, this analysis proves to be a valuable tool for investigating the initial geometry and the EoS of the quark-gluon plasma. The 3-dimensional flow structure is calculated for various centrality classes and energy levels, covering both RHIC and LHC collision energies. Additionally, the influence of initial geometry fluctuations on the 3-dimensional flow structure is analyzed. These findings are compared with experimental data from the ALICE collaboration. The 3-dimensional flow structure is also computed for a specific initial geometry configuration. Finally, the effects of varying model parameters on the 3-dimensional flow structure are explored. This research is intended to provide a foundation for future experimental and theoretical studies. The 3-dimensional flow analysis tool is available for use by the community. The ongoing COVID-19 pandemic has caused widespread disruption to daily life and global economies. While medical imaging serves as a vital tool for early diagnosis, the rapid expansion of related datasets raises significant privacy concerns. This paper introduces a novel framework for the early identification of COVID-19 that integrates adversarial training with differential privacy. We evaluate our model using the OpenI-COVID19 dataset, demonstrating that it maintains robust model performance while ensuring robustness against adversarial attacks and adherence to differential privacy standards. This study investigates the integration of Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) with wireless transmission systems, proposing a framework for decentralized training and inference. The objective is to enable collaborative learning among multiple GNNs without relying on a central server, thereby enhancing privacy and security. The research addresses two primary challenges: (i) the training of a multi-layer GNN for decentralized inference, and (ii) the optimization of a single-layer GNN within this decentralized environment. To solve these issues, the authors develop two distinct algorithms: a sub-optimal method for multi-layer GNNs and an optimal approach for single-layer GNNs. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the proposed algorithms achieve performance comparable to centralized methods while significantly reducing computational complexity. Furthermore, the study confirms that both algorithms outperform existing distributed learning techniques. Finally, the paper evaluates the efficacy of the proposed algorithms in decentralized wireless transmission systems. The results indicate that the proposed methods yield substantial improvements in both spectral and energy efficiency relative to current state-of-the-art solutions. Additionally, the analysis reveals that the proposed algorithms are more robust against channel fading than existing distributed learning approaches.
