Homicide rates in Brazil have historically been high, with recent data indicating a surge in violence. This study analyzes the temporal and spatial distribution of homicides in the Brazilian state of Goiás between 2002 and 2014. By applying the Scan statistic to homicide counts across 77 municipalities, we identified 147 periods characterized by significantly elevated rates. These findings were visualized using a space-time cube, which revealed that the highest homicide concentrations occurred in the northern and central regions of the state. The analysis also detected a spatial shift in these high-rate areas over time. Furthermore, the research examined the relationship between homicide rates and the state's economic cycle, finding that the surge in violence coincided with a period of robust economic growth. These results underscore the need for targeted public policies aimed at reducing violence in the most affected regions. The methodology employed is particularly valuable for guiding such interventions. Additionally, the study demonstrates the efficacy of integrating Geographic Information Systems (GIS) with advanced statistical techniques to analyze spatial-temporal crime data. The accompanying GIS dataset includes a shapefile of Goiás divided into 77 municipalities, along with supplementary files containing homicide data, population figures, and land area. The dataset also provides a file with homicide rates calculated per 100,000 inhabitants. All data are accessible via the provided link. The research was conducted using ArcGIS 10.2, ArcMap 10.2, and R version 3.2.2. The R package 'sweep' was utilized for spatial analysis, while the 'survival' package facilitated the application of the Scan statistic. Future work will explore the impact of specific socioeconomic variables on homicide rates. Accelerated Stochastic Gradient Descent (SGD) is a widely adopted optimization method for training deep neural networks. However, its convergence behavior varies depending on the underlying data, often performing poorly when data noise is high. This study investigates how noise levels impact accelerated SGD convergence and demonstrates that these effects can be mitigated by adjusting key hyperparameters. We introduce a straightforward, yet effective, technique to enhance accelerated SGD's robustness against noise by dynamically tuning hyperparameters based on the current batch. This approach requires no additional computational cost and is compatible with any loss function. We evaluate the method across various data scenarios, including different noise levels and convex versus non-convex loss functions. Experimental results indicate that our method yields substantial improvements in convergence speed and final test accuracy. Furthermore, we show that this approach can be seamlessly integrated into existing accelerated SGD implementations with minimal code modifications. The source code is publicly available at https://github.com/ashwinb/accelerated_sgd. The findings in this work have been accepted for publication in the 2021 IEEE International Conference on Data Mining (ICDM). Our implementation is also released as an open-source package, Noise-AccSGD, available at https://github.com/ashwinb/noise-accsgd. Axion-based detectors are anticipated to detect a significant flux of solar axion-like particles (ALPs), a signal expected to dominate the exposure of next-generation instruments. The BabyIAXO prototype is designed to achieve a sensitivity of $10^7$ photons/cm$^2$/s for solar axions, a threshold that will allow for the first direct observation of the solar ALP flux originating from the core. This study examines the ALP production mechanisms within the solar core and analyzes the resulting spectral and spatial distributions of solar ALPs. We demonstrate that the BabyIAXO sensitivity is sufficient to resolve the central source of solar ALPs, enabling the first direct measurement of the solar core's temperature and density. Furthermore, we show that the observed ALP flux can be used to constrain the strength of the axigluon coupling to gluons. Our findings indicate that the axigluon production rate is approximately 100 times lower than that of solar axions, a difference that will be clearly distinguishable by BabyIAXO. Additionally, we have developed a method to determine the axigluon decay length within the solar core, which can be derived from the angular distribution of ALPs. This approach allows for the measurement of the axigluon mass with a precision of about 10%. Finally, we have established a relationship between the axigluon lifetime and the mixing angle between the gluon and the coloron, a parameter that BabyIAXO can constrain to a precision of roughly 10%. These results underscore the scientific potential of BabyIAXO and highlight the importance of advancing solar axion physics. We conclude that BabyIAXO will provide the first direct measurement of the Sun's core properties, thereby significantly enhancing our understanding of solar physics. We also note that BabyIAXO will be the first experiment to directly observe ALP production within the Sun. This work was conducted within the Axion-GW initiative, a collaboration dedicated to developing axion and ALP astrophysics as a new field of study. The initiative aims to investigate the Sun, other stars, and the early universe to explore the dark sector. Axion-GW is a joint effort between the Axion-GW initiative and the International Axion Observatory (IAXO). IAXO is a global collaboration of over 100 institutions dedicated to building the world's most sensitive solar axion telescope. This paper introduces and examines a novel category of self-oscillating systems. While classical self-oscillating systems are governed by autonomous differential equations, the new systems discussed here are defined by non-autonomous differential equations featuring specific discontinuities. The study primarily addresses the global asymptotic stability of solutions within this framework. Initially, several examples are provided to demonstrate the feasibility and significance of analyzing such systems. Subsequently, the article establishes general conditions ensuring global asymptotic stability for specific oscillating systems and concludes with an outline of open research questions in this field.

Robot dexterous grasping remains a difficult task because of the vast array of object shapes, sizes, and orientations. While recent dexterous gripper systems have demonstrated promising results, the robotic community still lacks a comprehensive dataset covering a wide variety of objects. To address this gap, we introduce DexGraspNet, a simulation-based dataset featuring diverse objects and grippers. This resource includes 100,000 dexterous grasp samples across 100 objects, 10 gripper types, and 100,000 poses. We validate our findings using two methods: learning a dexterous policy via reinforcement learning and employing a geometric approach. Our results indicate that both strategies perform effectively on DexGraspNet. Furthermore, we demonstrate the dataset's utility by training a gripper adapter that enables a fixed gripper to achieve a 30% improvement in success rate on the GraspIt benchmark. The data and code are accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2000/DexGraspNet. Our repository also offers a user-friendly GUI for creating dexterous grasp samples, which can be exported in various formats, including URDF, OBJ, and JSON. This study introduces a free-breathing, motion-corrected 4D (3D plus respiration) T2-weighted turbo spin-echo (T2-TSE) sequence for body imaging. The approach employs a retrospective, data-driven method to reconstruct free-breathing 4D datasets. By utilizing a convolutional neural network (CNN) trained on a large collection of respiratory phases, the method automatically compensates for both respiratory and cardiac motions. The network was trained on 2D slices from 3D volumes, with the 2D data generated via a 3D fully convolutional U-Net architecture. The resulting 4D T2-TSE images demonstrate superior motion correction compared to existing techniques, as evidenced by higher signal-to-noise ratios, greater signal homogeneity, and reduced artifacts. These findings indicate that the proposed method holds promise for enhancing the quality of free-breathing 4D T2-TSE imaging in the abdomen and chest. Furthermore, the study confirms that the data-driven approach is robust, capable of generating high-quality 4D T2-TSE images even when applied to subjects outside the range of those used during training. Compressing deep neural networks (DNNs) is essential for enabling their deployment on resource-constrained devices. Current compression techniques typically involve training a smaller student network to replicate the behavior of a larger teacher network. However, these methods often fail to maintain the teacher's original information flow, which can result in a student model that is significantly harder to train than the teacher. This difficulty complicates the compression process and limits the achievable compression ratio. To address this, we introduce InDistill, a novel approach designed to preserve the teacher's information flow within the student. InDistill achieves this by extracting and transferring the teacher's internal information flow to guide the student's training. Our method demonstrates that transferring the teacher's internal representations is more critical than simply matching input-output mappings for effective compression. We validate the efficacy of InDistill across various compression strategies, including pruning, quantization, and distillation, showing that it consistently improves compression performance. Furthermore, we evaluate our approach on diverse model architectures, such as ResNet, MobileNet, and MobileNetV2, confirming its robustness across different model families. CountSketch is a widely used dimensionality reduction technique designed to compress high-dimensional vectors into lower dimensions while approximately maintaining their $L_2$ norm. This paper investigates the resilience of such compressed representations against adaptive inputs. We demonstrate that for a fixed number of rows, if the count of adaptive inputs grows sufficiently large, the resulting estimates fail to approximate the original vectors within the $L_2$ norm. Furthermore, we establish that this limitation is tight, as a number of rows that is linearly proportional to the total number of adaptive inputs is both necessary and sufficient to ensure that the estimates do approximate the inputs in the $L_2$ norm. Our findings are complemented by extensions applicable to sparse inputs and to norm definitions beyond the $L_2$ norm. Finally, we present experimental results indicating that the theoretical upper bound on estimates is tight. To our knowledge, this represents the first formal analysis of CountSketch's robustness against adaptive inputs. Additionally, we explore the algorithm's resilience to adversarial inputs, a topic that has received limited attention in prior research. Our results indicate that while the original CountSketch algorithm is not resilient to adaptive inputs, a modified version is. This research examines an economic framework involving intermediaries who facilitate transactions between buyers and sellers. It demonstrates that when intermediaries are permitted to retain a portion of the generated income, they will inevitably capture the surplus, leaving buyers and sellers with nothing. This outcome holds true even if buyers and sellers can form direct connections, provided these links are not publicly known. Furthermore, if the network of direct links between buyers and sellers is public, they will strategically construct a structure that allows intermediaries to appropriate the entire income. This finding underscores the necessity for buyers and sellers to collaborate in forming a joint venture to effectively compete with intermediaries. The study concludes by exploring the viability of such a partnership. Specifically, if buyers and sellers establish a joint venture, they can devise a mechanism that ensures the venture captures the income while allowing both groups to achieve their individual objectives. Additionally, the paper explores whether a similar mechanism can be designed for a scenario where buyers and sellers form separate joint ventures. Finally, the study addresses the challenge of identifying the optimal joint venture structure for a specific instance, given a target income level, and proves that this problem is NP-hard. We introduce a fully faithful embedding of lambda-S1, the simply-typed calculus of quantum manipulations, into the quantum channel category. This process manipulates the density matrices of pure states as if they were vectors, utilizing the corresponding von Neumann projections. We subsequently examine the categorical model for lambda-S1 and demonstrate that, despite the density matrices of pure states lacking closure under convex combinations, the category of manipulations for these matrices exhibits all the characteristics of a categorical model for a typed lambda calculus. We introduce DUVET, a survey designed to investigate how galactic outflows regulate star formation in starbursting disk galaxies. By utilizing the 30-meter telescope at the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), we conducted a deep, high-resolution continuum observation of the star-forming galaxy NGC 253. We successfully resolved the outflow's morphology and measured its kinematics, finding that the gas is expanding at a rate of 100 km/s. Furthermore, we determined that the outflow's mass is approximately 10% of the star formation rate (SFR) multiplied by the age of the starburst. These findings indicate that the outflow removes a substantial quantity of gas from the star-forming region, thereby significantly influencing the galaxy's star formation history. It rotates facets to ensure that each iteration either optimizes the linear program or strictly improves the objective function value. This paper focuses on linearity-constrained linear programs, demonstrating that for this specific class, the method achieves an iteration bound of $O(mn)$, where $m$ and $n$ represent the counts of constraints and variables, respectively. This result matches the bound established by the reoptimized simplex method and surpasses the $O(m^2n)$ limit set by the standard simplex method. Furthermore, the proposed bound is optimal up to a constant factor. The analysis relies on a new potential function that quantifies the distance to optimality, which is defined as the sum of the distances from all basic variables to their optimal values. This function is proven to decrease by a constant amount during every iteration. Additionally, the bound is derived by examining a sequence of linear programs generated through a specific graph construction. The paper concludes with a discussion on extending these results to general linear programs. A key contribution is a novel potential function that unifies the approaches of [10] and [11]. This function is constructed as the sum of two components: one measuring distance to feasibility and the other to optimality. The feasibility distance is defined as the $L_1$ norm of the dual infeasibility vector, while the optimality distance is defined as the $L_1$ norm of the dual objective function evaluated at the primal feasible solution. The authors conjecture that the $O(mn)$ iteration bound holds for all linear programs. We announce the confirmation of OGLE-2017-BLG-1434Lb, a super-Earth with a mass of 1.8 Earth masses orbiting a K-type star at a distance of 0.18 AU. This system was identified through a microlensing event that exhibited a brief deviation from the standard parabolic light curve, indicative of a planetary companion. To definitively confirm the planet and determine the host star's mass and luminosity, we conducted adaptive optics imaging using the Keck/NIRC2 instrument. The observed separation of 0.14 arcseconds aligns with the microlensing model, providing strong evidence for the planet's existence. Our analysis indicates that the host star has a mass of 0.62 M$_\odot$, a luminosity of 0.29 L$_\odot$, and an effective temperature of 3800 K. Consequently, the planet's equilibrium temperature is approximately 200 K, classifying it as a cold super-Earth. This discovery is significant because it demonstrates that microlensing can detect planets around low-mass stars at large distances from the Sun, a capability that has been difficult to achieve with other methods. Furthermore, OGLE-2017-BLG-1434Lb joins a growing list of planets discovered via microlensing, including OGLE-2012-BLG-0026Lb, OGLE-2016-BLG-1141Lb, and OGLE-2017-BLG-0509Lb, which share similar characteristics. These findings suggest that cold super-Earths are relatively common in the Milky Way. Additionally, the planet's proximity to the host star and its low mass suggest it may be migrating inward, a phenomenon that could be investigated through future infrared observations. This study underscores the complementary nature of microlensing and direct imaging, as the latter was essential for confirming the planetary nature of the microlensing anomaly. Our results highlight the potential for adaptive optics to detect and characterize exoplanets in microlensing events, thereby expanding the reach of both techniques. We investigate the Lindblad master equation featuring a rapidly oscillating Hamiltonian and a potentially time-dependent dissipative component. In the high-frequency limit, the effective dynamics are characterized by a time-averaged Hamiltonian, alongside a small correction term that scales with the inverse square root of the Hamiltonian's oscillation frequency. This correction arises from second-order Floquet theory applied to the non-oscillating Hamiltonian part and is derived using the Dyson series expansion of the time-ordered evolution operator. We demonstrate that this expansion converges for a broad class of smooth functions and establish the corresponding order of the correction term. Furthermore, we illustrate the expansion's utility in analyzing two specific systems: a driven two-level system with a time-dependent dissipative term and a driven three-level system. Finally, we propose several directions for future research. These include extending the expansion to regimes where the frequency is not strictly high, exploring its application in quantum control, and investigating its relevance for time-oscillating many-body systems. The latter area is particularly significant for understanding the Mott transition in the driven optical lattice model. Additionally, we outline potential extensions to non-Markovian dynamics and the derivation of effective Lindblad equations for weakly coupled quantum systems. Our findings are supported by numerical simulations. This result establishes a finiteness condition for intermediate $\beta$-shifts, thereby extending the work of Maass and Mummert. Furthermore, this finding provides the necessary conditions to apply the spectral theory of subshifts to intermediate $\beta$-shifts. Additionally, the proof yields a novel characterization of intermediate $\beta$-shifts through the lens of spectral theory. The article concludes with several open questions. Notably, it is currently unknown whether the property of having a gap in the space of invariant measures remains invariant under topological conjugacy. Consequently, it remains an open problem to determine if the converse of our main theorem holds. To address this, we examine the properties of invariant measures for specific classes of $\beta$-shifts. Our analysis reveals that the existence of a gap in the space of invariant measures for a $\beta$-shift with a gap is not merely a sufficient but also a necessary condition for the spectral theory to be applicable. This wordless note demonstrates that the count of right-angled triangles with hypotenuse $n$ within the triangular grid formed by the first $n$ rows equals the $n$th tetrahedral number, $\binom{n+2}{3}$, by presenting two distinct proofs. The first approach utilizes the property that the sum of the first $k$ odd numbers equals $k^2$. The second approach applies the property that the sum of the first $k$ triangular numbers yields the $k$th tetrahedral number, $\binom{k+2}{3}$. Both methodologies offer an elementary and engaging alternative to traditional number-theoretic proofs of these respective identities. Furthermore, we highlight that certain steps in the first proof can be extended to establish that the number of isosceles triangles with base $n$ in the corresponding grid also corresponds to the $\binom{n+2}{3}$th tetrahedral number. Finally, we explore the connection between these results and the well-known property that the sum of the first $n$ tetrahedral numbers results in the $(n+1)$th pentagonal number. As an application, we provide a combinatorial proof for the identity $\sum_{i=1}^n \binom{i+2}{3} = \binom{n+4}{4} - 1$. Additionally, we examine the relationship between our findings and a problem from the 2019 AMC 10B competition. Finally, we discuss the link between our results and the recently introduced concept of "Golomb's triangles." These connections offer a fresh perspective on Golomb's triangles and may inspire further research into this area. Our work also presents a novel application of the property that the sum of the first $n$ odd numbers equals $n^2$. Furthermore, we identified a diffuse, extended X-ray emission component located about 1.5 Mpc from the cluster center, which may represent a substructure. Legendre Memory Block (LMB) is a transformer memory module that utilizes Legendre polynomials to store and retrieve information within the transformer architecture. By replacing linear attention mechanisms with a compact, non-linear function, LMB significantly enhances performance while reducing memory usage. However, the training process for LMB is computationally intensive, often requiring days or weeks on high-performance computing systems. This paper introduces a parallelization strategy for LMB training based on the tensor parallelism framework. We demonstrate the implementation of this approach using PyTorch and the DeepSpeed library. Experimental results indicate that the proposed method accelerates training by a factor of 16 compared to the original implementation. Furthermore, we successfully trained a 137-billion-parameter LMB-based model on 128 A100 GPUs, achieving a throughput of 100 billion tokens per second. We investigate the emergence of consensus within a naming game framework involving the migration between two communities. In this model, agents from distinct communities initially possess random labels and develop languages through contact. Consensus is defined as a state where both communities converge on a single label. We demonstrate that consensus inevitably arises in this migration scenario, with the system's evolution characterized by two distinct phases: first, the rapid emergence of consistency in one community, followed by the slower emergence of consensus in the other. Furthermore, we show that the migration rate governing this consensus formation can be precisely determined by analyzing the timescales of these two evolutionary phases. Our findings indicate that the evolution toward consensus is driven by the competition between the rates of language emergence and migration. Additionally, we observe that this process is significantly influenced by the initial conditions, specifically the pre-existing languages in both communities. Finally, we demonstrate that these dynamics can be accurately captured by a simplified model featuring a single agent from each community. These results offer a quantitative framework for understanding how consensus forms in social systems through the interaction of two communities. This framework is applicable to diverse domains, including linguistic evolution, opinion formation, and the development of social norms. In the context of opinion formation, our findings suggest that the interaction between two communities with opposing views can lead to consensus on a third, intermediate opinion. This outcome is particularly likely when the migration rate is low, allowing sufficient time for the initial community to establish its own consistency before the second community influences the evolution. Our results also highlight the critical role of initial conditions, showing that the presence of an initial opinion can facilitate the formation of consensus on an intermediate opinion. These insights provide a framework for understanding how social systems can evolve toward consensus, emphasizing the importance of initial conditions and the rates of language emergence and migration. Overall, our findings provide a comprehensive understanding of the complex dynamics underlying consensus formation in social systems. However, it has been observed that PINNs often struggle to learn modes associated with high-frequency functions, a limitation attributed to spectral bias. This study demonstrates that incorporating momentum into PINNs significantly mitigates this spectral bias. Our findings indicate that these momentum-enhanced PINNs can successfully identify high-frequency modes that standard versions cannot, while also accelerating convergence. We validate these results through numerical experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets. This study examines a coupled wave system featuring mixed Dirichlet and Neumann boundary conditions, where only a subset of the Dirichlet boundaries incorporate a Kelvin-Voigt damping term. The analysis demonstrates that energy decay follows a polynomial order of $1/\log t$ under periodic obstacles, polynomial for coupled systems with Neumann conditions, and exponential when the coupled system is conservative. These findings extend our previous work, which addressed only the periodic obstacle scenario. Furthermore, the proof for polynomial decay relies on a novel approach to deriving an observability inequality. This new method is more straightforward and avoids the need for complex geometric arguments, such as the propagation estimate for the KVV damped wave equation or the deep geometric control condition. Additionally, the technique is versatile and can be applied to other coupled wave systems, such as the Euler-Bernoulli beam. Finally, the proof for exponential decay employs a frequency domain approach, which also facilitates the derivation of polynomial decay rates. Finally, numerical simulations are included to validate the theoretical results. This work represents a significant advancement over our earlier paper, as it employs a fundamentally different methodology to achieve the same objectives. The novelty of this approach stems from the author's prior research on the spectral asymptotics of non-self-adjoint operators, a field that has recently gained prominence. Consequently, this manuscript serves as a valuable introduction to the field of spectral asymptotics. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 reviews the necessary background on spectral asymptotics; Section 3 establishes the main results; and Section 4 provides the detailed proofs. Model-based reinforcement learning (RL) seeks to enhance sample efficiency by learning a compact representation of the environment to guide policy learning. However, this approach introduces a new challenge: the necessity to interpret the learned representations. This paper addresses that need by employing inductive logic programming (ILP) to derive symbolic rules from numerical features. Blind image restoration aims to recover a high-quality image from a degraded version without prior knowledge of the blur kernel. This paper introduces a novel blind deblurring technique leveraging a kernel mixture model. We hypothesize that the blur kernel is not uniform but comprises multiple sub-kernels, each representing a distinct blur type. To address the ill-posed nature of the problem, we develop a robust blind deblurring algorithm utilizing a non-negative matrix factorization (NMF) framework. This approach decomposes the blur image into a series of sub-kernels and a corresponding blur map. Additionally, we propose a regularization method to enhance the stability of the deblurring process. Experimental results demonstrate that our method effectively restores images with complex, non-uniform blurs, achieving superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques. This paper introduces and investigates the concept of a nonuniform associative Yang-Baxter equation (ary) across both commutative and noncommutative settings. A nonuniform equation is characterized by a pair of functions, f and g, mapping from a set S to the real numbers, where f(s) represents the exponent for g(s) within the equation. Canopus is a recent, high-performance, leaderless replicated state machine (RSM) designed for cloud environments. It leverages the cloud's massive scale and parallelism to ensure low-latency, high-throughput operations. However, Canopus is not fully compatible with the diverse workloads typical of general-purpose cloud systems, as it lacks mechanisms to handle node and service failures, as well as Byzantine faults. Deep object detectors are widely used across numerous applications, yet their inability to quantify prediction uncertainty hinders their deployment in safety-critical environments. To address this, we introduce BayesOD, the first Bayesian framework designed for uncertainty estimation in deep object detection. By modeling object locations and dimensions as latent variables, BayesOD approximates the posterior distribution of bounding boxes using a Bayesian neural network. This approach enables the generation of multiple plausible bounding boxes, allowing for the calculation of uncertainty metrics such as the mean squared error between the true box and the predicted mean, as well as the coefficient of variation of the predicted variances. Evaluated on the MS-COCO dataset, BayesOD surpasses state-of-the-art methods in both object localization uncertainty and class prediction uncertainty. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these uncertainty measures can effectively identify difficult samples and enhance the performance of ensemble classifiers. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/ashishkumar123/BayesOD. The source code for replicating our experiments can be found at https://github.com/ashishkumar123/BayesOD.

We examine the viewing characteristics of a rotating disk featuring multiple colored sections, commonly known as a color wheel. This setup serves to illustrate how a camera's discrete sampling method can create false color perceptions, an effect referred to as aliasing. By employing a continuous model of light based on transversal modes, we analyze the apparent colors seen by an observer on a camera. Our findings indicate that the visible color results from the superposition of the mode corresponding to the fundamental color and its higher-order harmonics. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the transversal mode framework offers a straightforward and effective means for calculating these perceived colors. Finally, we outline potential applications of this approach in color imaging and computational photography. Our research was conducted using an open-source Python package called `spinningdisk`, which we have made available to the community. This package enables users to simulate spinning disks, compute the spectral content of the light reflected from them, and generate images based on that data. We provide example code and images to highlight the package's capabilities. Additionally, we have released the package's source code, along with the code used to create the example images, on GitHub. We hope that this computational tool will assist researchers in studying color and computational photography. The package can be installed via pip using the command `pip install spinningdisk`. We propose that the planet's gap is sculpted by a pressure bump, which may facilitate the formation of a second-generation planet. Additionally, we observe a large-scale gap in the disk, hypothesizing that it results from the interaction between the binary system and the circumstellar disk. The presence of this gap, along with the planet and its associated gap, indicates that the disk is highly depleted, suggesting that planet formation has already commenced. These findings provide valuable insights into the early stages of planet formation around low-mass stars. Furthermore, the system's architecture offers a unique opportunity to study the interaction between the binary and the disk, as well as the formation of massive planets in the inner disk regions. The discovery of this massive planet around a low-mass star also supports the hypothesis that the planet formation process is universal across different stellar types. Finally, the system's characteristics may help explain the low frequency of giant planets observed around low-mass stars. The paper is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.00001. This paper examines the Most Taps problem, which involves determining the minimum number of button presses required to extinguish all lights on an $m \times n$ grid, where each press toggles a light and its orthogonal neighbors. We present a concise proof of a formula for square grids and another formula for grids with an even width, subsequently deriving additional formulas based on parity considerations. Furthermore, we provide Python code to validate our results and a calculator for computing the answer for any given dimensions. Finally, we conclude by outlining several open questions for future research. This project was developed as part of the 2021-2022 cohort of the MIT PRIMES program. This paper introduces a new vari-based segmentation model that integrates two recent image recovery techniques: nonlocal nonconvex low-rank matrix completion and nonlocal total variation denoising. The proposed approach is formulated as a multiobjective optimization problem, where the first objective function incorporates these recovery methods, and the second serves as a segmentation criterion. To address the computational challenges of solving this multiobjective optimization problem, we develop two efficient algorithms. The first is a nonconvex optimization algorithm that leverages the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM) and a majorization-minimization strategy. The second is a convex optimization algorithm that utilizes the concept of a segmentation criterion defined as a weighted sum of data fidelity and a segmentation energy term. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed model and its corresponding algorithms yield superior segmentation results compared to several existing methods. Furthermore, we provide a theoretical analysis of the proposed model, proving that its local minimizers satisfy the first-order necessary optimality conditions. Finally, we illustrate the application of this model in color image segmentation. Abstract Interpretation (AI) is a method that approximates the semantics of programs to achieve static analysis. It operates through two primary phases: the descending phase, which computes an over-approximation of program semantics, and the ascending phase, which refines this approximation to ensure it remains as precise as possible while maintaining soundness. This paper introduces a novel algorithmic framework for AI that decouples these two phases. This approach leverages the concept of widening, a technique that accelerates the descending phase by ensuring convergence within a finite number of iterations. By separating the phases, the framework allows for the execution of multiple ascending phases to achieve greater precision without compromising the convergence of the descending phase. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework by applying it to the design of a new algorithm for static analysis. This algorithm utilizes the $\textsc{FlowCov}$ abstract domain to analyze the termination behavior of C programs. Experimental results indicate that the algorithm significantly outperforms the state-of-the-art tool, $\textsc{Coverall}$, in both precision and performance. Furthermore, we show that our approach can identify termination behaviors that $\textsc{Coverall}$ misses, even when our analysis is slower. Finally, we illustrate the framework's versatility by applying it to various abstract domains, including $\textsc{Interval}$, $\textsc{Octagon}$, and $\textsc{Polyhedron}$. In all cases, the resulting algorithms outperform existing state-of-the-art techniques. Topological phonons have recently been identified in oxide perovskites, a phenomenon driven by the interaction between polar and optical phonon modes. This study demonstrates that the topological characteristics of these systems are highly sensitive to external perturbations, particularly those induced by laser excitation. By employing a multi-phonon model, we analyze how these perturbations alter the topological invariants of the system. Our findings indicate that the specific topology is determined by the relative phase between the polar and optical modes, a factor directly influenced by the excitation laser. Furthermore, we observe that these topological characteristics can be dynamically controlled through the intensity and frequency of the laser. These results offer new avenues for investigating topological states within excited materials and establish a foundation for developing laser-driven topological devices. Additionally, we have experimentally verified the existence of topological phonons in SrTiO$_3$ using inelastic x-ray scattering. By incorporating laser excitation into our measurements, we demonstrate the modulation of topological properties, thereby validating the theoretical predictions. These outcomes underscore the significant potential of oxide perovskites for advancing the fields of topological physics and photonics.

Identifying outliers within high-dimensional data is a critical task across numerous domains. This paper introduces a novel outlier detection approach utilizing metric proximity graphs, which are constructed to enable efficient nearest neighbor queries. By integrating these graphs with a new outlier definition based on the count of $\epsilon$-nearest neighbors, we develop a method that is both rapid and precise. We evaluate our approach against several state-of-the-art techniques on real-world datasets, demonstrating that it achieves up to two orders of magnitude faster performance while maintaining accuracy comparable to the methods being compared. The implementation is publicly accessible at https://github.com/robinwagner/pgod. Furthermore, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the method's accuracy and efficiency, supported by theoretical insights into its worst-case time complexity. Our results indicate that, given a fixed dataset, the algorithm can achieve linear time complexity under specific conditions. Finally, we outline potential applications in fraud detection and drug repurposing. We investigate the dynamics of an atom situated before a thin mirror by modeling it as a two-level system interacting with the electromagnetic field, where the mirror is represented by a time-dependent current. We derive an exact solution for the atom's state within a half-space, demonstrating that the atom experiences an enhanced stimulation effect from an incoming photon compared to free space. This effect is contingent upon the specific characteristics of the atom-mirror system. Furthermore, we calculate the mirror's response to a initially excited atom and determine the resulting radiation emitted into the half-space. Our findings indicate that the atom-mirror system can function as an efficient emitter, with the ability to direct radiation into either the half-space or the full space. Additionally, we observe that the atom's stimulation and its capacity to act as an efficient emitter are not mutually exclusive phenomena. Finally, we explore the implications of these results for quantum information processing involving atomic qubits. These outcomes are validated through numerical simulations. Our analysis reveals that the atom's stimulation is governed by the interference between its virtual transitions into states above and below the initial energy level, a principle applicable to any quantum emitter. Consequently, these insights are broadly relevant to quantum information processing involving quantum emitters. We also examine the impact of mirror thickness on the stimulation of a quantum emitter, showing that a thin mirror can significantly enhance stimulation. This capability may prove valuable for quantum information processing utilizing atomic qubits. Finally, we address the challenge of extracting quantum emitters from the vicinity of a thin mirror. These conclusions are supported by numerical simulations. Overall, our results indicate that the interaction between quantum emitters and thin mirrors can be harnessed to improve the performance of various quantum information processing tasks. We suggest that these findings can be extended to a broader range of quantum emitters and mirror materials. This paper introduces a novel framework for fair graph representation learning, designed to address biases inherent in graph data and algorithms. We propose the Localized Community Fairness (LCF) framework, which ensures that community detection and classification algorithms identify and learn from community structures in a fair manner. The framework comprises two components: the LCF objective, which enforces fairness constraints on community detection, and the LCF algorithm, which builds on the fair community detection method to deliver a fair graph representation learning algorithm. We demonstrate that the proposed objective is equivalent to a constrained optimization problem and develop an efficient algorithm to solve it. Furthermore, we prove that the proposed algorithm converges to a local optimal solution. Finally, we show that the LCF algorithm achieves fair community detection, classification, and representation learning, while also being computationally efficient and scalable to large graphs. Extensive experiments on both real-world and synthetic datasets confirm the effectiveness of our framework. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/Local-Fairness. This study examines kinetic models for reversible enzyme reactions, specifically $E+S\rightleftharpoons ES\rightleftharpoons E+P$ and $E+S\rightleftharpoons ES\rightleftharpoons E+S+P$. It demonstrates that the kinetic equations governing these models can be solved exactly to yield precise expressions for reaction rates. Furthermore, the approximate solutions derived via the homotopy perturbation method (HPM) and the iterative method (MIM) are evaluated and compared against these exact solutions. The analysis covers reversible Michaelis-Menten kinetics, the reversible Haldane equation, the reversible Briggs-Haldane equation, and the reversible Michaelis-Menten equation under the quasi-steady-state approximation (QSSA). Additionally, the validity of the pseudo-first-order and second-order kinetic equations under QSSA is investigated. Finally, the theoretical findings are corroborated through numerical analysis. The results indicate that both HPM and MIM produce comparable outcomes, with errors remaining below 10% for HPM and 5% for MIM. Consequently, the HPM is deemed applicable for deriving approximate solutions to the kinetic equations of reversible enzyme processes. The study concludes by outlining the limitations of the proposed models and suggesting avenues for future research. This work is anticipated to be valuable for researchers in the field of enzyme kinetics. This paper introduces a new econometric framework designed to identify and characterize rational expectation asset price bubbles. The proposed model features a latent stochastic duration process governing the bubble's existence, which is modeled as a mean-reverting process. This approach enables the simultaneous estimation of the bubble's existence and the precise moment it ceases to exist. Furthermore, the study offers a suite of diagnostic tests to detect the presence of such bubbles. We evaluate the framework's performance through Monte Carlo simulations and by applying it to historical data to examine the evolution of the S&P 500 and the Nasdaq indices. The empirical analysis reveals that both indices experienced multiple bubbles over the past four decades, with the most recent one concluding in 2019. Additionally, we demonstrate that the proposed model outperforms existing econometric methods in terms of both in-sample and out-of-sample predictive accuracy. Finally, we utilize the model to forecast the probability of bubble existence and the likelihood of the bubble ending within a specific future timeframe. These forecasts indicate that the current market environment is not free of bubble risk, and the probability of the existing bubble collapsing in the near future remains elevated. These findings underscore the necessity for investors to incorporate bubble risk into their investment strategies. The paper concludes by outlining potential avenues for future research. Notably, the model's ability to estimate the probability of bubble existence and the probability of its termination within a defined future period offers a significant advantage over other methodologies. This capability allows investors to integrate bubble risk into their decision-making processes, thereby enhancing their ability to navigate the inherent risks of financial markets. By understanding the likelihood of a bubble's existence and its potential collapse, investors can make more informed decisions regarding asset allocation, portfolio management, and risk mitigation. Ultimately, the proposed model serves as a valuable tool for investors seeking to navigate the complexities of the financial markets and protect their investments from the potential devastation of a bubble burst. In summary, the model's capacity to quantify bubble risk provides investors with a critical edge in the dynamic and often unpredictable world of finance. By leveraging this knowledge, investors can better position themselves to capitalize on the opportunities presented by bubbles while safeguarding their investments from the potential fallout of their eventual collapse. In essence, the proposed model represents a significant advancement in our understanding of financial market dynamics, offering investors a powerful means to navigate the inherent risks and rewards of the modern financial landscape. We present a path integral approach to numerically simulate the time evolution of a quantum harmonic oscillator subject to a stochastic force. This method employs the Langevin equation for the position operator, incorporating both quantum and thermal fluctuations. The path integral is evaluated using the Metropolis algorithm within a Monte Carlo framework. Our results demonstrate that the numerically computed two-time correlation function aligns with the known analytical solution for an undriven, damped oscillator. Additionally, the simulated time evolution of the position operator's expectation value matches the analytical expectation for a driven oscillator. We conclude that the driven quantum harmonic oscillator serves as an effective pedagogical example for illustrating the interplay between quantum and thermal effects. Furthermore, the method's versatility suggests it could be applied to other driven quantum systems. Finally, we propose that this approach offers a valuable tool for investigating the quantum-to-classical transition in driven systems. To facilitate broader application, we have included a Python code package in the supplementary material. This package features a user-friendly interface and includes a tutorial that guides users through the simulation of the quantum driven harmonic oscillator. We believe this resource will be beneficial for both teaching and research applications. User reviews serve as a vital source of information for potential customers, and the growing volume of online reviews has made automated sentiment analysis essential for extracting insights from this unstructured data. While recent Item Recommendation (IR) models have attempted to incorporate review information, they often overlook the nuanced sentiment within the text. This paper introduces the Sentiment-aware Interactive Fusion Network (SIFN), which leverages both the sentiment scores and review text from historical interactions to enhance IR. SIFN employs a bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (Bi-LSTM) network to capture semantic features, followed by a review embedding module that integrates these sentiments into a unified embedding space. Furthermore, the model utilizes a self-attention mechanism to identify key reviews and an interactive fusion module to combine them with user behavior data. Extensive experiments on two real-world datasets demonstrate that SIFN significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines. Additionally, case studies reveal that SIFN effectively captures user preferences through review analysis, offering valuable recommendations for customers. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2019/SIFN. The model's performance is also available on the Kaggle competition: https://www.kaggle.com/c/review-based-item-recommendation-challenge/data. Data augmentation has emerged as a vital technique for enhancing Neural Machine Translation (NMT) performance, particularly in low-resource scenarios. This study examines substituting lexical items within Arabic-English code-switched (ACS) text to create new training data. We evaluate various substitution strategies, including morphological, lemma-based, and word-level replacements, across multiple substitution lengths. Our findings indicate that word-level substitutions yield the most significant improvements, while longer sequences of substitutions offer only marginal gains. We achieved a 1.2 BLEU score increase over the base model using morphological substitutions. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this approach is resource-efficient, requiring no ACS-specific annotations or models, and can be readily applied to other code-switching domains. The code is accessible at https://github.com/abdelrahman-ahmed1234/cs-da. Finally, we release the resulting augmented dataset for community use. We demonstrate that any Roelcke precompact collection of orientation-preserving homeomorphisms acting on a compact surface must contain a non-constant constant sequence. This finding stands in contrast to the scenario involving groups of plane homeomorphisms, where a non-trivial Roelcke precompact sequence is feasible. Furthermore, we establish that for any compact surface $S$ and dimension $n \geq 2$, the group $\mathrm{Homeo}^+(S)$ equipped with the topology of uniform convergence on compacta possesses a dense subset that is Roelcke precompact. Additionally, we prove that the group $\mathrm{Homeo}^+(S)$ under the topology of uniform convergence on compacta admits a Roelcke precompact filter consisting exclusively of filters with cardinality greater than 1. These results highlight the distinct nature of precompactness in the context of surfaces compared to that of Euclidean spaces. Finally, we present several open questions and conjectures stemming from these findings. The terminology "filter" is employed here to encompass both sets and filters defined on the powerset of cardinality two. We introduce a new algorithm for solving the hexagonal board game Hex on uniformly distributed hexagonal meshes. The method employs a variant of the tets-and-nets algorithm previously developed for tetrahedral meshes. By applying a series of specialized moves, the algorithm bypasses the need for certain game configurations, thereby accelerating the solution process. The ventral temporal cortex (VTC) is hypothesized to encode visual stimuli based on their semantic categories, such as animals versus tools. However, the specific neural mechanisms driving this categorical representation remain unclear. This study investigates the role of a fundamental category: animacy (human faces, other animals, or objects). We developed a dataset comprising 10,000 images of faces, animals, and inanimate objects, which we used to train a convolutional neural network (CNN) to classify these three groups. Our findings indicate that the CNN's performance in mimicking animacy coding is highly dependent on the specific VTC region examined. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the pixel-level patterns identified by the CNN are functionally significant for animacy coding within the visual cortex. These results suggest that animacy codes are not an emergent property of higher-order categories but are instead grounded in low-level visual features. Additionally, we show that the CNN's performance can be enhanced by incorporating a more robust understanding of the visual features that drive animacy coding. Finally, we explore the implications of these findings for the broader debate regarding the nature of categorical coding in the ventral temporal cortex. This study employs the high-energy spectrometer of Insight-HXMT to investigate the evolution of the corona in the black hole X-ray binary MAXI J1535-571, utilizing quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) as a diagnostic tool. Our analysis of type-C QPOs across various spectral states reveals that the QPO frequency initially declines as the source transitions from the hadal state to the low/hard state, reaching a minimum during the low/hard state before rising again as the system moves toward the high/soft state. Furthermore, the amplitude of type-C QPOs is observed to be significantly larger in the low/hard state compared to other states. These findings suggest that the corona is most compact during the low/hard state, while the amplitudes of type-C QPOs are greatest when the corona is either highly turbulent or located far from the black hole. Additionally, we detected a correlation between the amplitudes of type-C QPOs and the photon index, indicating that the corona is more turbulent during the low/hard state. Finally, the evolution of the type-C QPO frequency aligns with the frequency evolution of type-C QPOs previously reported by other research groups. These results are consistent with the standard accretion flow model, which posits that the corona is compact during the low/hard state and that the frequency of type-C QPOs is governed by the size of the corona. Furthermore, our results support the hypothesis that type-C QPOs arise from the interaction between the accretion disc and the corona. However, the observed evolution of type-C QPO frequency contradicts the predictions of the frequency standard accretion flow model. Consequently, we propose that the frequency of type-C QPOs is determined by the size of the corona, the accretion rate, and the disc radius. Finally, we suggest that the frequency of type-C QPOs may serve as a valuable tool for measuring the mass of black holes. These conclusions are also applicable to other black hole X-ray binaries. We introduce a new end-to-end model for robust keypoint and feature matching that bypasses the traditional two-stage approach of keypoint detection followed by local matching. Instead, our model learns a single, end-to-end differentiable mapping between two images, directly generating pairwise correspondences. To achieve this, we developed LoFTR, a lightweight and efficient transformer-based architecture designed to extract local attributes from image patches and establish pairwise relationships between them. LoFTR integrates two complementary components: LoF-attention, which captures local attributes within a patch, and LoF-cross-attention, which links patches across different views. These components are combined into a unified transformer decoder that identifies and matches patches between two views. We demonstrate that LoFTR is both lightweight and effective, surpassing state-of-the-art methods in both speed and performance. Furthermore, we show that our model can be trained end-to-end without requiring a large-scale dataset, a significant advantage for real-world applications. We validate the efficacy of LoFTR across various real-world scenarios, including indoor and outdoor visual localization, visual SLAM, and visual place recognition. We introduce a novel method for detecting metal-poor stars using the broad-band photometry and low-resolution spectra from the Gaia mission. This approach relies on a supervised machine learning algorithm trained on BP/RP spectra and photometry from a curated sample of 1,000 stars with known chemical abundances. The technique achieves a 99.9% detection rate for stars with [Fe/H] < -2.0, while maintaining a false positive rate of only 0.001% for the general stellar population. Applying this method to the entire Gaia DR3 catalog yields approximately 1.5 million metal-poor stars, a figure that is 10 to 100 times higher than previous estimates. We demonstrate that these candidates are predominantly located in the Galactic halo and that their distribution aligns with the known spatial distribution of halo stars. Furthermore, we show that the spatial clustering of these candidates can be used to identify and correct for systematic errors in the Gaia DR3 data. Finally, we confirm that the [Fe/H] distribution of our candidates matches the distribution of stars with known abundances, indicating that the method successfully recovers the true population of metal-poor stars. This study marks the first time that the vast population of metal-poor stars in the Milky Way's halo has been identified. The identified candidates will enable astronomers to investigate the formation and evolution of the Galaxy, as well as the early history of the Universe. It compiles a dataset of 1,000,000 records from 1970 to 2019, covering 11 countries: Argentina, Australia, Brazil, Canada, Chile, China, Greece, Italy, Russia, Spain, and the USA. The data includes 15 fields, such as the count of affected individuals, the number of blazes, and the total area burned. The research addresses two primary objectives: first, analyzing the statistical properties of these variables to understand their distribution and correlations; and second, developing forecasting models for the total affected area and population. To achieve this, the study employs various statistical and machine learning techniques, including time series analysis, regression models, and time-decay methods. The findings offer valuable insights for stakeholders, including government agencies, insurance firms, and the general public. This study investigates the reliability of various metrics designed to assess morphological complexity. We gathered ten corpus-based measures from the literature and computed them across a dataset comprising 25 languages spanning diverse typologies. Our findings indicate that these measures are not entirely redundant, as they yield different rankings for the languages. Furthermore, we examined the inter-correlations among the measures and their relationship to established typological characteristics. Finally, we propose a new composite index that integrates all ten measures to provide a more robust evaluation of morphological complexity. This index demonstrates strong alignment with known typological features and successfully predicts the outcomes of language learning experiments. We conclude that this novel index serves as a valuable instrument for both describing and predicting language properties. The data utilized in this research is available at https://osf.io/57692/. We investigate gravitational lensing within galaxy clusters, focusing on the substructure signal generated by dark matter halos. Our analysis reveals that the observed signal aligns well with the standard cold dark matter ($\Lambda$CDM) model, which predicts a substructure-to-main-halo mass ratio of $f_{\rm sub} \sim 0.003$. However, self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) models, which typically suppress subhalo abundance, predict a significantly weaker signal. To reconcile SIDM predictions with the observed lensing data, we propose a scenario where the subhalo mass distribution follows a power law, $dN/dM \propto M^{-1.5}$, extending down to a minimum mass of $M_{\rm min} \sim 10^6 M_\odot$. This specific configuration allows SIDM to remain consistent with lensing observations while still addressing small-scale issues in $\Lambda$CDM, such as the core-cusp and missing satellite problems. Furthermore, we examine the implications of this scenario for the dark matter density profile in the central regions of galaxies. We find that SIDM models can successfully reproduce the observed flat rotation curves of dwarf galaxies, a feature that $\Lambda$CDM struggles to explain. Consequently, we argue that SIDM offers a more comprehensive framework for understanding both small-scale galaxy dynamics and cluster lensing phenomena. Finally, we outline the observational requirements necessary to test this hypothesis. Our findings suggest that future observations of dwarf galaxies and subhalos in galaxy clusters will be crucial for determining whether dark matter interacts significantly with itself. Specifically, we recommend that the Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope prioritize the study of subhalos in galaxy clusters to achieve this goal. Additionally, we note that the proposed Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope mission could enable the first direct detection of these subhalos. We conclude that the upcoming Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope will play a pivotal role in testing the hypothesis of self-interacting dark matter. We introduce a model simplification technique that operates under data privacy constraints by allowing the release of only a subset of data features. This approach is grounded in the assumption that the data originates from a probabilistic finite-state automaton (PFA). We demonstrate that the resulting simplified PFA can be derived in a decentralized fashion, with each participant utilizing exclusively their local data features. Furthermore, we establish that this method maintains the original data's statistical properties, specifically regarding likelihood and conditional likelihood, up to a controllable error margin. Finally, we validate the method's effectiveness through experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/robinwagner12/model-simplification.

This study introduces a real-time incident detection framework utilizing geotagged social media data. The approach comprises two core components: a location clustering algorithm that integrates geographic coordinates with social media posts, and an incident detection algorithm that identifies traffic jams by analyzing the temporal distribution of these clustered locations. This study employs evolutionary search to identify cobalt-abundant compounds within the Y-Co-B system. The resulting top 10 candidates, which contain 30% to 60% cobalt by atom fraction, are predominantly yttrium-based Laves phases. These compounds exhibit high kinetic stability, with formation energies ranging from -0.10 to -0.20 eV/atom and minimum diffusion barriers exceeding 0.20 eV/atom. Additionally, they demonstrate favorable magnetic properties, including magnetic moments between 4.0 and 6.0 $\mu_{\rm B}$/atom and Curie temperatures above 1000 K. Notably, the most promising candidate, Y$_2$Co$_3$, contains 60% cobalt and possesses a formation energy of -0.16 eV/atom, making it a viable alternative to the widely used NdFeB magnets. This work underscores the potential of evolutionary search as a powerful tool for discovering new materials with targeted compositions and properties. The identified Y-Co-B compounds are expected to be synthesized in future experiments. The source code for this study is accessible at https://github.com/evolveMaterials/YCoB. Wigner negativity is a well-known indicator of quantumness that enables quantum advantage in various tasks. This study examines its role in guiding quantum particles. We demonstrate that Wigner negativity is essential for achieving a quantum speedup when solving the black-box problem of estimating a function's integral. Furthermore, we show that a classical Monte Carlo method utilizing a Wigner-positive distribution can accurately estimate the integral of any target distribution, including those with quantum (Wigner-negative) characteristics. These findings suggest that, regarding the specific task of integral estimation, quantum negativity does not provide an advantage. Additionally, we explore the implications of these results for the field of quantum guidance. Finally, we outline potential avenues for extending these findings to broader contexts. Our work underscores the significance of carefully defining objectives when investigating quantum advantage. Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) serves as a secure method for two parties to generate a shared secret key, leveraging the principles of quantum mechanics. This paper introduces a novel approach to limit analysis for Quantum Key Distribution systems utilizing privacy amplification. The proposed scheme employs a non-uniform random seed generated by a seeded pseudo-random number generator (SPRG). By applying limit analysis, we evaluate the security of a generic QKD system, demonstrating that a specific set of parameters can be identified to ensure a defined level of security. Furthermore, we illustrate the application of this limit analysis to the BB84 protocol. Our findings indicate that the proposed method can enhance the security of a given QKD system. Additionally, we have developed a Python-based software tool capable of performing limit analysis for any arbitrary QKD system. This tool is accessible via a web interface at https://qkdtool.herokuapp.com/. The source code is available on GitHub at https://github.com/Ankit-2000/QKDTool. We believe this tool will be valuable for researchers in the field. This study examines the sampling and coalescence distributions for a broad category of pure jump Markov processes known as Feller processes. Specifically, for these processes, the $n$-point sampling distribution is defined as the probability law of the ordered vector containing $n$ distinct points selected from a single realization. The coalescence distribution describes the time at which the most recent common ancestor for a randomly chosen set of $n$ points originates. We derive formulas for both distributions across a wide class of Feller processes, which are characterized by a specific integral representation of their jump rates. Furthermore, we establish sufficient conditions guaranteeing that the coalescence time remains finite with probability one. As applications, we analyze the sampling and coalescence distributions for the classical Feller diffusion and a related two-dimensional process. Additionally, we demonstrate that the results apply to a class of processes modeling the evolution of a population's genetic structure. The proposed methods offer an alternative to the conventional approach that relies on the derivative of the $n$-point sampling distribution. Finally, we present a collection of Monte Carlo simulations to illustrate the theoretical findings. These simulations compare the performance of the proposed method against the traditional derivative-based approach. For the Feller diffusion, the classical method is shown to be invalid, whereas the new approach is effective. For the two-dimensional process, both methods yield valid results, but the proposed approach is significantly faster. For the genetic structure process, the traditional approach is invalid, while the proposed method provides accurate outcomes. In all cases, the proposed method proves to be substantially more efficient than the classical approach. The paper concludes with a discussion of potential future research directions. This work extends the findings of [10] to a wider class of Feller processes. This paper introduces a delay-enhanced variant of conventional non-coherent differential detection for continuous phase modulation (CPM), which leverages past signal energy to boost detection sensitivity. The approach retains the speed of traditional differential detection while utilizing energy from multiple previous signal intervals rather than just the immediate prior one. Analytical derivations of the equivalent differential phase transition are provided, alongside a comparison of the proposed method against conventional differential detection. Furthermore, simulation results for 4π-Mary modulation demonstrate that the proposed detector achieves a 2 dB sensitivity improvement over the conventional counterpart at a bit error rate of 10⁻⁵, while simultaneously reducing computational complexity. Additionally, the method exhibits superior performance compared to coherent detection when the roll-off factor exceeds 0.25. Reward learning (RL) has recently gained significant attention due to its capacity to automatically derive task rewards from demonstrations, thereby reducing the need for manual reward specification. However, existing approaches typically require a large volume of demonstrations to achieve effective learning. This paper introduces a novel visual-based cluster ranking method that enables the extraction of rewards from a minimal set of demonstrations. The proposed algorithm first clusters the demonstrations and then determines the optimal reward function by sequentially querying an expert to rank these clusters. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach can extract meaningful rewards from just a few demonstrations. Furthermore, when applied to robot manipulation tasks, the method successfully enables a robot to learn new skills from only two demonstrations. This paper investigates the topological characteristics of several frustrated Toric code models, with a specific focus on the topological line defects arising from open operators. We demonstrate that these lines are not always contractible and can exhibit non-trivial topology, such as possessing a winding number. Furthermore, we explore the potential for realizing such topological lines experimentally within Kagome Heisenberg antiferromagnets. Our findings indicate that these topological lines can be generated by applying a local magnetic field to a specific site, and we provide a detailed analysis of the resulting stability and detectability. Finally, we extend our framework to a broader category of topological phases, offering a comprehensive description of topological line defects in both Abelian and non-Abelian topological phases. Our results suggest that the topological nature of these lines can be more complex than previously understood, potentially featuring non-Abelian statistics. These insights offer a deeper understanding of topological line defects and propose new avenues for their experimental investigation. Our study paves the way for exploring topological lines in a wider range of physical systems, including topological superconductors and quantum Hall systems. Ultimately, our findings contribute to a more profound comprehension of topological defects and their potential applications in topological quantum computing. Algorithmic interpretability is a critical component of machine learning, yet it lacks a formal definition. This paper introduces a novel framework for measuring algorithmic interpretability, grounded in the premise that human learners can derive rules from data and that the complexity of these rules serves as a proxy for interpretability. We define a rule as a conjunction of literals, where each literal corresponds to a specific attribute value. The cognitive complexity of a rule is determined by the count of its unique attribute values. Consequently, the cognitive complexity of a rule set is the sum of the complexities of its individual rules. We introduce the Cognitive Complexity Score (CCS) as a metric for algorithmic interpretability, representing the average CCS across all test instances. We demonstrate that CCS is calculable in polynomial time and provide an algorithm to generate rule sets with a specified CCS. Furthermore, we establish a lower bound for CCS and prove that this bound is achievable. Finally, we validate the effectiveness of CCS through experiments on two real-world datasets. The results indicate that CCS effectively quantifies the interpretability of decision trees and rule sets, and that decision trees produced by our algorithm exhibit lower CCS compared to those generated by standard algorithms. These findings suggest that our algorithm is promising for enhancing decision tree interpretability. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ruixuanwang123/CCS.

Keywords: algorithmic interpretability, human learning, cognitive complexity, decision trees, rule sets.

This paper introduces a reparameterization of the standard extreme value model to facilitate the analysis of extreme events. The proposed framework interprets the classical model as a Poisson process defined by an event rate and a threshold distribution. We demonstrate that this reformulation eliminates the identifiability issue inherent in nonparametric threshold estimation within the standard approach. Furthermore, we establish that the rate event measure and the distribution function representing exceedances above a fixed threshold are both identifiable and possess sufficient regularity to support efficient Bayesian inference. A case study involving extreme sea levels in the North Sea illustrates the benefits of this new representation. Additionally, we provide a fully specified prior distribution for the parameters of this framework, which is conjugate to a noninformative prior under a flat prior on location and scale. Finally, we outline a straightforward algorithm for Bayesian threshold selection and present a simulation study that confirms the method's performance. The paper concludes with a discussion of the approach's advantages and limitations. All methods and data utilized in this study are accessible via the accompanying R package, {\tt exPois}. Quantum mechanics is a probabilistic framework that governs the evolution of quantum states and quantifies state transformations following measurements. To ensure that measurement outcomes align with the physical states of quantum systems, the consistency of state updates must be maintained. This paper introduces the Quantum Bayes' Rule, which defines the consistency condition for quantum measurement inferences. The rule is derived from the equivalence of two distinct procedures for determining the post-measurement state. Additionally, we examine the consistency of state updates in weak measurements and explore the relationship between Quantum Bayes' Rule and the diamond structure of quantum operations. Furthermore, we apply this rule to analyze the consistency of state updates in quantum feedback control. These findings establish a foundational principle for interpreting measurement results within quantum mechanics. The Lyman-alpha filter is a critical instrument for studying the early universe, yet its use in ground-based telescopes is hindered by the Lyman-alpha emission line's absorption by telluric oxygen. This paper introduces a novel filter design that enables the observation of Lyman-alpha radiation from the universe with a wavelength resolution of 0.01 A. The filter's transmission curve is engineered to be centered on the 1215.67 A wavelength, while maintaining a passband width of 0.01 A at the 50% transmission point. This design is realized through a multi-layer thin-film structure composed of magnesium fluoride and chromium. We have successfully fabricated a prototype of this filter and conducted transmission measurements using a spectrophotometer. The measured transmission curve aligns closely with our design specifications. Furthermore, we have developed a transmission curve fitting model to accurately describe the prototype's transmission profile. This model demonstrates a high degree of accuracy, with a maximum relative error of 0.001% across the entire transmission curve. Additionally, we have created a transmission curve fitting model for Lyman-alpha photometry, which is essential for analyzing the transmission curve and determining the photometric system. This model is applicable to Lyman-alpha photometry utilizing the newly fabricated filter. Our research demonstrates that the proposed filter design is feasible and can be effectively applied in astronomical observations. This paper introduces a distributed algorithm designed to address graph symmetric systems within graph filters, achieving optimality with communication costs comparable to centralized methods. The symmetric nature of these systems stems from the inherent structure of the underlying communication network. By leveraging the normal matrix property of graph filters, we formulate an optimization problem that minimizes a cost function by jointly designing the filter and its associated state. Crucially, this cost function can be decomposed into per-node components, enabling the distributed solution of the normal form optimization problem through local computations and exchanges among nodes. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the proposed algorithm successfully solves the optimization problem and converges rapidly. Furthermore, the approach is applied to distributed graph compression, yielding significant improvements in performance. Additionally, we establish that the proposed method achieves an optimal convergence rate for the distributed solution. Finally, the algorithm's efficacy is validated through simulations involving graph compression and distributed Kalman filtering. The code implementing this algorithm is accessible at https://github.com/ahmedhassan1995/GaussianGraphFilters. This paper introduces a new image indexing approach designed for video sequences, leveraging dynamic feature extraction and matching. R-trees are widely recognized for their efficiency in managing spatial objects, and we demonstrate that they are equally effective for indexing images based on features extracted from similar frames within a video sequence. We illustrate the application of DIM to a video database comprising 1,000 sports images from 100 football matches, where consecutive frames are highly similar. The method is evaluated through both quantitative and qualitative experiments, including a real-world application in football video analysis. In this framework, verification refers to the receiver's ability to detect if a different message was sent, while authentication involves the receiver accepting a message only if it is correct and rejecting any altered message.
