We present a theoretical framework for the interplay between strong spin-orbit coupling and electron-electron interactions, utilizing a three-band Hubbard model that incorporates both orbital and spin degrees of freedom. Our analysis of the self-consistent mean-field phase diagram reveals a novel phase termed the ferromagnetic spin liquid (FMSL), characterized by ferromagnetic order within the spin sector and orbital liquid order. We demonstrate that this FMSL phase emerges in regimes where spin-orbit coupling is significantly stronger than previously anticipated. Furthermore, we identify an instability toward a ferromagnetic metal state, which exists without orbital ordering and lies outside the scope of mean-field theory. These findings underscore the critical role of electron-electron interactions in enhancing spin-orbit coupling effects, a mechanism that may explain the unexpectedly high Curie temperatures observed in various ferromagnetic materials. Additionally, we discuss the potential existence of the FMSL phase in the context of recent experiments on the correlated metal Sr$_2$IrO$_4$. Finally, we explore the implications of our results for the classification of quantum phases in strongly correlated systems. This work is dedicated to the memory of A. M. Tsvelik. We introduce a new class of metastable matter fields, termed "shadows," which possess a conformal symmetry that is spontaneously broken by the matter sector. The associated Goldstone bosons are notably stable, with their decay mediated by higher-dimensional operators. We examine the phenomenology of these shadow fields, which include both fermionic and scalar variants. Shadow fermions can acquire a mass comparable to the electroweak scale through their interaction with the Standard Model Higgs boson. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the decay of shadow scalars into electroweak gauge bosons can be suppressed, resulting in decay lengths that extend to cosmological scales. Consequently, these particles may constitute a significant portion of dark matter. We also explore the cosmological implications of such long-lived particles, including their potential to generate significant gravitational wave signals. Finally, we outline the experimental constraints on these metastable states and outline future research directions. This framework offers a novel approach to dark matter, featuring a rich phenomenology that can be investigated through direct detection experiments, collider searches, and analyses of gravitational wave observatories. Additionally, we propose that the decay of shadow particles could account for the observed matter-antimatter asymmetry in the universe. This scenario is consistent with the standard cosmological model and can be tested using Big Bang Nucleosynthesis data. Moreover, we show that this mechanism can be embedded within a broader framework incorporating a strongly coupled hidden sector, where the decay of composite shadow states into electroweak gauge bosons is suppressed by the compositeness scale. This allows for the coexistence of both composite and elementary shadow states within the dark matter sector. Finally, we discuss the implications of this scenario for the dark matter self-interaction cross section. Regulatory authorities are increasingly scrutinizing the validity of clinical trials for AI medical devices, particularly when performance distribution shifts occurs between training and deployment environments. This study introduces a statistical testing framework that integrates distribution-free validity with strong power against common AI models. Our approach employs a two-stage strategy: first, a screening phase that bypasses complex modeling to rapidly identify potential distribution shifts, and second, a formal efficacy test that leverages this initial finding to maximize power. We demonstrate that this method surpasses existing techniques in both validity and power. Furthermore, we establish the asymptotic distribution of the test statistic under the null hypothesis, enabling precise power calculations for practical applications. Extensive simulations and a real-world case study confirm that our proposed method achieves superior power compared to current solutions. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2020/conformal_test. The findings presented here were initially shared in the arXiv preprint "Valid and Powerful Testing for Distribution-Free Efficacy of AI Medical Devices under Distribution Shift" (arXiv:2209.01002). This arXiv version incorporates several enhancements, including a more rigorous asymptotic analysis, the introduction of a novel testing method, and the inclusion of a case study. Additionally, the arXiv preprint has been updated to align with this version. The efficacy testing methodology described in the arXiv paper is now fully implemented in the provided code. While the code includes minor modifications to the original implementation, the core methodology remains unchanged. The paper itself has been revised to reflect these updates. Enhanced sampling of DNA conformations is a critical objective in biophysics, yet it remains a significant challenge. This study introduces Rigid Substrate Biasing (RSB), a novel force-based approach designed to improve the sampling of rare events. RSB functions by biasing the system toward a reference configuration, which can be either rigid or flexible. When applied to DNA, this method effectively increases the occurrence of rare events, such as kinking, without necessitating the selection of specific reaction coordinates. The efficacy of RSB is demonstrated through its application to both short and long DNA sequences. Furthermore, the method is utilized to generate a ensemble of DNA conformations that exhibit a distribution of curvatures comparable to that observed in in vitro experiments. These findings indicate that RSB offers a versatile and robust technique for enhancing the sampling of rare events in molecular dynamics simulations. The ANS is a universal entropy encoding method grounded in the arithmetic coding technique. It functions as a single state machine that accepts one word at a time and emits the corresponding code. This paper examines the ANS's behavior when applied to entropy encoding for various compression algorithms. The analysis covers the standard binary ans-encoder, which transforms the ANS into a base-$b$ ans-encoder, and the more recent zig-ans-encoder. The study evaluates the ans-encoder's performance across a range of base $b$ values, as well as its effectiveness in conjunction with zig-ans-encoders using different parameters. Additionally, the impact of employing a zig-ans-encoder with a non-zero parameter is assessed. The results indicate that the ans-encoder's efficiency is highly dependent on the specific encoding algorithm used. The paper concludes by outlining potential future research directions.

Pore solution, the liquid phase within cement-based materials, plays a critical role in determining their mechanical strength and durability. Its dielectric constant is a key property influencing the material's overall dielectric response, which can be analyzed using techniques like broadband dielectric spectroscopy. However, the dielectric constant of the pore solution is not static; it varies with the chemical composition of the cement and the specific pore size. This study investigates these dependencies by examining how the dielectric constant of the pore solution responds to changes in alkali metal cation concentration and pore radius. The findings indicate that the dielectric constant of the pore solution is highly sensitive to the type of alkali metal cation present. Furthermore, the results align with the concept of hydration, where the dielectric constant of the water film surrounding the pore solution increases as the pore radius decreases. These insights are derived from a model that incorporates the dielectric constants of both the pore solution and the hydration layer, alongside the specific surface area of the cementitious material. This model successfully explains the observed trends in dielectric constant across varying alkali metal cation concentrations and pore sizes. Ultimately, this research provides a valuable framework for interpreting dielectric measurements in cement-based materials. By utilizing these measurements, one can determine the dielectric constant of the pore solution, thereby gaining insight into the material's microstructure and its interaction with the environment. This capability is particularly significant for applications such as monitoring the aging process in concrete structures. Additionally, the study offers a method for calculating the specific surface area of cement-based materials, which is essential for understanding their microstructure. The proposed approach is applicable to various types of cement-based materials, including concrete, mortar, and geopolymer concrete. It is important to note that this method is most effective for materials with a well-defined microstructure, such as those with a relatively uniform pore size distribution. In contrast, materials with a highly heterogeneous pore size distribution, like some types of concrete, may present challenges for accurate specific surface area calculations using this approach. Nevertheless, the method remains a valuable tool for gaining a qualitative understanding of the material's microstructure. This paper provides a comprehensive review of recent findings on massive-heavy hadronic molecules, covering both experimental and theoretical perspectives. It begins by outlining the fundamental properties of heavy hadronic molecules, followed by an overview of experimental results on charmonium-like states, bottomonium-like states, and open-charm states. The discussion then shifts to theoretical advancements, including the heavy hadronic molecular framework, the heavy quark spin symmetry analysis of bottom-charmonium-like states, and the heavy diquark effective theory for heavy-open charm states. Finally, the paper examines the implications of these findings for future research. Given that the systematic study of heavy hadronic molecules is still in its early stages, this work aims to offer a broad perspective on the field and to inspire further investigation. Additionally, it seeks to clarify the current status of the field and to propose new directions for upcoming research. This review is intended to serve as a reference for scholars entering the area of heavy hadronic molecules. We introduce a novel method for cosmological parameter estimation that utilizes three-point correlation functions of the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest. By employing the emulator of the BAHAMAS suite of hydrodynamical simulations, we demonstrate that the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest's sensitivity to the Hubble parameter ($H_0$) and the matter density parameter ($\Omega_m$) surpasses that of the matter power spectrum. Consequently, we propose that three-point correlation functions of the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest serve as a potent probe for these parameters. Our analysis of the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest within the redshift range $2 < z < 3$ indicates a $3\sigma$ tension with Planck results regarding the Hubble parameter, a discrepancy that persists even when accounting for the impact of the neutrino mass density. Furthermore, we observe a $2\sigma$ tension concerning the matter density. These findings suggest that the observed tension between the Hubble parameter derived from the early universe and that inferred from the late universe may be more significant than previously thought. We conclude that the three-point correlation function of the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest holds promise for resolving this tension. Additionally, we demonstrate that the BAO scale can be accurately recovered from the three-point correlation function of the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest, thereby establishing a new avenue for measuring the baryon acoustic oscillation scale. Finally, we show that the three-point correlation function of the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest is sensitive to the dark energy equation of state, a property that could be leveraged to constrain the dark energy equation of state using future data. This study represents the initial step toward developing a new technique for cosmological parameter estimation based on the three-point correlation function of the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest. Future investigations will focus on extending this approach to real data. Our findings suggest that the three-point correlation function of the Lyman-$\alpha$ forest will become a valuable tool for cosmological parameter estimation. We anticipate that this method will enable the measurement of the Hubble parameter with a precision of approximately 1% and the matter density with a precision of roughly 2%. These results will significantly contribute to the ongoing debate regarding the Hubble tension. Our findings will be highly relevant to the upcoming DESI and Euclid surveys, which are expected to provide a substantial number of Lyman-$\alpha$ forest data points. The reevaluation process iteratively refines future trajectories by analyzing historical data and the intended directions of surrounding agents. The CSSVAE model generates diverse, socially-aware predictions by incorporating the attention maps of neighboring agents. This study examines the information-theoretic complexity of learning within undirected Boltzmann machines. We demonstrate that mutual information between training samples and model parameters serves as a robust proxy for expected test error, a finding that aligns with recent theoretical work on mutual information in related machine learning contexts. Furthermore, we establish that information bottleneck mutual information provides a lower bound for this parameter, a result that holds a theoretical significance comparable to its practical utility. Finally, we validate these theoretical insights through numerical experiments. Our results indicate that mutual information effectively predicts test error across various scenarios, including different sample sizes, feature counts, and noise levels. Additionally, we observe that the lower bound predicted by information bottleneck mutual information remains tight in most instances. These findings offer valuable guidance for selecting appropriate models and hyperparameters when applying Boltzmann machines to real-world datasets. This paper introduces a novel, intuitive interaction framework designed for human control of a decentralized swarm of mobile robots. Unlike traditional master-slave architectures, this approach leverages sequential hand gestures to establish a high-bandwidth communication channel between a human operator and the robot collective. The system relies on a deep learning algorithm capable of recognizing these gestures in real-time, even amidst occlusions and varying lighting conditions. We demonstrate the system's effectiveness through a proof-of-concept deployment featuring a physical swarm of 12 robots, which successfully translates recognized gestures into specific movement commands. Furthermore, we present the initial findings of a user study aimed at evaluating the overall performance and usability of this proposed interaction method. Our results indicate that the system is intuitive and easy to use, achieving a recognition accuracy of 96.6% and a user success rate of 94.2%. These findings suggest that the framework holds significant potential for real-world applications, including search and rescue operations, and may inspire new directions for human-robot interaction research. Counterdiabatic driving (CDD) is a technique designed to accelerate quantum evolution along the shortest path between two states. This study investigates the application of CDD to the one-dimensional Hubbard model, aiming to prepare the ground state starting from a completely mixed initial state. We derive an analytical expression for the Lagrangian density and a corresponding counterdiabatic drive that ensures rapid convergence to the ground state. Numerical simulations demonstrate that the proposed drive successfully generates the ground state from a completely mixed initial condition. Furthermore, we examine the impact of experimental noise on this process and find that the drive remains robust against such disturbances. These findings suggest that the method could be effectively applied to other quantum systems. Additionally, we outline a potential implementation using trapped ions. Ultimately, this work establishes a foundation for developing efficient protocols to generate ground states from highly excited initial conditions. This paper introduces a novel, high-speed color constancy algorithm designed for tone mapping. It is the first method to demonstrate that human perception of local luminance can be modeled using the ratio of red and green channel intensities. By applying this model to images, we achieve tone mapping that preserves local luminance while enhancing contrast. The proposed approach is both computationally efficient and effective, yielding visually superior results compared to other fast algorithms. Furthermore, we have developed a GPU-accelerated implementation, enabling real-time processing of 4K video at 60 frames per second on a single GPU. This paper introduces a novel approach to extending Taylor expansions to complex numbers. While the traditional Taylor series for $e^x$ converges for all $x \in \mathbb{C}$, the new "exponential Taylor expansion" (ETE) is defined as $\sum_{n=0}^\infty \frac{x^n}{n!} \left( \prod_{k=1}^n \left( 1 + \frac{1}{k} i \right) \right)$, where $i$ denotes the imaginary unit. The study demonstrates that the series (ETE) converges for every $x \in \mathbb{C}$ and provides an efficient approximation for any given value. Furthermore, it is proven that the first $n+1$ terms of (ETE) yield a highly accurate approximation for $e^x$ when $x$ is a real number within the interval $[-n, n]$. Additionally, the first $n+1$ terms of (ETE) evaluated at $x = ni$ produce a very precise approximation for $ie^n$. The paper also examines the second-order approximation of (ETE) and its application in deriving a new formula for calculating $\pi$. Finally, the authors propose a conjecture regarding the second approximation of (ETE) and its potential to generate a new formula for $\pi$. This work was conducted by high school students. Keywords: exponential, Taylor expansion, complex numbers, approximation, conjecture, $\pi$. MSC 2010: 11B83, 11Y55, 26C06, 26C10, 41A60. Classification: Primary 26C10, Secondary 41A60.

This finding extends a result by Schoen-Yau, which was limited to minimal immersions into the sphere. Additionally, we establish that any harmonic map from a closed Riemann surface to a compact non-positively curved manifold is also a topological covering map. Our approach leverages the theory of harmonic branched coverings developed by Eells and Wood. The second part of the paper examines harmonic maps targeting specific classes of manifolds, including the product of spheres, the product of complex projective spaces, and the product of spheres equipped with specific metrics. In these scenarios, we prove the existence of harmonic maps that are topological covering maps, provided the genus is sufficiently large. Furthermore, we outline a method to construct harmonic maps with arbitrary degrees for closed Riemann surfaces into products of spheres and complex projective spaces. Finally, we outline an approach to the uniformization problem for CAT($m$) spheres, which relies on the existence of harmonic maps with high degrees. This solution is particularly effective for spheres endowed with metrics close to the round metric. The techniques employed herein are applicable to various other geometric contexts. For instance, we outline a strategy for the uniformization of non-positively curved manifolds, with specific applications to tori and infranilmanifolds. We introduce a computational framework designed to simulate photon-photon interactions within intense laser-platan environments. This approach employs a hybrid Monte Carlo method, where photon propagation is modeled using Monte Carlo techniques and their coupling with the plasma is handled through a kinetic equation. The framework is validated by replicating established results from the literature. Additionally, it is utilized to investigate photon-photon scattering during the propagation of a 100 GeV photon beam through a plasma generated by an ultra-intense laser. Our findings indicate that the primary interaction mechanism is Compton scattering, which significantly degrades the beam's spectral quality. Furthermore, we observe that photon-photon scattering can occur when the beam interacts with plasma density fluctuations caused by the ponderomotive force. These outcomes suggest that photon-photon scattering represents a critical process in laser-plasma physics, particularly for the development of high-energy photon sources. Consequently, our framework is poised to serve as a vital tool for the design and analysis of such systems. Additionally, we demonstrate that the simplified model employed in the ATLAS and CMS Higgs mixing studies adheres to these constraints. Although conversion strategies exist for isolated data, translating data sets poses significant challenges due to complex correspondences between relational and RDF models. This paper introduces a novel algorithm for converting relational data into RDF that includes both shape expressions and instance data. The method generates an equivalent RDF instance along with an equivalent (or compatible) schema, ensuring that valid data is preserved during the transition from relational to RDF format. A preliminary implementation of this approach is also presented. The proposed method is applicable to specific cases, such as converting a relational schema into an RDF class schema, or to general scenarios where a mapping between relational and RDF schemas is provided. Furthermore, the algorithm supports the transfer of data constraints, such as referential integrity, from relational to RDF contexts. Finally, the paper explores extensions of the method to address additional challenges, including handling data loss and managing data that lacks a valid target representation. The algorithm's complexity is analyzed, and various strategies for determining equivalence between validated data sets are examined. Finally, the method is illustrated through several examples. The paper concludes with a discussion of open issues and potential future research directions. This work extends the authors' prior publication, which introduced a similar algorithm for translating single relational tables into RDF. That earlier version did not account for foreign keys, lacked a complexity analysis, and offered no discussion on equivalence between validated data sets. We conducted a spectroscopic analysis of 12 Be-type stars located in the 30 Doradus region, utilizing spectra obtained from the ESO Very Large Telescope. Our primary objective was to determine the effective temperatures of these stars and to investigate the relationship between their rotational velocities and temperature excesses. Our findings indicate that the temperature excesses of the Be stars in 30 Doradus are comparable to those observed in the Large Magellanic Cloud and the Small Magellanic Cloud. Additionally, we identified a correlation between temperature excess and rotational velocity, which aligns with results from Be stars in the LMC and SMC. However, the slope of this relationship for the 30 Doradus stars is steeper than that found in the LMC and SMC. This discrepancy may be attributed to the fact that the stars in 30 Doradus are more evolved than their counterparts in the other Magellanic Clouds. Furthermore, we observed that the most rapidly rotating Be stars in 30 Doradus exhibit the highest temperature excesses. Finally, we compared our derived temperature excesses with those predicted by the theoretical model of Be stars developed by Maeder and Huber. This comparison reveals that the model's predictions for temperature excess are lower than the observed values for the Be stars in 30 Doradus. The model's underestimation of temperature excess is likely due to its reliance on a single set of parameters for all Be stars, whereas in reality, these parameters vary depending on the evolutionary stage of the stars. Additionally, the model fails to account for the observed correlation between temperature excess and rotational velocity. Consequently, the theoretical model requires further refinement to accurately represent the properties of Be stars. This study is the first to provide a comprehensive analysis of the Be-type star population in 30 Doradus. Our results suggest that the stars in 30 Doradus are more evolved than those in the LMC and SMC, and that the Be stars in 30 Doradus are more massive than those in the other Magellanic Clouds. These conclusions are based on the observed correlations between temperature excess, rotational velocity, and mass. The paper also includes a table listing the effective temperatures and rotational velocities of the Be stars in 30 Doradus. The data presented in this study can be accessed via the following link: https://www.aanda.org/articles/aa/full_html/2021/01/abstract/stell202000

Inverse text normalization (ITN) transforms spoken input, initially converted to lowercase text, into properly formatted strings. This study introduces a data augmentation technique designed to boost the performance of data-driven ITN models. Deep neural networks (DNNs) are widely used for modeling complex data, yet they often suffer from overfitting when trained on small datasets. Recent research has shown that integrating a DNN's tangent kernel with a pre-trained model kernel can enhance generalization. However, these approaches typically assume that different tangent kernels are exchangeable, meaning their order does not matter. This paper challenges that assumption by demonstrating that the ordering of tangent kernels significantly impacts performance. To address this, we introduce a novel non-exchangeable kernel combination method that outperforms current techniques. Our proposed NFT-K model is flexible, capable of accommodating various pre-trained models and architectures, and can be trained efficiently using a closed-form solution. We introduce a framework to analyze the impact of correlations on the topological classification of non-Hermitian systems. This is achieved by extending the generalized bulk-edge correspondence to correlated settings, thereby defining a correlation gap. Applying this concept to the one-dimensional Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, we demonstrate that correlations can eliminate point topology even when the system remains in the same phase as uncorrelated cases. Furthermore, we show that the presence of topological states can be identified by the existence of a correlation gap. Finally, we uncover a novel correlation-induced topology in the one-dimensional Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model, characterized by a correlation gap that persists despite the absence of topological states. These findings highlight the pivotal role of correlations in the topological classification of non-Hermitian systems. Additionally, our results offer a new perspective on the topological classification of correlated systems, which is essential for advancing the field of topological quantum chemistry. We introduce a neutrino mass model grounded in the $A_4$ discrete flavor symmetry combined with the gauged $U(1)_{B-L}$ symmetry. The model incorporates two right-handed Majorana neutrinos, which remain massless at the tree level due to the unbroken $U(1)_{B-L}$ symmetry. These massless neutrinos acquire a small mass through a mechanism involving two additional sterile neutrinos that function as dark matter candidates. Furthermore, the framework successfully accounts for the observed quark mass ratios and mixing angles. This study examines the impact of a quantum gravitational effect, represented by a minimal length, on the collective motion of triaxial nuclei. Utilizing the algebraic approach, we derived the minimal length Hamiltonian for the generalized dynamical symmetry (GLD) scheme GL(3,1)⊗GL(1,1) and calculated its eigenvalues and eigenstates. Our findings indicate that the quantum gravitational effect significantly alters the energy spectrum of the collective motion, with the magnitude of these changes scaling linearly with Planck's constant. Furthermore, we observed that this effect is more pronounced in nuclei exhibiting soft collective motion. These results suggest that the influence of the minimal length on nuclear collective motion could be detectable through experimental measurements. Additionally, we propose that the deformation parameters of such nuclei are closely linked to the magnitude of this quantum gravitational effect. Finally, we recommend that future research should explore the relationship between deformation and the minimal length effect using both algebraic and geometric frameworks. This work represents the inaugural application of the minimal length concept to nuclear collective motion. The associated data are accessible at https://github.com/abdullahkaya1992/MinimalLength. Polyphase Golay complementary arrays (PGCA) are recently introduced two-dimensional structures that extend the concept of polyphase Golay complementary sequences to the array domain. These structures exhibit an array processing auto-correlation response that remains identically zero across all lags, making them highly valuable for array signal processing applications. This paper introduces a novel class of PGCA derived from Golay complementary arrays (GCA) and sequences. We present two specific construction methods: the first yields PGCA with a sidelobe suppression ratio (SSR) of 1, while the second achieves an SSR of 3, surpassing the performance of the first class. Additionally, we propose a generalization of these constructed PGCA that maintains the zero sidelobe suppression ratio. Finally, we demonstrate the application of these structures in array processing, specifically within array processing gain (APG) optimization. The performance of the proposed PGCA is validated through numerical examples. To the best of our knowledge, this work represents the first effort to construct PGCA with an SSR of 1 or 3 using GCA and GCA sets, or to apply these structures to optimize array processing gain. Furthermore, the proposed designs offer a straightforward approach to constructing PGCA with an SSR of 1, achieving high array processing gain, and supporting flexible array configurations. Detecting changes in remote sensing imagery is a critical yet difficult task, particularly when dealing with data from different sensors or across varying times. This paper introduces an unsupervised, end-to-end deep learning approach for change detection in multispectral and hyperspectral images. The proposed method utilizes a deep convolutional neuromodulator architecture to extract features from two input images, subsequently fusing these features to identify differences. The model operates in two modes: first, as a feature extractor, and second, as a change detector. To enhance feature quality, the system employs a novel feature fusion strategy that integrates both spatial and spectral information. The proposed model was evaluated on two benchmark datasets, MSRC and Pavia University, with results demonstrating its effectiveness. Additionally, the model's performance was tested on real-world satellite imagery from the Sentinel-2 and Landsat 8 satellites. This study investigates the link between residual entropy and viscosity in molecular fluids, as well as polar and non-polar Lennard-Jones (LJ) systems. We demonstrate that entropy-entropy scaling (EES) successfully predicts relative viscosity across a broad spectrum of temperatures and densities. Furthermore, we show that entropy scaling (ES) remains effective for more complex fluids, including polar and non-polar LJ systems, as well as square-shoulder LJ and hard-sphere mixtures. Finally, we find that the most accurate scaling framework combines both entropy scaling and EES. These results indicate that the proposed scaling approach is universally applicable to molecular fluids, polar and non-polar LJ systems, and hard-sphere mixtures. Additionally, we extend this scaling to several model potentials, including the Weeks-Chandler-Andersen, Yukawa, and inverse power potentials. Our findings suggest that entropy scaling provides a universal method for predicting the relative viscosity of molecular fluids and model potentials. These insights are derived from an analysis of simulation data for polar and non-polar LJ systems, square-shoulder LJ and hard-sphere mixtures, and various model potentials. Furthermore, we examine the relationship between residual entropy and viscosity in these systems. We observe that while the ratio of residual entropy to viscosity is nearly constant for polar and non-polar LJ systems, square-shoulder LJ and hard-sphere mixtures, and some model potentials, this ratio varies significantly for others. This variability is attributed to the presence of a low-density plateau in the entropy-activity correlation. Consequently, we conclude that the entropy scaling law is not universal for all molecular fluids and model potentials. Instead, we propose that the most reliable scaling method involves incorporating both entropy scaling and EES. This approach is demonstrated to be universally applicable to molecular fluids, polar and non-polar LJ systems, square-shoulder LJ and hard-sphere mixtures, and certain model potentials. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for future research. We outline a cyclical $\Lambda CDM$ cosmology, where the universe's expansion is periodically halted by Big Crunches, followed by Big Bangs that initiate new expansion phases. These transitions occur when the scale factor reaches a maximum, $a_{max}$, at which point dark energy is assumed to exist in a metastable state capable of decaying into stable dark matter. This mechanism offers a straightforward explanation for the apparent coincidence between dark energy and dark matter densities. We demonstrate that the model's parameters can be constrained using observational data regarding the density parameters, the Hubble constant, and the age of the universe. Furthermore, we show that this framework can account for the observed distribution of galaxies in the 2dFGRS. Although the cyclical nature of the universe is not directly observable, it provides a compelling explanation for several cosmological puzzles, including the flatness problem, the horizon problem, the density parameter issue, and the problem of initial conditions. Additionally, it offers a natural resolution to the coincidence problem. Consequently, we argue that the cyclical $\Lambda CDM$ model should be considered a viable alternative to the standard Big Bang model. Finally, we discuss the potential for testing this model using future cosmological data. This study investigates the applicability of hidden-variable techniques to superdeterministic theories, specifically focusing on John Archibald Wheeler's W82 scenario and the superdeterministic Invariant-set theory proposed by Nima Karimipour and Ali Mohseni. By employing a local hidden-variable framework, we demonstrate that the quantum correlations associated with entangled singlet states can be replicated through carefully designed correlations between the hidden variables of the particle pair. Furthermore, we show that the detection loophole inherent in Wheeler's W82 scheme can be closed. Our methodology involves substituting the projection postulate with a more detailed description of the measurement process, which is essential for modeling the interaction between the quantum system and the measuring device. This approach enables us to derive the quantum probability distributions for measurement outcomes. Additionally, we examine the testability of the Invariant-set theory and suggest a specific experimental proposal to distinguish it from standard quantum mechanics. Our findings indicate that this proposed experiment can be executed using existing technology. Ultimately, we conclude that the local hidden-variable model utilized in this work is incompatible with the Invariant-set theory. We also address the issue of nonlocality, arguing that Invariant-set theory does not violate Bell's inequality due to its superdeterministic nature. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the broader field of quantum foundations. Automated keyphrase spotting involves segmenting audio streams into distinct units and ranking them to identify the top keyphrases. While this task has garnered significant research interest recently, current state-of-the-art models are too computationally intensive for deployment on IoT devices. This paper introduces a novel neural network architecture designed for efficient keyphrase spotting on resource-constrained hardware. We evaluate our model against leading approaches using the Speech Separation and Recognition 2019 (SSR19) KWS dataset. Our approach achieves a 10x reduction in model size and a 2x decrease in inference time compared to the winner of the SSR19 KWS challenge, while delivering superior performance. Additionally, we demonstrate that quantization techniques can further lower both model size and latency. The implementation is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar12345/Neural-Network-for-Keyphrase-Spotting. Finally, we have released a demo application for keyphrase spotting, which can be downloaded from the Google Play Store at https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.ashishkumar12345.keyphrasespotting. This work examines the relationship between the dimer model and massless Dirac fermions interacting with background gauge fields. We demonstrate that the dimer partition function, when perturbed by a background gauge field, precisely matches the fermion partition function under identical conditions. Furthermore, we show that the fermion partition function aligns with that of a height model representing a specific perturbation of the dimer model. Consequently, we establish a strong equivalence among these three systems. Additionally, we compute the fermion partition function on a torus and calculate the resulting current, confirming that it exhibits a fractional charge of $1/2$. Finally, we offer a comprehensive discussion of the broader implications of these findings. This research was conducted within the framework of the 2020 Les Houches summer school. Group lasso methods are widely utilized for high-dimensional regression and classification tasks, particularly when data includes both continuous and categorical variables. However, standard approaches typically require a one-hot encoding scheme for categorical variables, which can lead to an excessive number of parameters and consequently suffer from reduced predictive accuracy. This paper introduces an enhanced group lasso method specifically designed for categorical data. The proposed approach employs a novel penalty function that effectively manages the degrees of freedom in group lasso models. Furthermore, an efficient iterative algorithm is developed to solve this new optimization problem. Theoretical analysis demonstrates that the categorical group lasso achieves the optimal minimax rate of convergence for estimating parameters in high-dimensional settings. Additionally, extensive numerical experiments confirm that the categorical group lasso outperforms existing methods in terms of both prediction accuracy and computational efficiency. Finally, the application of this method to a real-world dataset is also presented. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1996/CategoricalGroupLasso. Embedded systems are increasingly prevalent in daily life, yet their growing complexity necessitates more flexible and efficient management strategies. Virtualization offers a promising solution by enabling multiple operating systems to coexist on a single hardware platform. However, current virtualization technologies are primarily designed for general-purpose computing environments, rendering them ill-suited for mixed-severity embedded real-time systems. This paper introduces T-Visor, a hypervisor tailored for such environments. It supports the concurrent execution of a hard real-time operating system (RTOS) and a soft real-time operating system (SRTOS) within the same hardware, ensuring that the hard RTOS maintains strict timing guarantees while the soft RTOS operates with looser constraints. T-Visor leverages hardware virtualization capabilities to deliver deterministic scheduling for hard real-time tasks and facilitates the sharing of soft real-time resources between the two operating systems. This study addresses the synthesis of robust controllers for continuous-time systems subject to both parametric uncertainties and disturbances. We introduce a learning-based algorithm capable of automatically generating robust regulators that ensure robust stability for a broad spectrum of plants within a defined uncertainty set, while simultaneously optimizing a specified performance metric. The proposed method relies on a model-based approach that utilizes a linear control-affine system representation of the continuous-time dynamics. By integrating a discrete-time approximation with a parameterized control policy, we formulate the regulator synthesis task as a discrete-time stochastic optimal control problem. This problem is subsequently solved using a model-based policy search technique. We demonstrate the method's effectiveness through numerical experiments on a continuous-time inverted pendulum system. The results indicate that the proposed approach can synthesize regulators that not only guarantee robust stability but also surpass the performance of the best existing robust regulator found in the literature. Furthermore, the method exhibits robustness against model mismatches between the training and execution environments. Finally, we establish that the method can achieve any desired level of robustness, provided such a regulator theoretically exists. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ashishgupta12/RobustRegulator.

We calculate the leading twist distribution amplitudes for vector and pseudoscalar mesons by utilizing their nonrelativistic wave functions, which are derived from the potential model of two nonrelativistic quarks. Our approach employs the potential derived from the Wilson loop in the large $N_c$ limit of QCD. Furthermore, the leading twist amplitudes for vector mesons and pseudoscalar mesons differ markedly. Finally, we observe that the leading twist amplitude for a pseudoscalar meson is approximately half that of a vector meson. These findings are consistent with the leading twist amplitudes of the pion and rho meson computed via QCD sum rules. Additionally, our results align with the leading twist pion amplitude derived from QCD hard scattering theory. We contend that the success of QCD sum rules and QCD hard scattering theory in describing pion properties stems from the fact that the leading twist amplitude of the pion is nearly identical to that of the $\rho$ meson. However, our calculations demonstrate that the leading twist amplitude of the pion is not universal; it varies depending on the specific hadron under consideration. We investigate the BMS phase of four-dimensional gravity, focusing on the non-linear realization of BMS symmetry and its connection to soft theorems. We demonstrate that the BMS phase of four-dimensional gravity is equivalent to the BMS geometry arising from a top-down dimensional reduction of three-dimensional gravity. This equivalence offers a new perspective on the relationship between soft theorems and BMS symmetry, as well as on the black hole information paradox. Furthermore, we examine the holographic dual of this BMS phase and explore the link between soft charges and boundary diffeomorphisms. Finally, we analyze the implications of this equivalence for the cosmological constant and the black hole information paradox. Additionally, we establish the equivalence between the asymptotic symmetry of three-dimensional gravity and BMS geometry, and we show that the asymptotic symmetry of two-dimensional Jackiw-Teitelboim gravity corresponds to the product of two BMS groups. These findings provide a fresh viewpoint on the holographic dual of the BMS phase in four-dimensional gravity. In our conclusion, we outline the future directions of this line of research. Addressing the challenges of catastrophic forgetting and spurious bias in neural networks, ensemble methods have emerged as a promising solution. However, traditional ensembles typically require storing multiple models, which is impractical for online continual learning scenarios. This paper introduces a novel structure designed to train an ensemble of neural networks within a single model, enabling the dynamic addition of new networks as novel classes are introduced. The proposed approach utilizes a shared representation space for all classes and employs a new mechanism to mitigate interference between subsequently learned networks. We validate this method across various benchmark continual learning tasks, demonstrating that it surpasses state-of-the-art ensemble techniques. Furthermore, our experiments reveal that the network addition strategy is highly effective in reducing interference, even when the order of learning is reversed. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi1997/OnlineEnsemble.

We examine the geometric properties of these metrics, including their associated complex structures, Kähler forms, and closed, parallel four-forms. Additionally, we explore the connection between the closed, parallel four-forms and the Courant bracket. The paper concludes with a classification of Ricci-flat generalized Kähler metrics according to their four-forms.

This study addresses a non-zero-sum stochastic differential game concerning shared risk between an insurer and an investor within a regime-switching environment. The insurer manages both investment and reinsurance strategies, while the investor controls the amount of capital invested. The joint dynamics of the regime-switching process and the firm's value are modeled as a non-linear Markov process. The objective is to determine the optimal value functions and Nash equilibrium strategies for both parties. By leveraging the properties of value functions, we construct a system of backward stochastic differential equations (BSDEs) linked with the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman (HJB) equations. Furthermore, utilizing the verification theorem, we derive sufficient conditions for the existence of a Nash equilibrium. Finally, we propose an iterative algorithm to approximate these equilibrium strategies and provide a numerical simulation to demonstrate the method's effectiveness. Additionally, we examine the scenario where the regime-switching process is reduced to a simple on-off model. In this simplified case, we analyze the convergence of the proposed iterative scheme and its associated error. Finally, we illustrate the application of these findings through a specific example. This paper introduces a novel control algorithm designed to enhance the stability and robustness of smooth flight trajectories for Unmanned Aerial Vehicles (UAVs). The proposed Probabilistic Dual Simplex Algorithm (PIDA) is developed to optimize a cost function that simultaneously ensures minimal control effort and high trajectory stability. By integrating a noise-robust state estimator, the Genetic Filter, PIDA demonstrates superior performance in both indoor and outdoor environments. Simulation results indicate that the UAV equipped with PIDA achieves a 20% reduction in control effort compared to a standard model predictive control (MPC) system. Furthermore, the algorithm exhibits strong resilience to wind disturbances, maintaining stable flight with only minor deviations from the desired path. Experimental data confirms that PIDA effectively tracks trajectories with an average error of 0.01 meters. Additionally, the algorithm scales efficiently to larger UAV fleets, requiring only 0.001 seconds to solve the optimization problem for each flight control cycle. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ahmedhassan2000/PIDA. We present a low-energy expansion framework for the pion-nucleon interaction that maintains gauge invariance and a model-independent description of the low-energy region. This approach offers a systematic method for deriving effective low-energy Lagrangians, which are then utilized to calculate the pion-nucleon scattering amplitude. Our analysis of low-energy parameters reveals that the effective low-energy Lagrangian is not merely a convenient mathematical tool but also encodes genuine information regarding the low-energy dynamics of the pion-nucleon system. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the low-energy parameters of this Lagrangian possess a direct relationship with the low-energy parameters of chiral perturbation theory. Finally, we provide an explicit low-energy expansion of the pion-nucleon scattering amplitude, showing that it adheres to the low-energy Lagrangian and satisfies Weinberg's low-energy theorems. These findings are expected to significantly enhance our understanding of the low-energy structure of the pion-nucleon interaction. Additionally, we explore the implications of our results for the $\pi$-nucleon $\sigma$-term and the low-energy constants of chiral perturbation theory. Our results indicate that the low-energy parameters of the low-energy Lagrangian serve as a crucial link between these two quantities. Finally, we examine the low-energy parameters of the pion-nucleon Lagrangian within the context of a specific model. This work is the first in a series of papers that will provide a comprehensive analysis of the low-energy parameters of the pion-nucleon system. Subsequent papers will offer a detailed investigation of these parameters using various methods, including dispersion relations, QCD sum rules, and lattice QCD. We anticipate that this series of studies will significantly advance our understanding of the low-energy structure of the pion-nucleon system. Ultimately, we believe that the low-energy parameters of the low-energy Lagrangian will play a pivotal role in future research on the pion-nucleon system. The Large Hadron Collider (LHC) at CERN has undergone a significant upgrade to prepare for Phase 2 operations, which are expected to commence in 2027. This upgrade includes a comprehensive renovation of the CMS detector's pixel detector, designed to enhance its performance under the increased luminosity and background conditions anticipated during Phase 2. The pixel detector was engineered to achieve a 10-fold improvement in both spatial and temporal resolution compared to its predecessor. This paper presents the results of a reconstruction software benchmark conducted on the pixel pilot blade 11, which was installed in the CMS detector during the initial phase of the upgrade. The study compares the reconstruction performance of the new software against the previous version, demonstrating that the updated algorithms successfully maintain the targeted improvements in spatial and temporal resolution. Furthermore, the new software exhibits greater robustness in handling challenging data scenarios, such as data from dead or partially functional sensors. These findings indicate that the new reconstruction software is ready for deployment on the remaining pilot blades currently under testing. Additionally, the software is being prepared for integration into the CMS data acquisition system, with a planned installation scheduled for the end of 2023. This timeline ensures the system is fully ready for the start of LHC Phase 2 operations in 2027. We introduce a new machine learning approach designed to identify host galaxy structures for active galactic nuclei (AGN) at redshifts $z<1$ using $H$-band imaging from the Hyper Suprime-Cam Wide Survey (HSC-Wide). This method is trained on a dataset of 1,000 galaxies with known morphologies, sourced from the Sloan Digital Sky Survey (SDSS) and the Hyper Suprime-Cam Subaru Strategic Program (HSC-SSP). The approach classifies galaxies into three categories: disk, elliptical, and irregular. We evaluated the model's performance on 1,000 AGN galaxies from HSC-Wide that were not included in the training set, achieving an accuracy of 80.3% and a macro-average F1 score of 79.1%. The primary source of misclassification was distinguishing between elliptical and irregular types. Furthermore, we developed a model capable of estimating the probability of each morphology for individual galaxies. This model is publicly accessible via a web interface at \url{https://hsc-morphology.herokuapp.com/}. This tool will facilitate the selection of galaxies for follow-up spectroscopic observations to measure their redshifts. Ultimately, we aim to apply this methodology to the entire HSC-Wide survey dataset to statistically investigate the morphological characteristics of $z<1$ AGN host galaxies. Nuclear short-range correlations (SRCs) are investigated through various phase-space representations, utilizing a two-body correlation operator derived from high-momentum components of the Faddeev-Yakubovsky eigenstate wave function. The study demonstrates that the operator's momentum distribution aligns with findings from (e,e'p) experiments regarding two-body momentum distributions. Additionally, the calculated three-body and four-body momentum distributions are compared against results from Gaussian and Fermi hypernetted chain (FHNC) theories. The three-body momentum distribution exhibits strong agreement with both Gaussian and FHNC predictions, whereas the four-body distribution shows only qualitative similarity to the FHNC outcome. Furthermore, the phase-space representations indicate that SRCs are predominantly localized in the high-momentum region. Finally, the influence of long-range correlations on these representations is examined. The findings suggest that while SRCs are primarily responsible for the momentum distribution of high-momentum components, long-range correlations significantly affect the three-, four-, and five-body momentum distributions within the low- and medium-momentum ranges. Consequently, low- and medium-momentum data obtained from (e,e'p) experiments can be utilized to refine theoretical models of long-range correlations. Additionally, the impact of three-body correlations on two-body momentum distributions is explored, revealing that including such correlations in SRC calculations leads to a reduction in the SRC strength. This reduction is more pronounced in the four-body case compared to the three-body scenario. These results underscore the necessity of incorporating three-body correlations when analyzing SRCs. Finally, the study highlights the critical role of three-body correlations in shaping nuclear SRCs. The calculated SRC strength is found to be approximately 10% lower than that of the free nucleon-nucleon interaction, a discrepancy that is significantly larger than the effect of three-body correlations on the high-momentum components of the Faddeev-Yakubovsky eigenstate. This suggests that three-body correlations play a crucial role in the formation of nuclear SRCs. Amplitude variations in young stars are frequently linked to the presence of large-scale starspots. While the size of these spots is expected to correlate with stellar rotation, recent studies have identified a broader relationship between stellar age and spot size. This research investigates the origin of this age-related trend by analyzing the amplitudes of 1,000 low-metallicity stars from the Kepler mission. By examining the amplitudes of 1,000 low-metallicity stars, we determine that the observed trend arises from a combination of factors: younger stars exhibit larger amplitudes due to having larger spots, whereas older stars show smaller amplitudes because their spots are smaller. Furthermore, we find that this age-amplitude relationship is more pronounced in rapidly rotating stars compared to those rotating more slowly. Finally, our findings support the hypothesis that the spot sizes of young stars evolve over time, potentially driven by the decay of a stellar dynamo. These results offer a new perspective on the nature of spot sizes in young stars and their connection to the dynamo mechanism.

Quantum machine intelligence (QMI) represents the convergence of quantum computing and machine learning, offering a promising avenue to tackle complex problems that are beyond the reach of classical computing. This paper introduces SQUID, a new QMI framework that integrates quantum computing with deep learning. This paper investigates pointwise inclined submanifolds, both with and without boundary, embedded in almost contact manifolds. We establish that no non-trivial pointwise inclined submanifolds exist when the dimension is 1 or 2. Furthermore, we demonstrate that any non-trivial almost contact manifold cannot be expressed as a non-trivial warped product of such submanifolds. Additionally, we prove that any non-trivial pointwise inclined submanifold with boundary is isometric to a specific model space. Finally, we examine the existence of these pointwise inclined submanifolds within Sasakian manifolds. As an application, we show that no non-trivial pointwise inclined submanifolds exist in Sasakian manifolds of dimension 1 or 2. We also provide examples of such submanifolds in Sasakian manifolds of dimension 3 and 4, and finally, we establish the existence of non-trivial pointwise inclined submanifolds with boundary in Sasakian manifolds of dimension 2. The paper concludes with an overview of pointwise semi-inclined submanifolds that possess a boundary. We demonstrate that the existence of non-trivial pointwise semi-inclined submanifolds with a boundary in Sasakian manifolds is contingent upon the dimension of the manifold. Specifically, such submanifolds do not exist in Sasakian manifolds of dimension 1 or 2, whereas non-trivial examples do exist in Sasakian manifolds of dimension 3 and 4. Additionally, we present examples of non-trivial pointwise semi-inclined submanifolds without a boundary in Sasakian manifolds of dimension 3 and 4. We further illustrate that these submanifolds can exist in Sasakian manifolds of any dimension greater than 2. Finally, we explore the relationship between pointwise inclined submanifolds and pointwise semi-inclined submanifolds. We establish that the product of two pointwise inclined submanifolds is pointwise inclined, while the product of two pointwise semi-inclined submanifolds is pointwise semi-inclined. We also note that the product of a pointwise inclined submanifold and a pointwise semi-inclined submanifold is pointwise semi-inclined. However, we provide an example showing that the product of two pointwise inclined submanifolds can be pointwise semi-inclined without being pointwise inclined

We introduce a novel concept for a large-scale, low-threshold, passive neutrino and dark matter detector that utilizes color centers in diamond as its target medium. This approach leverages the ability of color centers to retain trapped excitations for extended periods, enabling the detection of low-energy nuclear recoils. By utilizing existing, widely deployed technologies for both color center creation and diamond handling, we aim to achieve a detector with a total mass of several hundred kilograms at a cost of approximately one US dollar per kilogram. The proposed design, named PALEOCCENE, is intended to be deployed underground to ensure high sensitivity for both neutrino and dark matter research. Furthermore, we outline a comprehensive strategy to advance this proposal from its current developmental stage to a fully operational detector. This includes establishing a dedicated R&D program to refine the technology and implementing a phased deployment strategy, starting with a prototype of roughly 10 kg followed by a full-scale installation of approximately 200 kg. We anticipate that the initial prototype could be ready for deployment within the next decade. Additionally, we have identified potential facilities for these detectors, including the Sanford Underground Research Facility, the SNOLAB, and the proposed Deep Underground Science and Engineering Laboratory. We strongly encourage the international community to pursue this proposal, as it offers a unique and complementary avenue for investigating neutrino and dark matter physics. Our goal is to initiate the development of the prototype within the next five years. We have already secured initial funding from the US Department of Energy and the US National Science Foundation to support this endeavor. We invite interested parties to contact us to discuss this proposal further. Our website, www.paleocene.org, provides additional details. We introduce a straightforward theoretical framework for dynamic colloidal molecules, where an attractive colloid interacts with a repulsive one that responds to activity gradients. This system yields structures that defy intuition, including the stabilization of a single bond between large particles and the creation of effective negative charges through careful selection of colloidal sizes and activity profiles. Furthermore, the model accounts for the self-assembly of these molecules into larger aggregates. Finally, we demonstrate that incorporating active fluctuations can generate anomalous diffusion and facilitate the design of a tunable, activity-dependent effective potential. These findings establish a foundation for constructing complex functional systems using building blocks that react to non-equilibrium conditions. Additionally, the framework is applicable to various systems involving active interactions, such as cells within chemical gradients, nanoparticles in acoustic fields, and granular particles under vibration. Finally, we provide open-source code for the theoretical model and associated experiments. This study investigates the quantum states of fractional quantum Hall systems within a strong magnetic field using the lowest Landau level projection method. By incorporating magnetic translation symmetry, we construct trial wavefunctions for the lowest energy states. We then analyze how these states transform under magnetic translations and determine their quantum Hall conductivities. Furthermore, we examine the impact of particle number and system size on these trial states. Our findings reveal that magnetron orbits can be divided into distinct regions, with multiple magnetron branches existing within each. Additionally, we demonstrate that the spectral total rule holds for the ground state as well as excited states. Finally, we explore the relationship between the quantum Hall conductance of trial wavefunctions and the filling factor. These results offer valuable insights into the quantum states of fractional quantum Hall systems. This work was supported by the National Natural Science Foundation of China (Grant No. 11974390). This paper introduces a geometric framework for analyzing and forecasting the evolution of outbreaks on networks. The approach begins by defining a geometric representation of the network, where each node is assigned a position in a metric space. This geometric model is then utilized to propose a data-driven algorithm for forecasting outbreak dynamics. The method involves clustering nodes based on their geometric proximity and subsequently modeling the temporal evolution of these clusters. The proposed algorithm is evaluated using both synthetic and real-world datasets, demonstrating its effectiveness in predicting outbreak progression. This study examines the impact of point sources on the convergence estimator derived from the maximum likelihood (ML) method. We demonstrate that the ML approach is highly sensitive to X-shaped artifacts generated by point sources, which can introduce significant biases into the resulting estimator. To mitigate these artifacts, we propose a method that removes the most prominent point sources prior to applying the ML technique. Our results indicate that this subtraction strategy effectively eliminates the X-shaped patterns, thereby preventing substantial biases in the estimator. Furthermore, we show that the root mean square (rms) of the bias in the estimator is significantly reduced when point sources are removed before the ML analysis. Finally, we establish that the bias in the estimator scales linearly with the rms amplitude of the point sources. These findings are validated using both simulated data and observations from the Planck satellite. We conclude that accounting for point sources is essential when utilizing the ML method to generate CMB maps. Additionally, we provide a Python package named `ml_map` to facilitate the implementation of this methodology. This study addresses the challenge of ambiguity in language-driven, goal-conditioned reinforcement learning, where a policy learns from natural language goals to reach a target state. The core issue arises because words can refer to multiple instances within the environment, causing the policy to potentially target the incorrect object. To mitigate this, we introduce a reward mechanism that reduces the likelihood of selecting an incorrect reference. Employing the renormalization group approach, we determine the dependence of the many-body gap on the interlayer distance and the dielectric constant of the surrounding medium. Our findings indicate that this gap can be eliminated through moderate increases in either the separation distance or the dielectric constant. Furthermore, we observe that the renormalization group flow exhibits a fixed point, suggesting that the system approaches a fixed state at long distances. Finally, we demonstrate that the bilayer system remains stable against the formation of a many-body gap. These results offer valuable insights for the design and manipulation of bilayer graphite-based devices. Additionally, we provide an open-source Python package implementing the renormalization group method for interacting bilayer graphite. The Ramsey sequence is a fundamental technique in quantum physics, widely utilized for high-precision measurements of atomic transition frequencies and magnetic fields. However, the Ramsey sequence protocol is not inherently optimized for efficient data collection. This work introduces a sequential decision-making framework designed to determine the optimal phase accumulation phase for each experiment within a Ramsey measurement. By applying this method to measure the 1S-2S transition frequency in hydrogen, we demonstrate that it yields a 1.5-fold improvement in precision compared to a standard Ramsey sequence requiring the same number of experiments. Furthermore, this approach is applicable to other spectroscopy tasks and can be extended to broader quantum measurement scenarios. The methodology is detailed in an accompanying Python package. Additionally, we show that a similar strategy can identify the optimal operating point for a superconducting qubit's frequency-phasing relationship. This finding is significant for quantum computing, as it enables the precise calibration of two-qubit gates by optimizing operating points. The method is also available through a Python package. Finally, we illustrate that the proposed approach can be adapted to other contexts, such as the quantum phase estimation algorithm. All associated Python packages can be accessed via a provided link. We demonstrate that, under a mild additional assumption, the limit set of any orbit is guaranteed to be non-empty, compact, connected, invariant, and possesses a dimension no greater than that of the state space. Variational quantum algorithms (VQAs) represent a promising method for solving complex problems on near-term quantum hardware. However, their practical utility is often constrained by the limited number of iterations required for convergence. This study introduces a novel adaptive strategy for VQA parameter optimization driven by qubit excitation dynamics. By modeling the initial state as a collection of non-interacting qubits, we derive an analytic expression for the average excitation probability, which serves as a robust metric for solution quality. This formula enables rapid assessment of VQA performance and facilitates the identification of optimal parameter values. We demonstrate the efficacy of this approach by applying it to the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) for molecular systems, showing that it significantly enhances convergence. Furthermore, we extend this framework to optimize other VQA applications, including the ground state search algorithm and the variational quantum compiler. Our findings indicate that the proposed method is broadly applicable, offering a general-purpose tool for accelerating VQA parameter optimization. The recent detection of a stochastic gravitational-wave background (SGWB) by the NANOGrav collaboration has sparked significant interest in identifying its source. While a supermassive black hole binary (SMBHB) origin is a leading hypothesis, it requires fine-tuning to align with the observed amplitude and frequency. In this study, we explore an alternative explanation: a background of gravitational waves amplified during cosmic inflation. This scenario arises from the interaction between primordial fluctuations and a stiff equation-of-state fluid, which can be naturally produced by a spectator field in the early universe. We demonstrate that this inflationary SGWB model can account for the NANOGrav signal without requiring parameter fine-tuning. Furthermore, we show that this model can simultaneously explain the recent tension between the Hubble constant measurements derived from the early and late universe. Finally, we examine the detectability of this SGWB by current and future gravitational-wave observatories, including NANOGrav, LIGO, Virgo, and the Cosmic Explorer. Our findings indicate that next-generation detectors will be capable of testing this model with high precision. Additionally, we find that the Cosmic Explorer can distinguish between this model and the SMBHB hypothesis, whereas LISA will be able to differentiate these scenarios based on their distinct spectral shapes. Our results suggest that the NANOGrav signal will be resolved by future gravitational-wave detectors. This study underscores the critical role of future gravitational-wave observations in advancing our understanding of cosmology. We present the first interferometric observations of a cometary coma using a submillimeter molecular tracer, specifically the rotational transition of CS at 4.89 mm. These observations were conducted with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) in its Atacama Compact Array (ACA) configuration, offering a unique capability for observing cometary atmospheres. The study targets the recently discovered comet C/2015 ER61 (PanSTARRS), which was observed approximately 1.5 years after its last perihelion passage. Our analysis reveals that the CS emission is spatially resolved, with a full width at half maximum (FWHM) of 1.2 arcseconds, corresponding to a physical scale of roughly 1.5 x 10^5 km at the comet's distance. This spatial resolution allows us to constrain the production rate of CS to 1.1 +/- 0.2 x 10^27 molecules per second. We further explore the potential for a dispersed source of CS, which could be attributed to the sublimation of CS ice or the photodissociation of HCS+ ions. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive analysis of the coma's H2O and CO2 production rates, deriving values of 1.1 +/- 0.2 x 10^28 and 1.1 +/- 0.2 x 10^27 molecules per second, respectively. These results are consistent with a dispersed source of both species, likely resulting from the sublimation of H2O and CO2 ice. Our findings suggest that the PanSTARRS comet possesses a diverse volatile inventory, including CO, CO2, H2O, and CS, which may have been delivered by a parent body that experienced a catastrophic disruption. This scenario is supported by the comet's high dynamical excitation and its membership in the recently identified Atira group. Our work demonstrates the effectiveness of submillimeter observations in probing the volatile inventory of comets, a method that can be applied to other cometary objects. Furthermore, we have developed a new data reduction pipeline for cometary observations, which is publicly available. This pipeline is designed to be easily adaptable for observations of other molecules and comets. The data presented in this study are accessible via the ALMA archive (project code 2019.1.00001.S). This study examines Tsallis holographic dark energy by incorporating it as an essence model, utilizing the generalized form of the uncertainty principle. Multi-Objective Mixed-Integer Non-Linear Programming (MO-MINLP) problems are prevalent in numerous real-world scenarios. Although these problems can be addressed using standard techniques, the resulting solutions often suffer from low quality and high computational costs. This paper introduces a novel Branch and Bound (B&B) method enhanced by the NSGA-II algorithm to efficiently identify high-quality solutions. The proposed approach addresses two primary challenges: (1) the need to solve a subproblem at each branch node, and (2) the necessity of maintaining the branch-and-bound search process. To address the first challenge, the method employs a subproblem solver that utilizes the NSGA-II algorithm to obtain a set of Pareto-optimal solutions for the subproblems. To tackle the second challenge, the algorithm maintains a set of Pareto-optimal solutions throughout the search, utilizing this set to generate initial solutions for each new subproblem. The performance of this approach is evaluated against the standard NSGA-II algorithm and the MOBOA algorithm from the literature. Numerical experiments demonstrate that the proposed method outperforms both benchmarks in terms of solution quality and computational time. Furthermore, the method is applied to a multi-objective portfolio optimization problem, yielding promising results. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ahmedgaber1998/NSGAII-BB. Aspect-based sentiment analysis (ABSA) is a critical research area within sentiment analysis, focusing on identifying the sentiment polarity of specific aspects within product reviews. However, the inherent subjectivity of human emotions makes it challenging to capture nuanced emotional expressions in reviews. To address this, we introduce a novel pre-training strategy that leverages explicit emotion expressions to facilitate the learning of implicit emotion representations. This approach utilizes a new loss function designed to pull representations of texts sharing the same explicit emotion expression closer together while pushing apart those with different expressions. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques. Additionally, we validate the effectiveness of the implicit emotion representation learning through various analyses. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi-00/SC-PABSA. Given its reliance on explicit emotion expressions, our method is particularly well-suited for applications where such expressions are readily available. Furthermore, the pre-trained model can be readily applied to other domains that utilize explicit emotion expressions. The comprehensive dataset required for our method is available at https://github.com/ChenYi-00/ABSA-ExplicitEmotion. The associated paper can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.03500. This study addresses the identification and estimation of causal effects within a binary outcome framework that incorporates a binary mediator. We demonstrate that a specific causal parameter can be identified through a linear combination of two naturally defined subpopulation causal parameters. Furthermore, we show that a weighted two-stage estimator yields an asymptotically unbiased and consistent estimate of this parameter within a general sampling framework. Our findings are applicable to designs utilizing stratified or case-control sampling, which is particularly relevant for analyzing data from nested case-control studies. We evaluate the performance of the proposed estimator using both Monte Carlo simulations and a real-world application involving a nested case-control study of HIV infection. In this application, we investigate the indirect effect of CD4 cell count on HIV status, which is determined by the treatment level of zidovudine. Additionally, we introduce a weighted estimator designed for general sampling schemes that accommodates multiple strata. Finally, we discuss the identification of continuous causal parameters within this binary outcome setting. Supplementary materials are available online. The Parker Solar Probe (PSP) mission has provided the first in-situ measurements of solar breeze energy flux within the inner heliosphere. By analyzing these new data, we have established the energy flux as a function of heliocentric distance and examined its relationship with the Parker spiral angle. Our results indicate that energy flux rises sharply as distance decreases, reaching a maximum of approximately 0.5 mW/m² at the closest PSP approach. Furthermore, we observed that energy flux increases with the Parker spiral angle, a trend that aligns with the inverse relationship between solar wind speed and this angle. These findings offer valuable insights into the energy transfer mechanisms operating in the inner heliosphere. Additionally, we compared our observations with existing theoretical models and found that the model predicting the strongest dependence of energy flux on heliocentric distance is the most consistent with the data. Finally, we propose that the observed dependence of energy flux on the Parker spiral angle can be explained by the model developed by Jian et al. (2019). These outcomes underscore the critical role of Parker Solar Probe in advancing our understanding of energy transfer processes in the inner heliosphere. The results indicate that adverse scissors resonances are more readily observed in the single rotor model, whereas the two-body rotor system exhibits a greater complexity.
