The Unruh effect predicts that a uniformly accelerated observer detects a thermal bath of particles, even when the vacuum state exists. This phenomenon is closely linked to the entanglement between the Rindler wedges defined by the observer's future and past light cones. In this work, we demonstrate that the Unruh effect can be detected through the nonlocal geometric phase acquired by a quantum system evolving within one of these wedges. Specifically, we find that a particle governed by a non-Hermitian Hamiltonian, which remains in its eigenstate during time evolution, acquires a Berry phase when controlled by the accelerated observer. This phase exhibits a singularity at the Unruh temperature, a feature that can be interpreted as the geometric phase contribution from the Unruh effect. Furthermore, we show that this Unruh-induced Berry phase manifests as a nonlocal geometric phase in the system's time evolution, offering a potential method to detect the phenomenon. Additionally, we establish that the Unruh effect is intrinsically connected to the entanglement between the future and past light cones of the accelerated observer. Finally, we examine the relationship between the Unruh phenomenon and the gravitational Berry phase arising from the entanglement of spacetime regions. These findings suggest that quantum systems can serve as detectors for the Unruh effect and provide new insights into the interplay between quantum mechanics and gravity. Our results also highlight the significance of non-Hermitian quantum systems in exploring fundamental aspects of quantum field theory in curved spacetimes. The accretion of a weak stellar wind onto a compact object in high-mass X-ray binaries (HMXBs) is thought to significantly influence the X-ray spectrum and timing of the system. This study utilizes data from the 2013 outburst of the HMXB Cyg X-1, which was in a hard spectral state, to investigate how the breeze from its O-star companion affects the system's X-ray output. We employed a model comprising a constant disk component, a blackbody, and a cutoff power law to analyze the data. Our results indicate that the breeze's contribution to the X-ray spectrum is minimal, accounting for less than 1% of the total luminosity. Furthermore, we examined the correlation between the blackbody temperature and the cutoff energy, finding a strong positive correlation with a Pearson coefficient of 0.92. This finding contradicts the hypothesis that the blackbody represents the breeze's contribution, as such a hypothesis would predict a negative correlation. Additionally, we observed a strong anti-correlation (Pearson coefficient of -0.94) between the blackbody temperature and the cutoff energy, a relationship that aligns with the hard-state spectral evolution model. Finally, we analyzed the cross-correlation between the constant component and the blackbody, noting a time lag of approximately 100 seconds where the blackbody lags behind the constant component. This lag supports the interpretation that the blackbody originates from the accretion disk's boundary layer, rather than from the breeze. Consequently, our findings suggest that the contribution of the breeze to the X-ray spectrum of Cyg X-1 is negligible. Furthermore, the observed time lag between the constant component and the blackbody is consistent with the blackbody arising from the disk's boundary layer. These results are also applicable to other HMXBs in the hard state. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the boundary layer model and the standard accretion disk model. Fast radio bursts (FRBs) represent brief, millisecond-duration radio signals of extragalactic origin that remain enigmatic. While some FRBs are accompanied by radio afterglows, the presence of optical or radio waves during the burst phase remains uncertain. This study reports the detection of a radio burst within the FRB 20200428E outburst on April 28, 2020, using the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical radio Telescope (FAST). Simultaneously, the burst was observed by the Liverpool Telescope and the Liverpool Telescope II at the Canary Islands. The radio signal exhibited a flat spectrum and a duration of 1.2 ms, with a fluence of 1.1 Jy ms. The optical emission was characterized by a continuum spectrum with a flux density of 0.015 Jy at 550 nm. This event marks the first simultaneous detection of a burst from FRB 20200428E and the second well-localized FRB to exhibit radio emission during the burst phase. Furthermore, we conducted a deep search for delayed optical emission from this burst using the Liverpool Telescope, finding no significant signal. These observations establish an upper limit on the ratio of optical to radio flux at 550 nm of $f_{\rm opt}/f_{\rm rad} < 10^{-3}$, a constraint that is approximately two orders of magnitude tighter than the most stringent previous limit. Additionally, we set an upper limit on the ratio of delayed optical to radio flux at 550 nm of $f_{\rm opt}/f_{\rm rad} < 10^{-2}$ for delays ranging from 10 to 100 ms. These findings suggest that the radio emission from FRB 20200428E is not primarily driven by the same mechanism responsible for the optical emission. The simultaneous radio and optical signals from this burst may be attributed to a magnetar wind shock model. Furthermore, the absence of delayed optical emission from this burst helps constrain the parameter space for the synchrotron self-absorption model. These results underscore the necessity of deploying a global array of radio telescopes to investigate the origins of FRBs. We introduce Delegated RingCT, a novel ring signature framework designed for privacy-preserving payment systems. This approach substantially lowers computational demands for both signing and verifying transactions, making it especially beneficial for verifiers. By leveraging the concept of a succinct set signature, our method ensures that verifier computation remains independent of the ring size. We have successfully deployed this system in a real-world application and benchmarked it against existing ring signature schemes, demonstrating significant performance gains. Specifically, verification takes only 0.001 seconds, and the signature size is 1000 times smaller than that of other practical solutions. These advantages are particularly critical for ring signatures used in payment systems, where verifiers often include users with limited computational resources. Furthermore, we outline how to extend the system to support multiple currencies and multiple signatures per currency. Finally, we address the challenge of ensuring that signers possess the authority to use the digital credentials within the ring. Our findings indicate that Delegated RingCT is ideally suited for privacy-preserving payment systems, offering superior performance compared to current solutions. Additionally, we have developed a prototype utilizing this system, which is available for download. The brightness of charged particle beams is a critical parameter for many applications, yet it is difficult to measure due to the beam's high intensity and small scale. This paper introduces a new method for brightness diagnostics that leverages the non-linear dynamics of a beam passing through a thin, weak-focusing solenoid. The technique is applicable to diverse beams, including electron beams in free-electron lasers, electron and ion beams in accelerators, and ion beams used in material irradiation. It offers a non-invasive approach to determining beam brightness without disrupting the primary application. The proposed method involves three steps: (1) measuring the beam's spot size at three longitudinal positions upstream of the scanner; (2) passing the beam through a thin, weak-focusing solenoid to induce a slight change in spot size; and (3) measuring the spot size at three positions downstream. By comparing these measurements, the initial beam brightness can be calculated. This paper presents the theoretical foundation of the method, derives the governing equations, and demonstrates its validity through particle-in-cell simulations. Additionally, a proof-of-principle experiment was conducted using a 100 MeV electron beam from the University of Michigan's Test Stand 1, which successfully confirmed the theory. The results indicate that the technique is feasible and can achieve brightness measurement precision within 10%. Finally, the paper discusses potential applications and outlines a roadmap for future development. This work focuses on mathematical models that are both interpretable and generalizable. We begin by defining these models and their significance. A mathematical model is considered interpretable if its parameters possess a clear physical meaning, and its structure and parameter values can be deduced from observed data. Generalizability refers to a model's capacity to perform accurately on data outside its training set. We argue that achieving both interpretability and generalizability is essential for mathematical models.
The remainder of this paper explores the challenges and limitations inherent in current physics-based and data-driven modeling approaches. We then propose a novel framework for collaborative data-driven modeling, which leverages both physics-based and data-driven methods to construct models exhibiting both desirable traits. Finally, we illustrate the effectiveness of this framework through a numerical example.

Soft robotics is a rapidly evolving field that leverages the inherent compliance of its components to excel in tasks demanding adaptability, dexterity, and robustness. These systems are typically characterized by their lightweight design, low cost, and high portability. However, despite these advantages, soft robots often suffer from sluggish dynamics and a lack of precision, largely due to the absence of effective control strategies. This limitation stems from the difficulty in creating accurate models for soft robots, which are difficult to characterize using traditional rigid-body dynamics. Consequently, researchers have increasingly turned to model-driven control approaches, which utilize mathematical models to formulate control laws. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of model-driven control techniques for soft robots, examining both the current landscape and future challenges. It begins by outlining the fundamental concepts of model-driven control, followed by an analysis of the various modeling and control methods employed in this domain. The discussion also addresses the specific challenges associated with these approaches and concludes by proposing promising future research directions. By synthesizing existing literature, this survey aims to offer a clear overview of model-driven control for soft robots and inspire further advancements in the field. The source code for this survey is accessible at https://github.com/softroboticslab/MDControlSurvey. Additionally, the authors invite researchers to share their work on model-driven control for soft robots to facilitate a more thorough examination of the topic. Distance labeling serves as a compact alternative to adjacency matrices for representing graphs. Although these labels are significantly smaller, they must remain at least as large as the edges to fully capture the graph's structure. This paper demonstrates that for every planar graph $G$ with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges, there exists a distance labeling where each label contains $O(m^{1/2}n^{1/3})$ bits. Crucially, we also provide a fault-resilient variant of this labeling. Specifically, for any subset of $k$ vertices, the induced labels on the remaining $n-k$ vertices allow for the reconstruction of the original graph's labels. This capability is essential for fault-tolerant graph algorithms, enabling the adaptation of non-resilient methods to handle faults. Our results improve upon the best-known bounds by a factor of $n^{1/3}$. Furthermore, we show that for graphs with maximum degree $\Delta$, a fault-resilient distance labeling with $O(m^{1/2}n^{1/3}\log\Delta)$ bits per label exists. Additionally, we establish a lower bound of $\Omega(m^{1/2}n^{1/3})$ bits per label for planar graphs, proving that our upper bound is tight. Finally, we extend these findings to $c$-excluded minor graphs, which encompass all planar graphs. For such graphs, we present a fault-resilient distance labeling with $O(m^{1/2}n^{1/3}c^{2/3})$ bits per label. Our analysis indicates that this bound is nearly tight for planar graphs, with only a minor loss in the $n$ term. To our knowledge, this represents the first construction of fault-resilient distance labelings for planar graphs. We also introduce a fault-resilient distance labeling for general graphs with $n$ vertices and $m$ edges, achieving $O(m^{1/2}n^{1/3}\log\Delta)$ bits per label. This improves upon the previous best lower bound of $\Omega(m^{1/2}n^{1/3})$ by a factor of $\log\Delta$. Our approach relies on a novel application of the Erdős-Hajnal theorem, which we believe will be valuable for other problems. This study investigates two-particle correlations within a driven-dissipative Bose-Hubbard model, examining them across both time and frequency domains. The analysis covers two distinct dissipation regimes: one where dissipation is weak relative to the driving force, and another where it is strong. In the weak dissipation regime, the system reaches a quasi-steady state characterized by a distribution of quasi-energy states. Correlations are analyzed using the two-particle density matrix in the quasi-energy basis, revealing that at short times, the system exhibits memory of its initial conditions, a feature absent in the long-time limit. Conversely, in the strong dissipation regime, the system is described by a non-equilibrium steady state (NESS). Here, correlations are characterized by the two-particle density matrix in the energy basis, with the two-particle density matrix at the driving frequency serving as a key indicator. Furthermore, the study demonstrates that the NESS can be effectively modeled as a thermal state at a non-thermal temperature, which is derived from the two-particle density matrix. These findings are validated through numerical simulations of a two-site system. Additionally, the results are compared against an analytical model for a mean-field system, showing qualitative agreement. Finally, the paper outlines potential experimental applications of these theoretical results. The accompanying code is accessible at https://github.com/Ankit-1234/Correlations_Bose_Hubbard. This paper introduces a novel method for detecting out-of-distribution (OOD) data by utilizing Gaussian Processes (GP). We achieve this by modeling the data distribution as a Gaussian Process and defining a new class of functions termed "strata." These strata are derived from the probability density function of the data and represent level sets of the GP. We establish the theoretical properties of these strata, demonstrating that they partition the input space into regions where data points share identical likelihoods. Furthermore, we prove that these strata possess a specific geometric structure that enables effective OOD detection. We validate the efficacy of our approach through experiments on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Driven open quantum systems frequently develop chaotic dynamics that cause rapid heating, a phenomenon that hinders the creation of macroscopic quantum states. In this study, we demonstrate that a specific scarring-like state within an optical lattice, which is weakly coupled to a thermal reservoir, remains protected against both environmental and internal heating sources. Consequently, the system achieves a non-equilibrium Bose-condensed state at a finite Bose-condensation temperature. This finding suggests that engineering scar-like states in open driven systems offers a viable pathway for generating non-equilibrium Bose-condensed phases. Furthermore, we propose that this Bose-condensation mechanism can be observed experimentally in a driven lattice of ultracold atoms interacting with a reservoir of another atomic species. Notably, the resulting Bose-condensed state exhibits unique properties, such as a non-thermal distribution for the reservoir species and a non-monotonic relationship between the Bose-condensation temperature and the coupling strength between the two species. These distinctive features offer a means to detect the Bose-condensed state and provide a method to control its temperature. Additionally, we show that the Bose-condensation temperature can be tuned by adjusting the Floquet-driving frequency. These findings may also extend to other scarring-like states in various open driven systems. Finally, we highlight that the Floquet-driving frequency can be utilized to manipulate the size of the Bose-condensed condensate. These results offer new avenues for investigating non-equilibrium Bose condensation and may contribute to the development of non-equilibrium quantum technologies. This study establishes a unified approach to deriving quantitative Alexandrov maximum principle estimates for the Monge–Ampère equation within a bounded domain, utilizing a specific class of functions defined on the product of Euclidean spaces. This methodology yields a novel proof of the Alexandrov–Petrovskii theorem regarding the uniform Hölder continuity of the Monge–Ampère equation's solutions, applicable to both the global and local contexts. Furthermore, the proof demonstrates robustness by accommodating various elliptic operators beyond the standard Monge–Ampère equation. The Alexandrov maximum principle is also extended to the broader category of superminima. The findings are supported by illustrative examples and counterexamples. Additionally, the Alexandrov maximum principle is derived for elliptic equations expressed in divergence form, featuring uniformly elliptic coefficients and right-hand sides belonging to a suitable function class. These results are subsequently employed to derive quantitative Alexandrov–Bakelman–Protter estimates for this class of equations. The paper concludes with a set of open questions. This study introduces a joint failure restoration, fault prevention, and energy-efficient resource management strategy designed for software-defined networks (SDN) within fog computing environments. The primary objective is to minimize total power consumption by dynamically adjusting the number of active switches based on current service demands, while simultaneously optimizing failure resilience through the rapid recovery of failed flows. To achieve this, the paper formulates the problem as a Mixed-Integer Linear Program (MILP) and proposes a corresponding heuristic algorithm. These codes are defined by the presence of a bulk boundary isometry, which ensures that any $k$ qubits within the boundary correspond to $d$ qubits in the bulk, thereby achieving a $k/d$ code distance. However, the local structure of TPS restricts these codes to linear scaling in both code distance and minimum distance. This limitation is overcome by Holographic Multiscale Entanglement Renormalization Ansatz (H-MERA), which utilizes a more complex network structure capable of supporting power-law scaling for both code distance and minimum distance. This paper introduces Hyper-MERA, a novel holographic code that maintains power-law scaling while enhancing the $k/d$ ratio. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the hypergraph structure inherent in Hyper-MERA can be effectively approximated using a hyperbolic tensor network, thereby enabling the application of bulk boundary isometries to this class of codes. This ability to construct explicit bulk boundary isometries for Hyper-MERA distinguishes it from other holographic codes that rely solely on tensor contraction networks. Additionally, we examine the relationship between the code distance and minimum distance of Hyper-MERA, showing that the minimum distance scales as $k^{1/2}$. Finally, we explore the potential of Hyper-MERA for holographic quantum computing, specifically regarding the complexity of decoding and the capacity for geometric local encoding. This paper introduces a distributed optimization framework designed to implement Optimal Conservation Voltage Decrease (OCVD) within Integrated Primary-Secondary distribution systems. The objective is to minimize total network losses by determining the optimal voltage profile across all buses, utilizing only local voltage measurements. This distributed strategy is specifically tailored for distribution systems featuring significant amounts of inverter-based resources (IBRs). The proposed method relies on a distributed algorithm capable of solving OCVD problems formulated as Second-Order Cone Programs (SOCPs) or Mixed-Integer SOCPs (MISOCs). To address the MISOC variant, which incorporates binary variables for IBR operational modes, the study employs a distributed cutting-plane method. This approach iteratively refines a linear approximation of the original problem by exchanging only local data between IBRs and smart meters. Simulation results using a 69-bus test feeder demonstrate the method's effectiveness, scalability, and robustness. Furthermore, the approach is shown to be resilient against communication delays and failures. Finally, the paper outlines potential extensions applicable to broader power system optimization challenges. The proposed framework is implemented in Python and made available as an open-source software package. This work investigates a stochastic nonstochastic hybrid framework where an advisor recommends arms to a learner, characterized by arm-dependent delays affecting both entities. The advisor observes the entire history and arm outcomes but experiences delays specific to the suggested arm, whereas the learner shares this information yet suffers additional arm-dependent delays in identifying selected arms. We introduce two novel models featuring a finite set of arms with varying success probabilities: the \emph{Full Information} model, where the learner accesses the advisor's complete history, and the \emph{Partial Information} model, where the learner's history is a subset of the advisor's. We propose two algorithms, \texttt{FIA} and \texttt{PIA}, for the Full Information and Partial Information models respectively, demonstrating that both achieve finite-time regret bounds that are nearly optimal up to logarithmic factors. Furthermore, we establish that any algorithm operating under the Partial Information model incurs a regret lower bound of $\Omega(\sqrt{T})$, where $T$ represents the time horizon. This document serves as a review of Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD) based on the Lattice approach, with a specific focus on non-zero temperature and chemical potential. It begins by outlining the theoretical foundations of the QCD Lagrangian within the lattice framework. Subsequently, it examines the primary challenges associated with QCD simulations, including the sign problem, the necessity of reweighting, and the application of improved actions. The discussion then shifts to results derived from these lattice calculations, covering the chiral phase diagram, the behavior of the equation of state, and the phase structure of QCD at finite temperature and density. Finally, the document concludes with an outlook on future research directions. This text is intended to provide a pedagogical introduction to the subject for graduate students and early-career researchers. This study introduces a novel probabilistic surrogate modeling approach designed to estimate the stochastic stress response of offshore wind turbines. The method employs a sequence of Gaussian process (GP) models, where each model is conditioned on the output of the preceding one, forming a chained GP structure. This framework is applied to a simplified two-degree-of-freedom (2DOF) offshore wind turbine system. The chained GPs are trained using a dataset of stress time histories generated via time-history analysis, which accounts for the statistical dependence among input wave variables. The model's performance is evaluated by comparing its predictions against a dataset of stress time histories created through a Monte Carlo simulation that captures the statistical dependence of wave inputs. Results demonstrate that the chained GPs effectively predict the statistical characteristics of the 2DOF system's stress response. Furthermore, the approach is shown to be computationally efficient, capable of generating a probabilistic model for stress response within minutes. These findings indicate that chained GPs offer a promising solution for modeling the stress responses of complex offshore wind turbine systems. Finally, the paper outlines the necessary extensions to adapt this methodology for use in wind-turbine reliability assessment. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/abdelrahimhassan/chained-GP. This study introduces a new method for reconstructing time-resolved data, utilizing a forward-optimization strategy applied to a parametric inversion framework. The approach employs a parametric representation of data trajectories, specifically Fourier series, to model data evolution over time. By integrating this representation into a Bayesian inversion model, the method accounts for data correlations across time, enabling robust reconstruction from noisy measurements. The forward-optimization technique is utilized to infer the Fourier parameters that best explain the data. We demonstrate the application of this approach to two data types: (i) the temporal dynamics of a single particle's position, and (ii) time-resolved fluorescence emission spectra. In both scenarios, the method successfully reconstructs data from noisy measurements, even when the sampling rate is insufficient to fully capture the data's time evolution. Furthermore, the method is shown to be robust against model errors, such as those caused by an incomplete basis for the data trajectories. Finally, we discuss the method's computational efficiency, which stems from the use of forward-optimization and the efficient parameterization of data trajectories. The method is implemented in Python and made available as an open-source package. The associated code and data required to reproduce the results presented in this work can be accessed at https://github.com/andreasgustafsson2020/PyTrajectoryBasis. The Coronavirus-SUS application, developed by the Brazilian government, serves as a contact tracing tool for COVID-19. It utilizes Bluetooth technology to anonymously identify and notify users when they have been near individuals who later test positive. This study evaluates the privacy of the system by analyzing its source code and comparing its design against established theoretical and empirical privacy metrics. Our findings indicate that the application fails to meet these metrics, thereby exposing its users to significant privacy risks. We conclude that the developers should prioritize privacy as a core design principle and implement the necessary adjustments to align with the established theoretical and empirical measures. Additionally, we propose a set of empirical measures that can be applied to any contact tracing application, regardless of the specific programming language used. Finally, we offer a set of recommendations for the developers of Coronavirus-SUS to enhance the application's privacy protections. This research underscores the critical need for a standardized approach to measuring privacy in contact tracing systems. Furthermore, it demonstrates that source code analysis is a valuable method for assessing the privacy of such applications. We believe these insights will assist developers in creating more privacy-preserving solutions and enable researchers to establish more effective metrics for privacy evaluation. To support this, we have made the code and data utilized in this study publicly available. We introduce a code creator for functional language ACL2 that automatically generates proofs verifying programs written in the C-like language ACL2-C. This code creator operates based on a shallow embedding of C within ACL2, where every C program is represented as a mathematical function in the same way as in existing work. However, unlike previous approaches, our method automatically generates proofs for the correctness of these C programs. Users can specify the correctness theorem using a new, user-friendly notation, and the tool automatically generates the corresponding proof script. This generated script is subsequently translated into a proof script for the original program in the target language. We have implemented this code creator as a tool called C2P4ACL2 (C to Proofs for ACL2) and have applied it to verify the correctness of C programs from various domains, including operating systems, embedded systems, and web browsers. Furthermore, we have evaluated C2P4ACL2 using a set of industrial cases, demonstrating that it can automatically verify the correctness of C programs in these domains. Finally, we show that C2P4ACL2 can be effectively utilized by industrial engineers who are familiar with either ACL2 or ACL2-C. To our knowledge, this is the first work to achieve both the automatic verification of C programs and their accessibility to industrial engineers. Solar irradiance follows a predictable daily pattern, peaking at solar noon and tapering off toward the early mornings and late evenings. This article introduces a new quadrature rule designed to accurately compute functions of this specific form. The method is rooted in Gaussian quadrature, where the weight function is defined as $w(t) = \sqrt{t(1-t)}$ on the interval $[0,1]$. By mapping this to the physical time interval $[t_0, t_1]$, the weight function effectively models solar irradiance, remaining near zero at the start and end of the day while approximating a flat profile around midday. The resulting solar-weighted Gaussian quadrature rule utilizes seven nodes and seven weights, delivering exceptional accuracy for this class of weighted functions. Its primary application is in numerically solving ordinary differential equations (ODEs) that are driven by solar irradiance. To demonstrate this, the paper presents a numerical model of a photovoltaic-powered water pump. The model's ODEs are solved using the solar-weighted Gaussian quadrature rule, and the results are compared against solutions obtained via standard ODE solvers. The comparison reveals that the solar-weighted rule achieves accuracy comparable to standard methods while offering a significant computational advantage. Consequently, the proposed quadrature rule is presented as a valuable tool for applications involving solar irradiance. The source code for the PV pump model is available at https://github.com/andrewsds/solar-weighted-GQ.

Keywords: solar irradiance, Gaussian quadrature, ordinary differential equations, photovoltaic, optimization, water pumping.

While position estimation for novel categories is essential for robotics, it remains largely unexplored in computer vision. This paper introduces a new end-to-end zero-shot category-level object position estimation method that utilizes a single category name as input. We developed a novel network architecture that integrates a 3D convolutional backbone with a multi-scale feature fusion module to enhance position estimation accuracy. While imputation is a common approach, it is particularly critical for queries that require learning from interventions or counterfactuals. This study introduces VACA, a new class of variational graph autoencoders that utilizes interventional and counterfactual queries to enhance imputation. The VACA framework is straightforward to implement, supports both missing-at-random and missing-not-at-random scenarios, and is applicable to both linear and non-linear graphs. Experimental results demonstrate that VACA surpasses current state-of-the-art methods. Furthermore, we illustrate how VACA can be employed to generate synthetic data for interventional and counterfactual analysis. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/andrewkane/VACA. The Irish LOFAR station, situated in the West of Ireland, functions as a real-time transient acquisition backend known as REALTA. This system utilizes a dedicated 16 GHz receiver to monitor a 1.4–1.8 GHz frequency band with a 2048 MHz bandwidth, sampling data at 128 MHz. The system is currently operational and has already identified several known transients, including Fast Radio Bursts (FRBs), SGR bursts, and pulsars. This paper details the system's capabilities and highlights its initial scientific results. Furthermore, we outline plans for future enhancements, such as implementing a new pipeline for FRB detection and discovery. These improvements will expand the system's reach to 2048 MHz, thereby increasing sensitivity and enabling the detection of more distant FRBs. Additionally, we propose the development of a new real-time data analysis pipeline to facilitate the rapid follow-up of FRBs. This proposed system is designed to be easily adaptable for detecting other transient events, including solar bursts, pulsars, and magnetars. Ultimately, REALTA serves as a versatile tool for the real-time detection and follow-up of various transient phenomena. Its capabilities complement existing facilities, such as the CHIME FRB array in Canada, the Murchison Widefield Array in Australia, and the Low Frequency Array in the Netherlands. We anticipate that REALTA will significantly contribute to the growing field of multi-messenger astronomy. The REALTA system is publicly accessible at http://www.lofar.org/realtime. The software is open-source and available on GitHub at https://github.com/lofar/RealTime. The backend is also accessible via a web interface at http://realtime.lofar.org/. The synergy between machine learning and metaphotonics has recently sparked significant scientific and technological interest. This review examines the current state of this emerging field, exploring how machine learning can be leveraged to design and control light-matter interactions in hybrid systems combining meta-atoms with conventional microcavities. We outline recent advancements in applying machine learning to metaphotonics, detailing the fundamental principles of key machine learning techniques and their specific applications within metaphotonic platforms. Furthermore, we address the critical challenges and future directions associated with this interdisciplinary domain. We anticipate that the continued integration of machine learning and artificial intelligence into metaphotonics will unlock new capabilities for both the control of light-matter interactions and the design of next-generation devices. This synergy is poised to substantially advance the fields of quantum information science and nanophotonics. Additionally, we provide open-source Python code to facilitate the implementation of machine learning methods in metaphotonics. This resource is intended to inspire further research and foster collaboration between the machine learning and quantum optics communities. Our goal is to accelerate progress in this rapidly evolving area and to establish a foundation for future breakthroughs at the intersection of these disciplines. The code is available at: https://github.com/quantum-machine-learning/metaphotonics. By employing a quasi-steady-state approximation, the analysis demonstrates that a constant power-frequency dependence can stabilize voltage dynamics, transforming a saddle-focus bifurcation into a Hopf bifurcation. The theoretical findings are validated through simulations of a detailed model of the Western Australian power grid. Furthermore, the results are contrasted with those of droop frequency control, revealing that constant power-frequency dependence can mitigate saddle-focus bifurcations more effectively than the droop characteristic. Finally, the paper discusses the implications of these findings for the design of frequency control strategies. Notably, the proposed constant power-frequency dependence is shown to be realizable through droop frequency control, provided the droop characteristic is sufficiently nonlinear. Consequently, the study concludes that droop frequency control can achieve saddle-focus elimination if the droop factor is tuned appropriately. Specifically, we propose a model that represents CP-PhyS as a network of computing, communication, and physical subsystems, where each computing and communication component is modeled as a distributed system. We examine the challenges and methodologies for developing a framework that enables CP-PhyS to harness the diverse and heterogeneous resources of their embedded distributed systems. Furthermore, we outline a set of enabling technologies and demonstrate how this framework can be applied to a smart grid scenario. The primary objective of this work is to establish a foundation for the intelligent evolution of CP-PhyS, thereby enhancing their overall performance. To achieve this, we have developed a prototype implementation of the framework, which is currently being evaluated through various case studies. This paper details the implementation and its assessment within the context of a smart grid. The proposed framework is expected to significantly improve the efficiency of CP-PhyS, making them more intelligent, resilient, and responsive. Additionally, it is anticipated to enable the design of new CP-PhyS with superior performance and to support the development of a new generation of CP-PhyS. This study introduces MAPPIES, a novel Monte-Carlo code designed to simulate the production of ultraviolet (UV) and soft X-ray photons through the inverse external-Compton scattering of seed photons originating from the accretion disk around a supermassive black hole. The code's validity is confirmed by comparing its output with analytical solutions and by reproducing the UV/soft X-ray excess observed in the spectra of blazars. Additionally, we apply MAPPIES to analyze the emission from the active galactic nucleus 3C 273, utilizing the disk model established by Krawczynski et al. (2002). Our findings indicate that the radiation field generated by the accretion disk is sufficient to account for the UV/soft X-ray excess in 3C 273, with the scattering region situated approximately 100 gravitational radii from the black hole. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the polarization of this excess radiation is sensitive to the polarization of the accretion disk, offering a potential method to investigate the polarization of accretion disks in active galactic nuclei. Finally, we outline the future development of MAPPIES, which will incorporate the effects of magnetic fields and relativistic jets. This work is the second in a series; the first paper, by Krawczynski et al. (2002), details the derivation of the disk model and the development of the initial analytical code. We demonstrate that the saddle-point approximation serves as an efficient asymptotic expansion for the partition function within this framework. Furthermore, we explore the connection between these analytic extensions and replica methods. Finally, we apply these findings to the replica extension of complex landscapes, specifically addressing the replica symmetric approximation and the saddle-point approximation of the replica symmetric ansatz. These findings are supported by numerical experiments conducted on the Sherrington-Kirkpatrick spin glass model. Symmetric pure states are defined as quantum states that remain unchanged under any permutation of their component subsystems. This work introduces and examines a novel online detection protocol for these states. The proposed method is straightforward, resource-efficient, and capable of achieving perfect detection fidelity. Furthermore, we establish a necessary and sufficient condition for implementing this protocol using any arbitrary set of symmetric pure states. Finally, we demonstrate the method's practical utility by applying it to detect multipartite Bell states and Greenberger-Horne-Zeilinger states. Additionally, we explore the potential of this approach for generating multipartite entanglement. These findings may find broad applications in quantum information processing. Our results are validated through numerical simulations. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi-1999/Symmetric-Pure-States. Baryon production is investigated through the quantized fragmentation of a QCD string, incorporating a magnetic field generated by the helical motion of its endpoints. The study examines how this field influences baryon formation, specifically focusing on diquark creation. The resulting distribution of diquarks, which serve as the fundamental building blocks for baryons, is derived. Furthermore, the impact of the magnetic field on the fragmentation process is analyzed in detail. The findings indicate that while the field does not alter the total number of formed diquarks, it significantly shifts the average position of the first one along the string. This shift moves further from the string's center as the magnetic field strength increases. These results are compared with existing data on baryon production. Finally, the potential for extending this framework to include meson formation is briefly addressed. The research was conducted using the Lund string model enhanced with a magnetic field. The resulting diquark production rate aligns with experimental data, and the average location of the first diquark along the string agrees with predictions from the Lund Monte Carlo program. Additionally, the average distance between the produced diquark and the string's center exhibits a strong dependence on magnetic field intensity, a feature that can be tested against experimental results. The study also explores the possibility of extending this approach to meson production. Overall, the inclusion of a magnetic field in Lund string fragmentation proves essential for accurately modeling diquark production. Solar active regions (ARs) are known to influence the accuracy of helioseismic travel-time measurements. This study examines the contribution of currents surrounding these regions to the north-south (N-S) travel-time data. By analyzing the relationship between N-S travel-time variations and the magnetic flux of ARs, we identified a correlation. Furthermore, we calculated the current density around these flux concentrations and found a strong correlation between the current magnitude and the N-S travel-time variations. These findings suggest that the observed N-S travel-time asymmetries are likely caused by solar active regions. Consequently, we recommend excluding observations of regions with high current density to improve the reliability of helioseismic travel-time measurements. Additionally, we propose a method to identify such high-current regions using the SunPy Python package. This approach involves tracking the position of ARs over time and calculating the current density within a specified area surrounding them. We successfully applied this method to identify high-current regions in the solar cycle 24. Our results indicate that the N-S travel-time measurements from these identified regions are significantly larger than the global average. This research underscores the necessity of removing observations from high-current regions to ensure the reliability of helioseismic travel-time data. Furthermore, it demonstrates that the N-S travel-time asymmetry is a valuable tool for identifying ARs with high current density. Ultimately, this study provides a method for automatically detecting high-current regions and offers a new perspective on the impact of ARs on helioseismic travel-time measurements. We investigate the detection of gravitational wave (GW) backgrounds generated by primordial magnetic fields (PMF) within the Pulsar Timing Array (PTA) frequency range. Our analysis reveals that PTA experiments can constrain the amplitude of PMF up to $10^{-10}$ across a broad spectrum of power-law indices. Furthermore, we demonstrate that PTA observations can significantly enhance limits on PMF amplitude, reaching up to a factor of 100 beyond current constraints. These findings are particularly relevant for theories proposing a direct link between inflation and PMF, such as those involving magnetogenesis. Additionally, we show that PTA data can probe PMF amplitudes at levels significantly higher than those accessible through observations of the cosmic microwave background or the large-scale structure of the universe. Finally, we establish that the PTA can determine the power-law index of the PMF with a precision of approximately 10% for amplitudes near $10^{-10}$. These results underscore the critical role of PTA experiments in exploring the physics of primordial magnetic fields. Finally, we discuss the potential for future PTA experiments to further improve these limits. The code used for this analysis is accessible at [1].

Interactive retrieval models have recently surpassed traditional dense methods in monolingual settings by utilizing query-relevant documents to refine the search process through multiple iterations. However, these models demand substantial computational resources, rendering them impractical for cross-lingual applications where queries are typically translated via machine translation. This study introduces a straightforward and efficient approach to interactive retrieval that leverages pre-translated documents without incurring translation costs. By employing a lightweight, non-interactive model to identify query-relevant documents in the source language during the initial iteration, we can achieve high performance with minimal additional computation. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a small collection of high-quality pseudo-relevant documents from the first iteration significantly enhances vector-based cross-lingual information retrieval. Our results indicate that this method improves performance by 1.5 to 2.5 points on standard CLIR benchmarks. The code is accessible at https://github.com/abhi-1999/interactive-CLIR. Additionally, our approach ranks first on the CACM 2022 CLIR shared task, achieving a 1.5-point gain over the second-place method. Small-area estimation (SAE) is a statistical approach designed to derive reliable estimates for small populations within specific geographic regions. This paper reviews the development and implementation of SAE models in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), with a specific focus on HIV prevalence estimation in sub-Saharan Africa. It outlines the essential design and operational requirements for SAE, including the necessary data infrastructure and human expertise. The discussion highlights the distinct advantages and limitations of both model-based and design-based SAE methodologies. Furthermore, it addresses the challenges posed by data scarcity in LMICs and the difficulties in validating model assumptions. Finally, the paper proposes future research directions aimed at enhancing SAE models and refining their application in these settings. Given the critical need for accurate estimates in LMICs, we advocate for the integration of model-based SAE into national statistical surveys. This approach would leverage existing survey infrastructure to generate actionable data for policy and programmatic decisions. We conclude by offering recommendations for practitioners and researchers working in this field. The manuscript also includes a technical appendix detailing the statistical models employed in the illustrative case study. This appendix provides an overview of the models, explains the rationale behind their selection, and presents the corresponding R code. Additionally, the appendix includes a discussion of the model's performance and an exploration of alternative modeling strategies. The R code is available at https://github.com/abigael/SAE. We investigate a scenario where an agent utilizes a continuous-variable quantum channel to place a wager on a sequence of independent and identically distributed events. The wagering strategy involves preparing a continuous-variable quantum state and distributing it across multiple copies of the channel. The sequence of events is then encoded into this state via a series of measurements, with the resulting outcomes determining the state's evolution through the channel. Finally, the agent settles the wager by measuring the final state and comparing the result against a predefined threshold. We demonstrate that an optimal betting strategy can be derived by solving a semidefinite program. Furthermore, we apply these findings to a specific case where the events follow a Bernoulli distribution. In this context, we show that the optimal wagering strategy enables the agent to achieve the min-entropy of the source. Additionally, we examine a scenario where the agent can manipulate the initial state of the channel, proving that this capability allows for the attainment of the min-entropy rate. These findings provide a novel operational interpretation for min-entropy and min-entropy rate within the framework of continuous-variable quantum information. Finally, we validate our theoretical framework through numerical simulations.

Transition metal and group-14 based dichalcogenides and dipnictides have garnered significant interest due to their potential applications in next-generation optoelectronic devices. This study employs first-principles calculations to investigate the quasiparticle band structures and excitonic properties of MA$_2$Z$_4$ compounds, where M represents Mo, W, or Ti, and Z represents Si, Ge, or N, P, or As. The results indicate that the quasiparticle band structures of these materials are highly sensitive to stacking configurations, whereas the excitonic characteristics remain largely unaffected by variations in atomic composition or stacking. Furthermore, the binding energies of excitons in these compounds are substantially higher than those in conventional semiconductors. We present a three-dimensional simulation of prestellar core collapse that incorporates both self-gravity and radiative transfer, specifically designed to model the formation of a protostar and its surrounding protoplanetary disk. Our analysis reveals that the disk's mass and radius are primarily determined by the initial mass and density profile of the prestellar core. The simulation results indicate that the final disk mass is approximately 0.01 times the stellar mass, with a characteristic radius of roughly 100 astronomical units. Additionally, we observe that the disk's surface temperature is significantly lower than its midplane temperature, a factor that substantially influences the disk's evolution. Finally, we demonstrate that the final stellar mass is primarily a function of the initial core mass and the ambient gas density. These findings offer valuable insights for interpreting observations of young stellar objects. Furthermore, the proposed methodology can be applied to investigate the formation of circumstellar disks around other types of stars. Atmospheric dispersion is a critical factor in astronomical observations, particularly for high-resolution spectroscopy. This paper introduces a novel atmospheric dispersion model designed to characterize the integrated refractive index profile of the Earth's atmosphere. The model's parameters are determined by fitting the model to measured zenith atmospheric dispersion data collected at the ESO La Silla Observatory. These measurements were obtained using a newly developed, compact, and cost-effective instrument called the Atmospheric Dispersion Monitor (ADM). The ADM operates by measuring the angular separation between the blue and red images of a star, utilizing a simple optical setup that directs starlight through a narrow slit onto a single-pixel detector. The paper provides a detailed description of the atmospheric dispersion model and its associated parameters, which are subsequently employed in a companion paper to evaluate the performance of high-resolution spectrographs under varying atmospheric conditions. We present a concise proof of the Pontryagin duality for locally compact abelian groups, situated within the framework of constant low-order arithmetic. This approach utilizes the language of ordered vector spaces, a method that is notably simpler than the $\mathsf{R}^4$ formulation found in [10]. Additionally, we establish a similar duality result for locally compact abelian groups equipped with the total topology. All groups under consideration are assumed to be uncountable. The proof relies on a novel characterization of Pontryagin duality through the topology of the groups and the ordering of their characters. Specifically, we demonstrate that the topology of a locally compact abelian group is entirely determined by the order structure of its character group. Furthermore, we provide an alternative characterization of the order structure of characters for such groups. We also examine the relationship between the topology of a group and that of its dual, proving that the topology of the dual group is dictated by the lattice of topological subgroups of the original group. These findings are derived using the techniques introduced in [1]. Finally, we illustrate that the topology of the double dual group can be recovered from the topology and order structure of the dual group. These results collectively provide a comprehensive characterization of Pontryagin duality within the context of constant low-order arithmetic. We conclude by outlining several open questions in this area. The paper includes an appendix detailing the foundational results of [1] regarding constant logic. This study examines a wireless powered network (WPN) augmented with an intelligent reflecting surface (IRS). The WPN comprises a power station (PS) and multiple receivers, where the PS transmits wireless energy to the receivers while they simultaneously harvest data. The received signals are further corrupted by interference from an external source. We propose a two-stage approach to maximize the sum throughput of the receivers: first, optimizing the IRS phase shifts to mitigate interference, and second, determining the optimal power allocation for the PS to ensure receivers meet minimum energy requirements. To accomplish this, we develop a deep unsupervised learning (DUL) framework that jointly optimizes IRS phase shifts and power allocation to boost WPN throughput. The DUL model is trained offline using a dataset generated from various interference conditions, allowing it to function without real-time access to current interference states. Simulation results demonstrate that the DUL approach significantly enhances WPN throughput compared to existing methods. Furthermore, we analyze the DUL model's performance under different network configurations, such as varying numbers of receivers and interference sources, as well as under diverse channel conditions. Finally, we evaluate the computational complexity of the proposed method. Our findings indicate that the DUL approach is highly effective in improving WPN throughput and is computationally efficient, making it suitable for practical deployment. We introduce a unified framework that simultaneously accounts for dark matter and neutrino masses, utilizing a gauge symmetry to stabilize a dark matter candidate and employing a discrete symmetry to safeguard the asymmetry of heavy neutrinos. This approach allows us to address both phenomena while naturally incorporating a neutrino mass hierarchy. We calculate the dark matter relic density and perform a comprehensive parameter space analysis, finding that the neutrino mass hierarchy can be derived without relying on fine-tuning. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the dark matter relic density can be explained through annihilation into heavy neutrinos, with the resulting neutrino asymmetry remaining consistent with the dark matter density. Finally, we discuss the implications of this model for future experimental searches. This study is a collaborative effort by the authors of reference [1]. This paper introduces a data-driven control framework designed to learn control policies for generic dynamical systems using minimal data. The proposed method relies on two core components: a data-driven predictive control law and a data-driven approximate value function. The control law is derived by approximating the optimal value function via a deep neural network, which is trained on a limited dataset of state-control pairs. To address the limited data, we propose a novel approach that incorporates side information to enhance the quality of the data. Simulation results demonstrate that this framework can successfully train a single policy capable of executing multiple behaviors—such as reaching, swimming, walking, and flying—across various systems, including a 2-link robot arm, a quadcopter, a quadbike, and a quadpod. Furthermore, the framework enables the creation of a unified policy for a humanoid robot that can reach, walk, and swim. Additionally, we show that the framework can be extended to handle multiple behaviors beyond reaching, walking, and swimming, such as flying and sliding. Finally, we demonstrate that the framework can be adapted to execute these multiple behaviors sequentially. These findings indicate that the proposed approach offers a promising solution for data-driven control in scenarios characterized by limited data and a diverse range of behaviors. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ashishgupta12345/Unified-Policy.

Keywords: Data-driven control, predictive control, value function, side information, limited data, multiple behaviors.

Relation Networks (RNs) are a recent deep learning approach designed to model complex interactions between inputs by employing a fixed set of relations. While RNs have proven effective for tasks like image retrieval and similarity learning, they are typically trained using standard triplet loss. This paper introduces a novel Relation Generative Adversarial Network (RGAN) that integrates RNs with Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to enhance their training process. Specifically, we propose a new triplet loss function that leverages the relationship between real and fake samples to refine the representation learning of RNs. By combining the strengths of both architectures, RGANs learn representations that are more robust to variations in object appearance and pose. Extensive experiments on the Stanford Online Products (SOP) and Pascal VOC datasets demonstrate that our method surpasses state-of-the-art performance. Furthermore, we show that RGANs achieve superior results in image classification and generation compared to other GAN variants. The code is accessible at https://github.com/zhongyuanwang/RGAN. Additional details can be found at https://zhongyuanwang.github.io/RGAN/. The paper is available at https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.00220. We also invite contributions to our new dataset, Pascal VOC GANs, available at https://github.com/zhongyuanwang/PascalVOCGANs. This dataset includes 1,000 images from the original Pascal VOC dataset, divided into 80 classes, with 100 images per class. It features 10 object categories (airplane, bicycle, bird, boat, bottle, chair, dining table, elephant, horse, and person) and 10 background classes (bridge, building, cake, chair, cloud, mountain, river, sea, tree, and umbrella). The dataset is divided into 80 images for training and 20 for testing. We also provide a baseline implementation of a DCGAN, which can be trained and tested using the provided scripts. Twin-field quantum key exchange (TF-QKE) is a long-distance quantum key distribution protocol that leverages quantum entanglement to generate secure keys. Its primary benefit lies in its ability to scale transmission distances by allowing the communication rate to decline exponentially with distance. However, the implementation of TF-QKE has traditionally been hindered by the necessity of phase locking, a complex setup that demands the synchronization of optical phases across all transmitters and receivers. In this work, we introduce a phase-lock-free variant of the TF-QKE protocol. By employing a novel detection method, we demonstrate that this approach maintains performance comparable to the standard TF-QKE protocol while substantially simplifying the experimental requirements. Furthermore, we validate our theoretical predictions through experimental data obtained from a 100 km fiber link. These findings indicate that phase-free TF-QKE offers a more practical pathway for real-world deployment. Additionally, our results suggest that TF-QKE could potentially be extended to satellite-based quantum communication systems. Finally, we outline the necessary modifications to adapt the protocol for measurement-device-independent quantum key distribution. For a row contraction $X$ on a Hilbert space, the Toeplitz algebra $\mathrm{Toe}(X)$ is defined as the $C^*$-algebra generated by the Toeplitz operators $T_{\theta X}$, where $\theta$ ranges over the bounded analytic functions in the unit disk. This work investigates the structure of these Toeplitz algebras specifically for $X$ formed by the forward shift operators acting on the Fock space $\mathcal{F}^2(a)$ and the Hardy space $H^2$. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Toeplitz algebra associated with the shift on Fock space $\mathcal{F}^2(1)$ is isomorphic to the $C^*$-algebra of compact operators. Consequently, we derive that the Toeplitz corona algebra for Fock space, $\mathcal{T}_{\mathcal{F}}$, is isomorphic to $\mathcal{K} \oplus \mathcal{Q}$, where $\mathcal{K}$ denotes the compacts and $\mathcal{Q}$ represents the quotient of $H^\infty$ by the ideal of vanishing at the boundary. Additionally, we establish that the Toeplitz corona algebra for the shift on the Fock space $\mathcal{F}^2(\sqrt{N})$ possesses the property of real rank zero. Finally, we examine the case of a finite row of weighted shifts on the Hardy space $H^2$. In this context, we show that the Toeplitz corona algebra for the shift on Hardy space exhibits real rank zero, and we provide a complete characterization of its ideal structure. As a specific application, we determine the structure of the Toeplitz corona algebra for the shift on the Drury-Arveson space. This result confirms that the Drury-Arveson space is not essentially normal, thereby offering a negative answer to a question posed by Douglas and Yang. Moreover, we identify the ideal space of the quotient $\mathcal{T}_{H^2}/\mathcal{K}$ as the Shilov boundary of the unit disk. Finally, we note that the Drury-Arveson space is the only reproducing kernel Hilbert space on the unit ball for which the Toeplitz corona algebra of the shift possesses real rank zero. We introduce a pseudo-annotation technique that circumvents the need for bounding boxes during the training of object detectors. By leveraging a pre-trained model, we generate pseudo-bounding boxes for objects within an image dataset and subsequently filter these annotations using a rule-based system. This approach enables the training of an object detector on a dataset containing only image-level labels for all target classes. Furthermore, this framework supports the identification of novel object classes that were absent during training. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves performance comparable to state-of-the-art techniques on standard benchmarks like COCO and pascalVOC, while also exhibiting superior capabilities in open-vocabulary scenarios. We present a new study on the spatial distribution of ionized gas, atomic gas, and gas illuminated by photodissociation regions (PDRs) surrounding the Rho Oph S1 star. Utilizing the IRAM 30m telescope, we mapped the [CII] 158um, [NII] 205um, and [SIII] 907um lines, alongside the CO J=1-0 and 2-1 transitions. Our analysis reveals that the ionized gas is located in the northern and western sectors of the cloud, whereas the PDR gas occupies the southern and eastern regions. The atomic gas distribution aligns with the PDR gas, exhibiting a distinct separation from the ionized gas. We propose that the ionized gas originates from the cloud's surface, while the PDR gas is situated deeper within. The observed spatial segregation between ionized and PDR gas is attributed to the geometry of the cloud and the specific radiation field characteristics. Furthermore, the [CII] emission is primarily driven by the CO emission, indicating that the PDR gas resides in the shadow of the cloud. Finally, we estimate the mass of the PDR gas to be approximately 100 solar masses. These findings are consistent with the hypothesis that the Rho Oph S1 star formed from the collapse of a PDR. Additionally, the observed PDR gas distribution supports the theory that PDRs can trigger the collapse of molecular clouds. This study employs factor models to forecast mortality rates, utilizing the time-varying nature of common factors to project future mortality levels. We evaluate two distinct factor loading specifications: one where loadings are constant over time and another where they evolve over time. Our analysis utilizes the Lee-Carter model as a reference point, demonstrating that it is mathematically equivalent to a factor model with time-invariant loadings. Furthermore, we establish that a factor model with time-varying loadings can be expressed as a weighted average of several time-invariant factor models. Using data from the United States, we find that the model with time-varying loadings yields superior out-of-sample forecasts compared to the time-invariant version. Finally, we apply this approach to predict mortality rates for countries within the European Union. These predictions are subsequently used to estimate life expectancies and calculate the sensitivity of life expectancies to variations in mortality rates. This methodology offers a straightforward and efficient means to assess the potential impact of public health initiatives aimed at reducing mortality. The code required to replicate our findings is available on GitHub. (Accepted for publication in the Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series A). Keywords: Factor models, mortality prediction, life expectancy, European Union. (Accepted for publication in the Journal of the Royal Statistical Society: Series A). Neural Architecture Search (NAS) has demonstrated significant potential for automatically designing high-performing neural networks. However, the extensive search space and the need for repeated training make this process computationally demanding. To address these challenges, researchers have developed various methods to condense the search space, including weight sharing, hyper-architecture search, and performance prediction. This paper introduces a novel approach that leverages the inherent diversity of neural architectures to shrink the search space. By analyzing the diversity within a learned architecture space, we identify redundant components and eliminate them. Our method is versatile, supporting both supervised and unsupervised search scenarios. We validate our approach across multiple benchmarks, including Supervised MobileNet, Supervised CIFAR-10, and Unsupervised CIFAR-10. Experimental results indicate that our proposed method achieves superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art techniques. The code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2018/InterferenceReduction.

This paper investigates the properties of the \textit{boundary at infinity equipped with geodesic completeness}, originally introduced by D. D. Broomhead and J. R. Isbell in 1971. We demonstrate that for a proper geodesically complete CAT(0) space, the convergence structure on this boundary is uniquely determined by the space's metric. Furthermore, we establish that for any two such spaces, the wreath product's convergence structure is equivalent to the combination of their individual structures. We also provide a characterization of Cauchy sequences within this framework and examine the relationship between Cauchy sequences in the metric sense and those in this convergence structure. Additionally, we characterize the metric convergence structure on the boundary for specific examples, including hyperbolic spaces and products of hyperbolic spaces with Euclidean spaces. Finally, we characterize the topology of this boundary for geodesically complete CAT(0) spaces that are either products of hyperbolic spaces and Euclidean spaces or wreath products thereof. We conclude by posing an open question regarding whether this characterization extends to general geodesically complete CAT(0) spaces. The paper includes several examples and counterexamples to illustrate these findings. Notably, we show that the class of geodesically complete CAT(0) spaces is not closed under taking subspaces, even when those subspaces are closed, convex subspaces. We also construct a geodesically complete CAT(0) space where the Cauchy sequences in the convergence structure do not converge to a unique point. Finally, we characterize the Cauchy sequences in the convergence structure for products of these spaces and provide an example of a geodesically complete CAT(0) space where the convergence structure on its boundary is not metrizable. Throughout, we offer several theorems and conjectures concerning this convergence structure. We also characterize the boundary at infinity equipped with geodesic completeness for products of hyperbolic spaces and Euclidean spaces, and for specific examples involving geodesically complete CAT(0) spaces and their subspaces. In doing so, we characterize the boundary at infinity with this convergence structure for geodesically complete CAT(0) spaces that are either products of such spaces or specific examples thereof. We address whether this characterization applies to general geodesically complete CAT(0) spaces. The paper features numerous examples and counterexamples, including cases where the boundary at infinity is not metrizable under this convergence structure. We also explore whether this class of spaces is closed under subspaces, even closed convex ones.

In language services, ensuring quality and reliability is paramount. While human translators are responsible for the final output, their work is not always infallible; errors can occur due to factors such as fatigue, lack of subject-matter expertise, or insufficient proficiency in specific technical fields. To address this, a Bayesian approach has been developed to evaluate translator reliability. This method enables the calculation of the probability that a specific translator will err on a document of a given length, thereby facilitating more informed hiring decisions. The proposed methodology was validated using data from a translation service provider. The resulting probability estimates indicate that the model can effectively distinguish between highly reliable and unreliable translators. Furthermore, the method demonstrates the ability to differentiate between translators with varying levels of experience and those operating across different languages. Finally, the approach successfully identifies translators who are likely to reduce error rates when processing documents in their areas of subject-matter expertise. These findings suggest that the model can be extended to assess the reliability of translation teams, which comprise both translators and proofreaders. This extension would facilitate the selection of teams with a higher probability of producing error-free documents. Additionally, the model offers the potential to estimate the cost of errors, allowing clients to make more educated choices regarding the trade-off between the expenses of translation and proofreading services and the risk of incurring costs from document errors. The method is implemented in the R programming language, with the source code accessible at https://github.com/edgar-fernandez/bayesian-translator-reliability. The accompanying R package, bayesian-translator-reliability, can be installed via the command `devtools::install_github("edgar-fernandez/bayesian-translator-reliability")`. The package includes a function to estimate the probability of error for a translator working on a document of a specified length, utilizing a Bayesian framework based on beta-binomial distributions. This framework is parameterized by the translator's prior distribution, which is derived from a beta distribution informed by their previous performance. The model also incorporates a subject-matter expertise component, allowing for the estimation of error probabilities for documents in specialized domains. This capability is particularly valuable for determining whether a translator's error probability is elevated when handling documents in areas outside their expertise. The model is designed to be easily adaptable for estimating the reliability of translation teams, which include both translators and proofreaders. The paper concludes with a discussion of the method's limitations and potential future research directions. Keywords: reliability, translator, proofreader, subject-matter expertise, Bayesian, error probability

We introduce a general framework to analyze energy deposition across various scattering systems, ranging from quantum dots to graphene nanoribbons. Central to this approach are "energy deposition eigenchannels," which represent the most efficient pathways for delivering energy to a specific location. We establish sum rules for the spectral properties of these channels and derive an exact expression for local energy deposition following an ultrafast excitation. Furthermore, we develop a method to calculate these eigenchannels, illustrating their application in both quantum and high-energy regimes through specific examples. These findings offer a robust foundation for designing systems with optimized energy deposition characteristics. Additionally, our results are anticipated to facilitate the development of new algorithms for identifying similar eigenchannels in complex many-body systems. Finally, we demonstrate how this formalism can be utilized to construct a non-Hermitian effective Hamiltonian that captures the essential spectral features of energy deposition eigenchannels. This construction enables the application of established techniques from non-Hermitian physics to investigate phenomena such as exceptional points and non-Hermitian skin effects within the context of energy deposition. These insights are expected to significantly advance the design of systems tailored for specific energy deposition tasks. Finally, we discuss the potential applications of this formalism in energy delivery and harvesting. This work appears in Phys. Rev. Research 5, 013001 (2023). This study examines the optimal pricing and timing strategies for lottery tickets. We introduce a model where an agent's utility from winning a prize is diminished by the number of other winners, as shared prizes are divided among all successful participants. Consequently, an optimal pricing mechanism can be established to maximize the expected utility for a rational buyer. Furthermore, we propose a dynamic pricing framework where the cost of a ticket fluctuates based on the count of previous purchasers. Our findings indicate that when the prize-sharing effect is significant, lotteries should adopt a "high-low" pricing strategy, beginning with high prices and transitioning to lower ones over time. This approach is particularly advantageous when the marginal utility of additional wealth rises sharply at low income levels. We illustrate the practical application of this model using the Powerball lottery. Additionally, we develop a general analytical framework for determining optimal pricing and release schedules, which can be adapted to other scenarios involving diminishing returns, such as auctions, online advertising, and resource allocation. Finally, we explore extensions of this model, including the impact of risk aversion and the presence of impatient agents. Our results demonstrate that high prices attract only those with substantial wealth, whereas low prices are more effective at drawing buyers with limited financial resources. These insights are broadly applicable to various contexts, including the sale of housing, land, and online advertising. The valley degree of freedom in two-dimensional materials has garnered significant attention due to its potential for valleytronics. However, valley physics is not isolated; it is intrinsically linked to spin, charge, and electron-phonon coupling. This study employs a comprehensive theoretical framework to investigate how various electron-phonon coupling mechanisms impact valley properties. Specifically, we examine how different lattice deformation modes alter valley states and how the valley response to spin-orbit coupling is modified by electron-phonon interactions. Our findings indicate that these effects are highly material-dependent, with valley states in graphene and borophene being particularly sensitive to such couplings. These results offer a theoretical basis for understanding the role of electron-phonon interactions in valley physics and provide a pathway for manipulating valley properties through lattice deformations. Furthermore, this approach may facilitate the discovery of new two-dimensional materials with enhanced valley sensitivity. The accompanying code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi-1992/Valley_physics. This report presents our solution to the Visual Domain Adaptation (VIDA) challenge at NeurIPS 2022. The competition required training a model on the source domain (ImageNet) to achieve high accuracy on three target domains (CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and Caltech-100) through cross-domain training. The evaluation metric was defined as the average of the four domains' accuracies, calculated as:
$$\text{score} = \frac{1}{4} \left( \text{acc}_{\text{ImageNet}} + \sum_{\text{target}} \text{acc}_{\text{target}} \right)$$
Our approach leverages a pre-trained Swin Transformer, which is subsequently fine-tuned using a multi-task objective that combines classification with auxiliary tasks like pseudo-labeling and contrastive learning. This strategy yields a final score of 75.11, securing first place on the leaderboard. The source code is accessible at: https://github.com/ChenRongsheng/VIDA-2022.
Keywords: Visual Domain Adaptation, Contrastive Learning, Pseudo-Labeling.
