t-SNE is a widely used dimensionality reduction technique that has become a standard tool for visualizing high-dimensional data. However, its application to spherical data is constrained by t-SNE's reliance on Euclidean distance, which is not suitable for this context. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel t-SNE variant called spherical t-SNE (VMF-SNE), which substitutes the Gaussian distribution with a von Mises-Fisher distribution. This adaptation enables VMF-SNE to effectively capture the intrinsic geometric properties of spherical data. We evaluated VMF-SNE against t-SNE and other methods using both synthetic and real-world datasets. The experimental results demonstrate that VMF-SNE surpasses t-SNE in preserving the underlying data structure and outperforms competing methods on certain datasets. Additionally, we have made the source code available to the community. Our implementation is written in Python and utilizes the PyTorch library. The code can be accessed at: https://github.com/PyTorch/vmf-sne. Our implementation supports both 2D and 3D data. Furthermore, we have developed a Python package that integrates VMF-SNE with the scikit-learn API, allowing for seamless use of the method. This package is available at: https://github.com/PyTorch/vmf-sne. The package also supports 2D and 3D data. The authors acknowledge the contributions of the community to PyTorch. We investigate the two-dimensional Fermi polaron using a diagrammatic Monte Carlo approach. By extending the diagrammatic expansion to include diagrams with multiple loops, we achieve high precision in calculating the polaron energy. Our results reveal that as the impurity strength increases, the polaron transitions from a dressed state within the Fermi sea to a bound state with the Bose polaron energy, accompanied by the emergence of a di-particle bound state. Furthermore, we observe that the polaron's wave function evolves from a smooth, extended form to a localized one, while the self-energy shifts from a peak at the quasiparticle energy to a dip. Additionally, we analyze the impact of diagrams with a greater number of loops on the convergence of the series expansion. Finally, we explore the possibility of a quantum phase transition in this system. This study offers a comprehensive analysis of the two-dimensional Fermi polaron, delivering precise numerical data for the energy, wave function, and self-energy across various coupling regimes. These findings will be valuable for future theoretical and experimental investigations into this area. We introduce a quantum emulation method for fermionic systems that leverages the hybrid digital-analog computing framework. This approach utilizes a fermionic quantum simulator where native fermionic gates are digitally controlled by arbitrary single-qubit operations, alongside a lattice of interacting spins capable of hosting a large number of fermions through a Jordan-Wigner transformation. We demonstrate the emulation of various fermionic many-body systems, including free fermions, the Kitaev chain, and the Hubbard model. Furthermore, we validate the method's efficacy by calculating key physical observables, such as correlation functions and the density of states. Our findings indicate that the digital-analog hybrid scheme offers a viable pathway for executing quantum algorithms on fermionic systems. Additionally, we establish that the error in the physical observable scales inversely with the number of shots per run, a factor that can be adjusted by the user. This flexibility allows users to control the trade-off between computational resources and result accuracy. Consequently, this work provides a valuable resource for the development of quantum algorithms involving fermionic systems. Finally, we outline a roadmap for extending this approach to larger systems and discuss its potential applications in quantum chemistry and materials science. We establish links between the coefficients of powers of $p_{\mathbf{x}}(t)=\sum_{i=1}^n\lambda_i^{\mathbf{x}}t$, which represent eigenvalue moments for adjacency matrices of regular graphs, and the coefficients of a sequence of polynomials $\{P_k(t)\}_{k\geq 0}$ that obey a three-term recurrence relation. This approach yields novel identities for these identities and offers a new perspective on graph problems concerning adjacency matrices of symmetric and distance-regular graphs. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the polynomials $\{P_k(t)\}_{k\geq 0}$ linked to the Catalan numbers arise specifically from regular Hermitian graphs. Additionally, we derive an explicit formula for the $k$th root of $P_k(t)$ and provide a combinatorial interpretation of its coefficients. Finally, we present an algorithm to generate the coefficients of $\{P_k(t)\}_{k\geq 0}$ given a sequence of regular graphs $\{G_k\}_{k\geq 0}$ with adjacency matrices $A_k$ possessing a rank of $r_k\leq 2$. This method is applied to construct such sequences for $r_k=1$ and $r_k=2$. The findings in this study have applications in the theory of orthogonal polynomials and number theory. The paper concludes with several open questions. Keywords: adjacency matrix, regular graph, recurrence relation, orthogonal polynomials, number theory. This paper demonstrates that for any two smooth cubic curves, there exist finite multiples lying on the Veech curve, with their vertical coordinates matching those of the originals. This finding enables the commutation of Hitchin systems associated with smooth cubic curves. Furthermore, we establish that every integer located on the Veech curve is a valid vertical multiple for precisely one type of Hitchin cubic. These results are achieved through the analysis of a novel geometric object termed the "modular curve," which serves as the curve analogue to the modular curve. The study of the modular curve constitutes the primary component of this work. Additionally, we provide a geometric interpretation of the action of $SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$ on Teichmüller curves. The modular curve is anticipated to be valuable in addressing problems concerning the commutativity of other Veech curve analogues. As an application, we show that the Teichmüller curves within a specific family of prismatic curves are dense in the corresponding moduli space. This conclusion relies on the observation that the closure of the Veech curve intersects the family of moduli curves at exactly one point. We also present an alternative proof of this observation utilizing the modular curve. Finally, we offer a comprehensive discussion of the modular curve's properties, including its genus, fundamental group, and the structure of its fundamental group's abelianization. This discussion draws upon the theory of Teichmüller spaces and their associated curve analogues. The paper concludes with several open questions. The first addresses the commutativity of Hitchin systems for smooth cubic curves, while the second explores the application of the modular curve to the inverse problem of cubic surfaces. The third question examines the density of prismatic curves in the moduli space of smooth cubics. The fourth and fifth questions investigate the density of the closure of the Veech curve within the moduli space of all genus 3 curves and the structure of its fundamental group, respectively. The final question examines the relationship between the modular curve and the curve analogue of the moduli space of cubic surfaces. These inquiries are expected to have significant implications for understanding the geometry of cubic curves and their moduli spaces. The author intends to address these questions in future research. The modular curve is expected to play a crucial role in this future work. The author acknowledges the limitations of this paper and hopes to return to these topics with more complete results. This study investigates how remote work impacts Scrum project success. By integrating a systematic literature review with three primary empirical components—a survey of 100 practitioners, 14 in-depth interviews, and 10 case studies—the research identifies key challenges and solutions for remote Scrum teams. Findings indicate that while remote work introduces specific difficulties, it does not inherently hinder project success. The study concludes that success depends on adopting appropriate strategies to address these issues. Additionally, the research offers practical recommendations for managers and practitioners to mitigate problems and enhance the efficiency of remote Scrum projects. Finally, the paper outlines limitations and suggests directions for future research. This study examines the General Degrees of Freedom (GDoF) performance of optimal versus binary power control in a $K$-user interference network, where each user possesses a specific rate tolerance. We demonstrate that the maximum GDoF advantage gained by transmitters through optimal power control is $\Theta(\sqrt{K})$ bits per channel use. This finding is derived from a lower bound based on a specific subnetwork and an upper bound established through a novel genie-aided strategy. Furthermore, we illustrate that the performance gains of optimal power control are substantial only when rate tolerances are low and the number of users is small. Additionally, we show that for any user subset, the maximum possible GDoF improvement from optimal power control is bounded by the sum of individual gains achievable by each user in isolation. Finally, we extend these results to scenarios involving multiple rate tolerances and heterogeneous channel strengths. The paper concludes with an outline of the proof techniques and their application to related problems. This work was presented at the 2019 IEEE International Symposium on Information Theory (ISIT). The necessity to categorize transactions into distinct types has grown due to the increasing complexity of financial dealings. This paper introduces a novel categorization method designed to adapt to the introduction of new transaction types. The proposed algorithm operates in two stages: first, it identifies the types of existing transactions, and second, it determines the types for new transactions based on their similarity to the existing set. To address the first stage, we developed an adaptable categorization algorithm utilizing formal concept analysis, which successfully identifies transaction types even as new ones emerge. For the second stage, we introduced a new algorithm that leverages similarity measures derived from formal concept analysis to assign types to new transactions. We evaluated the proposed algorithms using a dataset of real-world transactions, demonstrating that they achieve high accuracy in both identifying and categorizing transactions. Furthermore, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of the algorithms' performance regarding various similarity measures and the impact of noise within the transaction data. The experimental results indicate that the proposed approach outperforms existing categorization methods. Additionally, the algorithm exhibits robustness against noisy data, and its performance is shown to be sensitive to the selection of similarity measures. Finally, the paper discusses the algorithm's performance across different transaction datasets. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/taiki-ito/adaptive-fca-categorization. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first application of formal concept analysis to the task of transaction categorization. The proposed approach is particularly well-suited for categorizing transactions in the financial sector.

The authors introduce a method for generating marked point patterns in space, termed the STC process, which combines the Strauss process with an identity transformation. This identity transformation, defined as a mapping that leaves its input unchanged, is applied with a specific probability. The study demonstrates that the STC process is both ergodic and fully specified by its pair correlation function. Furthermore, simulation results indicate that the process can exhibit clustering behavior. The paper concludes by outlining potential applications of the STC process. Additionally, the authors provide a R package, also named stc, to facilitate the simulation of this model. The package includes functions for simulating patterns, visualizing them, and calculating the pair correlation function. A reference to the stc package is included. Finally, the paper presents a simulation study comparing the performance of the pair correlation function estimator across the Poisson process, the Strauss process, and the STC process. This study utilizes the same data sets for the Poisson and Strauss processes as those used to illustrate the stc package. The results show that the estimator performs well for both the Poisson and Strauss processes. However, for the STC process, the estimator appears to overestimate the pair correlation function at small distances. This overestimation is attributed to the presence of spurious pairs generated by the identity transformation. Consequently, the STC process is not considered a fully repulsive process. The authors suggest that future research should explore methods to mitigate the effects of the identity transformation.

We examine a multitasking allocation framework where agents handle multiple tasks, each demanding a specific processing duration. Agents may process these tasks sequentially or concurrently, with parallel work requiring specialized equipment. The objective is to assign agents to either a shared processor or to rent this equipment to minimize the total processing time for all tasks. We analyze two scenarios: first, where every agent requires the shared processor or equipment for parallel work, and second, where some agents can perform tasks without either option. For the first scenario, we propose a constant-factor approximation algorithm for both sequential and parallel objectives. In the second scenario, we present a constant-factor approximation algorithm for the sequential case and demonstrate that achieving a constant-factor approximation for the parallel objective is NP-hard. Furthermore, we establish that the problem is APX-hard even when the number of tasks per agent is limited to two. Finally, we explore extensions where agents possess private information regarding their processing times. Our findings indicate that while truthful mechanisms can achieve constant-factor approximations for the sequential case, no such mechanisms exist for the parallel objective. Additionally, we show that a constant-factor approximation is achievable for the parallel objective if agents' processing times are publicly known. Finally, we present a constant-factor approximation algorithm for a scenario where agents can utilize either the shared processor or equipment for all tasks. All results are supported by tight lower bounds. This work is partially funded by the National Science Foundation under grant CCF-1908831.

Firmware updates are essential for maintaining the long-term functionality of Internet of Things (IoT) devices. However, the inherent risks associated with the update process and the need for high availability in IoT services make it difficult to perform these updates reliably. This paper presents an investigation into the performance of firmware updates within a large-scale IoT environment, specifically targeting the critical issue of network partitioning. We outline a novel approach to mitigate network partitions during the update procedure and validate its efficacy through a real-world deployment. Our findings indicate that this method can reduce the likelihood of network partitions occurring during firmware updates by a factor of 10. Additionally, we demonstrate that the proposed solution is compatible with existing IoT firmware update systems, requiring only a straightforward extension. To our knowledge, this is the first study to address network partitioning in IoT firmware updates. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/DependableIoT/FU4IoT. We investigate the multifractal characteristics of eigenstates within the one-dimensional many-body localization (MBL) phase of interacting disordered spin chains. By employing Fock-space renormalization group techniques, we calculate scaling exponents for the Fock-space propagator across the MBL-thermal phase transition. Our results indicate that the shift in the critical disorder strength, determined by the propagator's scaling behavior, aligns with findings from entanglement entropy scaling and the two-point correlation function of the emergent $\mathbb{Z}_2$ symmetry-breaking order parameter. Furthermore, we observe that the $\mathbb{Z}_2$ order parameter exhibits a power-law decay as the disorder approaches the critical point, a feature that distinguishes this first-order phase transition from the power-law decay of entanglement entropy at the criticality of other interacting disordered systems. These findings offer a novel perspective on the nature of the one-dimensional MBL phase transition. Additionally, we discuss the potential for extending this approach to the study of many-body criticality in higher dimensions. Finally, we explore the implications of our results for the existence of a fractional moment scaling crossover in the MBL phase. These insights are derived from a comprehensive analysis of the full set of multifractal exponents of the Fock-space propagator, which are determined by solving a nonlinear set of equations. We also examine the stability of the multifractal spectrum against variations in the system size of the renormalized blocks. Our results demonstrate that the multifractal spectrum of the MBL phase is not stable, a feature that differentiates it from the multifractal spectrum of the critical phase. This paper addresses the Interactive Search for Multiple Targets (ISMT) problem, a recently introduced framework where a searcher must locate $k$ hidden targets within a grid using a limited search budget. The process is interactive, meaning the searcher receives feedback after each move to determine if a target is present, absent, or if the current cell is occupied by a wall. We present a novel algorithm that identifies all hidden targets within the searcher's reachable range in $O(k)$ time. This approach outperforms existing methods, which are restricted to finding only a single target per iteration and require $O(n^2)$ time for an $n \times n$ grid. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our algorithm is optimal by establishing a lower bound of $\Omega(k)$ for the time complexity of any solution to the ISMT problem. Finally, we validate the efficiency of our method through extensive experiments. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2000/BILISMT. This paper investigates Steklov eigenvalues within two-dimensional nearly round domains. We demonstrate that for a given eigenvalue $\sigma_j$, the value $\sigma_j(D)$ strictly increases as the domain $D$ becomes more circular, provided $j \neq 1$. The circularity of a domain is quantified using the Fraenkel asymmetry metric. Conversely, for the specific case where $j=1$, we establish that $\sigma_1(D)$ remains invariant and equals $1$ for any domain $D$ with a Fraenkel asymmetry $\delta_D$ satisfying $\delta_D \leq 1/2$. This result contrasts with the well-established fact that the first Steklov eigenvalue is precisely $1$ exclusively for round disks. Furthermore, our methodology yields a novel, streamlined proof of the classical inequality $\sigma_1(D) \geq 1$, which holds for all bounded domains in $\mathbb{R}^2$. Finally, we offer a discussion regarding the optimality of the bound $\delta_D \leq 1/2$. Additionally, we extend these findings to $n$-dimensional domains, proving that $\sigma_1(D) \geq \lambda_1$, where $\lambda_1$ denotes the first eigenvalue of the Laplacian on a round sphere. The proof relies on an extension of the classical Faber-Krahn inequality to the Steklov eigenvalue problem, which was originally formulated by Henrot and Nguyen Van Tran. This paper introduces a formal semantics for temporal planning languages based on the logic PLPL, which extends PTL with planning-specific constructs. We demonstrate that this semantics is both sound and complete with respect to the standard model-based definition for a substantial subset of the language. Additionally, we provide a sound, complete, and decidable abstract interpretation of PLPL that serves as the foundation for a formally verified temporal planning system. Our approach to verified planning follows the strategy established by Bhat et al. (2019), where the planner acts as an oracle for the verified logic solver. We illustrate this by formally verifying the core components of a temporal planning system, including the initial release of Temporal Planning Graphs (TPGs), and subsequently present an experimental evaluation of this verified TPG solver. Finally, we discuss several open research questions arising from our work.

The formalizations developed in this study are accessible via the Coq Proof Assistant at https://github.com/veridicalai/plpl. The codebase includes formalized definitions for PTL and PLPL, along with sound, complete, and decidable abstract interpretations for both languages. Furthermore, we have developed a verified algorithm that constructs TPGs from a given plan, ensuring that the resulting TPG accurately represents the plan's temporal structure.

This study examines global existence issues concerning Vlasov-type equations with boundary conditions. Specifically, we demonstrate that global well-posedness for the Vlasov-Poisson system within a bounded container can be achieved by appropriately selecting boundary conditions. Furthermore, we extend these findings to global well-posedness in global mean field models, including the Hubbard-Stratonovich transformation and the classical spin-boson model. Finally, we establish the global existence of solutions for a generalized Vlasov-Poisson system featuring a nonlinear source term. Additionally, we provide the first global well-posedness proof for a quantum fluid model incorporating a nonlinear source term. These outcomes encompass the global existence of solutions for the Hartree equation with boundary conditions. The methodology employed relies on the regularity of boundary layer solutions and the application of weighted norms. To address the boundary layer issue, we utilize the Fourier transform in tangential variables alongside the Laplace transform in the normal direction. This approach enables the derivation of regularity estimates for the solution and its derivatives up to any order. Weighted norms are applied to derive a priori estimates for the solution. We anticipate that the techniques developed herein will be valuable for addressing other boundary value problems in both classical and quantum physics. As an application, we show that the results in this paper can be utilized to prove the global well-posedness of the time-dependent Hartree-Fock equation in a bounded domain. This achievement marks the first instance of such a result for a nonlinear Schrödinger equation featuring boundary conditions. The paper is structured as follows: Section 2 presents the main results; Section 3 reviews preliminary knowledge and essential lemmas; Section 4 addresses the linear problem; Section 5 focuses on the nonlinear problem; and Section 6 concludes with an application to the time-dependent Hartree-Fock equation. Developing effective techniques for concept location is crucial for enhancing software maintenance productivity. This paper introduces STRICT, a novel approach that leverages information retrieval to identify search keywords for concept location. STRICT constructs a software model from source code and applies information retrieval techniques to extract relevant identifiers. The resulting identifiers are used to retrieve concepts from a pre-trained code embedding model, with the most frequent concepts selected as optimal candidates. An extensive evaluation using the Defects4J dataset demonstrates that STRICT outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving a 10.5% improvement in F1-score. Additionally, an ablation study confirms the effectiveness of STRICT's design decisions. The implementation is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2000/strict.

Colloidal gels are extensively utilized in rheo-acoustics, where high-frequency vibrations imparted to the liquid phase can significantly alter their mechanical and flow characteristics. This study investigates the rheo-acoustic response of a colloidal gel to ultrasonic vibrations across varying amplitudes and frequencies. We demonstrate that applying ultrasonic waves can either stiffen or soften the gel, contingent upon the specific amplitude and frequency applied. By combining these experimental findings with Brownian dynamics simulations, we elucidate the underlying mechanisms driving these rheo-acoustic effects. Furthermore, we introduce a simple yet effective model that accurately predicts the observed gel responses to ultrasonic vibrations. These insights offer a straightforward method for tuning the mechanical and flow properties of colloidal gels, a capability with potential applications in both fundamental research and technological advancements. Our findings are validated using a model system composed of polystyrene spheres suspended in an aqueous sodium alginate solution. Additionally, we examine the rheo-acoustic response of a biologically inspired gel formed by the bacteria *Pseudomonas aeruginosa*, which exhibits similar behaviors to those of the synthetic colloidal gel. These results underscore the fundamental nature of rheo-acoustic effects in colloidal gels. Finally, we discuss the potential applications of these rheo-acoustic phenomena in both colloidal and biological systems. The stable matching problem involves a set of agents partitioned into two groups, where each pair from opposite groups has a ranked preference list over one another. A matching is considered stable if no two agents can mutually benefit by deviating from their current assignments. While the classic version assumes every agent prefers being matched over remaining single, this paper examines a more general scenario where each agent holds a specific threshold for acceptable matches. We investigate the computational complexity of identifying stable matchings in this context and demonstrate that a unique stable matching always exists when a single agent is present. Furthermore, we introduce a novel algorithm that identifies all stable matchings for any given instance in polynomial time. Finally, we explore the problem of maximizing the total number of matches within the set of all stable matchings, proving that this optimization is NP-hard. Additionally, we present a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme for instances where all agents prefer being matched over staying single. These findings are supported by a comprehensive computational study. Our results indicate that, in practice, the objective of maximizing the total number of matches is rarely necessary, as the optimal solution typically yields only a marginal increase in the number of agents who secure a preferred match compared to a standard stable matching. However, we also identify a specific class of instances where this optimization problem is solvable in polynomial time. Our work extends the stable matching framework to a broader context, offering a unified framework that encompasses both the classic problem and its more general variant. The proposed algorithms are efficient and applicable to a wide range of practical scenarios. Our findings demonstrate that these algorithms can effectively identify all stable matchings, even in large-scale instances, thereby facilitating decision-making for a diverse array of real-world applications. By enabling the selection of the most suitable stable matching based on specific criteria, our approach enhances the flexibility and effectiveness of these solutions. Ultimately, this research advances the field of stable matching and holds significant potential for real-world implementation. This work investigates the recovery of a real-valued signal using quadratic measurements. By integrating results from compressed sensing and statistical physics, we establish the exact phase diagram for a specific instance of this problem. This exact solution is achieved by demonstrating that the statistical mechanics of the associated optimization problem are equivalent to those of a well-known problem in statistical physics. Our methodology is applicable to deriving the phase diagrams of various signal recovery problems. Furthermore, we empirically validate the phase diagrams for several other recovery scenarios, including those involving random Gaussian and random real symmetric matrices. These empirical findings suggest that the derived phase diagrams are likely exact. Collectively, these results provide significant insight into the fundamental limits of signal recovery from quadratic measurements. Additionally, we demonstrate that a specific algorithm achieves optimal performance across all problems where phase diagrams were derived. This algorithm is a variant of the message-passing technique originally developed for the large system limit of error correction in low-density parity-check codes. Finally, we explore the relationship between this approach and the replica method used in statistical physics. These outcomes offer a comprehensive framework for comprehending the fundamental limits of signal recovery from quadratic measurements. This framework enables the derivation of phase diagrams for novel problems and facilitates the design of efficient algorithms for signal recovery. The framework is sufficiently general to be applicable to a broad range of signal recovery problems. The results presented herein were recently announced in a talk at the 2019 International Congress of Mathematicians. This manuscript serves as a detailed exposition of those results. LiDAR and camera sensors are extensively deployed in autonomous driving systems, yet their inherent limitations necessitate effective data fusion to enhance perception capabilities. This paper introduces a straightforward yet powerful LiDAR-camera fusion framework that integrates a lightweight, real-time, and robust fusion module into the common multi-modality perception pipeline. Unlike previous approaches, our method directly fuses raw data from both sensors within the common bird's-eye view (BEV) representation, thereby eliminating the need for complex alignment mechanisms. Specifically, we employ a multi-scale feature fusion strategy to combine camera and LiDAR features, followed by a decoupled refinement module that independently adjusts the spatial and channel dimensions of camera features before re-combining them with LiDAR features. This design effectively mitigates the adverse impacts of camera degradation caused by adverse weather and lighting conditions. Extensive experiments on the nuScenes benchmark demonstrate that our approach achieves significant performance gains, delivering a 1.5x improvement in detection and 2.5x in keypoint estimation compared to existing methods. Furthermore, our model attains 3.0x and 2.0x improvements in detection and keypoint estimation, respectively, over the second-best model when evaluated on the CarPK benchmark. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/IDEA-Research/BEVFusion. This study examines the stability of a natural language extraction approach applied to design discussions. We evaluate multiple models and techniques to identify the most effective configuration for an information extraction task focused on design discussions. Our findings indicate that a combination of BERT and Bi-LSTM proves to be the most suitable model for this specific application. Furthermore, we demonstrate that integrating both linguistic and non-linguistic features enhances performance. Finally, we assess various methods for handling out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words, revealing that a vocabulary expansion strategy yields the best results. Additionally, we explore the use of a language model to generate candidate sentences for discussion extraction, showing that this method performs comparably to other approaches. However, we also note that this language model-based approach offers greater conclusion stability than the other techniques evaluated. These results suggest that while current language models are not yet optimal for the specific task of discussion extraction, they hold significant promise for future advancements in the field. Ultimately, this research underscores the value of information extraction techniques in supporting design processes. By leveraging these methods, designers can more effectively manage large volumes of data, thereby improving their overall efficiency. Our work provides a foundation for future studies in this area. Specifically, we aim to investigate how information extracted from design discussions can be utilized to support designers, with an initial focus on developing a system capable of automatically identifying relevant discussions for a given design problem. This paper introduces H-STREAM, a new analytics pipeline designed for querying big streams and data histories. Built upon the STREAM architecture, H-STREAM is engineered to deliver high-performance, low-latency analytics on large datasets. It features a data model that integrates both stream and history storage, enabling queries against massive data histories. The architecture supports two distinct query modes: stream processing for low-latency real-time analytics, and history processing for high-performance batch analytics on big data. Additionally, the system provides a unified query interface for both modes, allowing users to issue queries against big streams and data histories seamlessly. The study also presents a query processing algorithm and its implementation, which are optimized to minimize resource consumption and latency. Furthermore, the paper details the implementation of H-STREAM and evaluates its performance through extensive experiments. Results from these experiments demonstrate that H-STREAM achieves high performance and low latency, outperforming both standalone STREAM and other state-of-the-art solutions. Finally, the paper concludes with a discussion of H-STREAM's advantages and potential future research directions. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ChenYi2016/H-STREAM. We present non-resonant visualizations for the single production of top and bottom partners at the LHC, which arise from the interference between vector-like (VL) and Standard Model (SM) currents. These images serve as a complementary tool to the well-known resonance plots used for identifying potential new physics signals. The color patterns in our illustrations reveal the relative contributions of individual quark flavors to the cross-section, thereby indicating the optimal channels for experimental searches. Furthermore, we show that the shapes of these images remain largely independent of the specific quark partner model, the particle's spin, and the final-state kinematic variables. This universality suggests that such non-resonant images can be effectively utilized for the discovery of new physics at the LHC. Additionally, we provide the corresponding python code for generating these images. Our findings are also applicable to the electroweak production of top partners. Neural Machine Translation (NMT) has emerged as a leading method for translating knowledge base (KB) elements, yet it frequently results in inconsistent handling of repeated entities, leading to repetition errors. COPY operates by copying source-side entities directly, bypassing the NMT model, and is compatible with any sequence-to-sequence architecture. This paper addresses the challenge of validating neural networks employed in nonlinear control systems. While recent literature has established rigorous validation techniques for convex approximations of neural networks, these methods are often computationally prohibitive for networks of moderate size. To overcome this barrier, we introduce a validation framework that is both efficient and effective. Our approach involves training a significantly smaller neural network to approximate the validation metric of the original network; this surrogate model enables fast validation checks with only a marginal reduction in accuracy. We demonstrate the efficacy of our method through several numerical examples. Furthermore, we apply this technique to validate neural networks designed for nonlinear $H_\infty$ control of a vehicle suspension system. Our results indicate that validation can be executed in under 10 milliseconds, a performance that is 1,000 times faster than the state-of-the-art approach. Additionally, the proposed method allows for the deployment of a high-performing neural network while maintaining a level of safety comparable to that of a convex approximation. To our knowledge, this represents the first successful validation of a neural network used in control applications. Finally, we discuss how this methodology can be extended to validate neural networks within broader control contexts. Our code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/abhishekgupta2000/NNValidation}. This study investigates the thermodynamic properties of a monolayer Graphene sheet subjected to a transverse electric field. The model incorporates both thermal fluctuations and the effects of a substrate. The resulting Hamiltonian is solved using the mean field approximation, and its partition function is derived via the saddle point method. These findings may assist in understanding the physical properties of suspended Graphene sheets. Additionally, the proposed theoretical framework could be applicable to other two-dimensional materials. Finally, these results may contribute to the design of future electronic devices. We report a decade-long radio observation of the binary system CR Draconis, a young, active star exhibiting frequent electron-cyclotron maser emission (ECME) at low frequencies. This study identifies a new radio source at 1.4 GHz, designated CR Draconis A, which is likely a compact region within the star's corona. The source's position angle aligns with the binary's axis, and its size is comparable to the corona of the Sun. The observed flux density of CR Draconis A fluctuates between 0.01 and 0.1 mJy, with a mean of approximately 0.05 mJy. These variations are attributed to changes in the magnetic field strength within the corona. Additionally, we detected a second source, CR Draconis B, at 1.4 GHz, which is likely a flare site. This source is located approximately 10 arcseconds from CR Draconis A, with a size of about 0.5 solar radii. The flux density of CR Draconis B varies between 0.01 and 0.1 mJy, with an average of roughly 0.05 mJy. The frequency of ECME in CR Draconis is comparable to that of the Sun, and the emission is primarily driven by flares. The low-frequency observations presented here are the first of their kind for this system. We conclude that ECME in CR Draconis is a long-term phenomenon, with a duration of at least ten years. This finding is significant for understanding the evolution of magnetic fields and the generation of ECME in young stars. Furthermore, the detection of low-frequency ECME in this young star suggests that such emissions may also be present in other young stars. These observations could be valuable for studying the magnetic field evolution of young stars and the mechanisms behind ECME generation. Finally, the low-frequency data may aid in searching for technosignatures. We compute the three-dimensional Chern-Simons link invariant for the Hopf link within $SU(2)$ at level $k$ by representing the link as the boundary of a surface embedded in three-dimensional Euclidean space. The resulting calculation yields the $q=ie^{\frac{\pi}{k+2}}$-specialization of the $q$-6j symbol, which corresponds to the connection between the Chern-Simons invariant and the quantum inverse scattering method. Furthermore, we derive the $q$-6j symbol using the Kauffman state model of the Hopf link, applying the skein relation to the diagram. This process generates a recurrence relation for the $q$-6j symbol that aligns with the orthogonality relations of the Askey-Wilson matrix. Consequently, this establishes a correspondence between the three-dimensional Chern-Simons link invariant and the Askey-Wilson matrix. Additionally, we provide the first rigorous derivation of the connection between the three-dimensional Chern-Simons link invariant and the quantum inverse scattering method. Finally, we discuss the extension of these findings to the torus knot.

We examine two-dimensional frustrated trimer antiferromagnets composed of interacting two-level systems. These systems are defined by strong intratrimer interactions and weak intertrimer couplings, with the latter modeled as either nearest-neighbor or triangular interactions. Cluster quantum Monte Carlo simulations are employed to investigate the phase diagram, specifically focusing on the competition between a ferromagnetic phase and two distinct antiferromagnetic phases. The ferromagnetic phase is characterized by equal populations of states $|000\rangle$ and $|111\rangle$ within the computational basis, whereas the antiferromagnetic phases arise from the populations of $|100\rangle$, $|010\rangle$, and $|001\rangle$. By analyzing the magnetic structure factor, we determine the system's ground state. Furthermore, we investigate the influence of intertrimer interactions on the ground state and the resulting phase diagram. Finally, we discuss the potential for extending this methodology to more complex systems. This research holds significant relevance for the study of strongly correlated systems, including those found in quantum information science and quantum biology. Additionally, the findings are applicable to the investigation of frustrated magnets, such as the $\mathrm{Na}_{10}\mathrm{V}_6\mathrm{O}_{13}$ compound. This material exhibits a unique geometric structure where vanadium atoms are grouped into trimers, and it displays a complex phase diagram featuring multiple magnetic phases. The present study offers a theoretical framework for analyzing the phase diagram of $\mathrm{Na}_{10}\mathrm{V}_6\mathrm{O}_{13}$. Finally, we outline the necessary extensions to the current model to accurately represent the quantum phase diagram of this compound. This study examines the nature of the electroweak phase transition (EWPT) within a discrete $Z_3$-invariant Next-to-Minimal Supersymmetric Standard Model (NMSSM) possessing a $\mu$-term. We analyze the Higgs boson mass ($m_h$) and dark matter phenomenology in light of recent LHC findings. Our findings indicate that, given the observed Higgs mass, the EWPT is typically of the first order, with a critical temperature ($T_c$) falling between 100 and 120 GeV. The latent heat released during this transition is substantial, ranging from 10 to 100 TeV. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the Hubble parameter ($H$) can be calculated using the latent heat and the energy density of radiation. Finally, we show that the ratio $\alpha = \Gamma/H$ serves as a measure of the departure from thermal equilibrium, where $\Gamma$ represents the decay rate of the Higgs boson. We conclude that the $\Gamma/H$ ratio is significant, spanning from 10 to 1000, thereby suggesting that the first-order phase transition in this model could generate detectable gravitational waves. Additionally, we note that the Higgs mass is closely linked to the dark matter mass, which may lie between 10 and 100 GeV. These characteristics are crucial for the detection of gravitational waves. Finally, we discuss the implications of our results regarding the detection of these waves. We introduce a novel technique for determining redshifts of distant galaxies by applying a two-dimensional discrete Fourier transform to their surface brightness profiles. This approach, which we term "Sudoku," leverages the self-similar structure of galaxy profiles to generate a one-dimensional representation of the source. By stacking multiple sources at the same redshift, we can determine the redshift of the group by matching the resulting pattern against a library of templates. We have developed a prototype implementation of this method and applied it to the 1.1mm and 1.3mm bands of the MAMBO-2 survey. Our analysis indicates that Sudoku achieves a median redshift accuracy of approximately 0.015 for (sub)mm sources at z ~ 2.5, with a 90% success rate within 0.025. We demonstrate that the method's robustness stems from its ability to mitigate the effects of surface brightness fluctuations caused by seeing and atmospheric transmission. Additionally, we show that the redshift distribution of the identified sources aligns with the expected distribution for the (sub)mm luminosity function at the survey's observed flux density level. We also examine the method's sensitivity to noise and surface brightness fluctuations, finding that it remains effective even in the presence of significant noise. Finally, we outline the method's potential for future (sub)mm redshift surveys. We anticipate that Sudoku will enable the identification of a substantial number of high-redshift (z > 3) sources in upcoming (sub)mm surveys, thereby enhancing the statistical significance of the sub-population at these extreme redshifts. Furthermore, the technique is applicable to optical and near-infrared imaging. The source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/andrewjbell/Sudoku. This research was conducted using the European Southern Observatory Very Large Telescope.

Our results indicate that the critical behavior of the $120^{\circ}$-ordered to spin-liquid transition is independent of the specific magnetic ion involved. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the spin-liquid state in the $J_1$-$J_2$ model. This study investigates the confinement-deconfinement phase transition within $3+1$-dimensional $SU(3)$-Higgs theory, which incorporates a complex scalar field in the adjoint representation. Utilizing the strong-coupling expansion, we determine the exact confinement-deconfinement order parameter and locate the phase transition. Our findings indicate that this transition is of the first order. Furthermore, we calculate the leading-order strong-coupling expansion for the deconfinement shift relative to the critical value identified by Monte Carlo simulations. These results are compared with analogous shifts observed in $SU(2)$ and $SU(4)$ theories. Additionally, we examine the confinement-deconfinement phase transition in the limit where the Higgs field becomes infinitely massive. In this scenario, the transition reverts to a second-order phase transition, mirroring the behavior of pure gauge theories. We also derive the strong-coupling expansion for the deconfinement shift in this second-order case and contrast it with the shifts found in $SU(2)$ and $SU(3)$ pure gauge theories. Finally, we discuss the implications of these results for the confinement-deconfinement phase transition of QCD. Specifically, we demonstrate that the strong-coupling expansion accurately predicts the deconfinement phase transition in QCD up to the leading order. Moreover, we show that the leading-order strong-coupling expansion for the deconfinement shift in QCD aligns with that of the $SU(3)$-Higgs theory. These outcomes suggest that the strong-coupling expansion remains a valuable tool for analyzing the confinement-deconfinement phase transition in QCD. Consequently, this work supports the hypothesis that the confinement-deconfinement phase transition in QCD is a first-order phase transition. Furthermore, we provide an estimate for the critical temperature of the deconfinement phase transition in QCD. Finally, we explore the implications of these findings for the existence of a critical point in the QCD phase diagram. Specifically, we show that the strong-coupling expansion predicts the presence of a critical point within the QCD phase diagram. Additionally, we estimate the location of this critical point. These results support the hypothesis that the QCD phase diagram includes a critical point situated near the crossover region. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the search for the critical point in the QCD phase diagram. Specifically, we demonstrate that the strong-coupling expansion can predict the existence of a critical point

Cr2Al crystallizes in the AlB2 structure and exhibits a high Néel temperature of 400 K. Neutron diffraction studies reveal that the antiferromagnetic order is characterized by in-plane ferromagnetic chains of chromium atoms coupled through antiferromagnetic interactions. The exchange interactions are primarily mediated by direct electron overlap and the p-d hybridization between chromium and aluminum. Additionally, the antiferromagnetic order induces a significant lattice distortion, transforming the initial hexagonal symmetry into a monoclinic one. This distortion arises from the competition between the elastic energy required to deform the lattice and the energy gained by lowering the symmetry. Furthermore, the antiferromagnetic order results in a substantial reduction of the Fermi surface volume, which is attributed to the exchange splitting of the chromium 3d bands. These findings are supported by detailed neutron diffraction data and first-principles calculations. The observed magnetic order in the AlB2 structure is also discussed in relation to other materials within this structural family. Finally, the potential for Cr2Al to serve as a component in magnetic devices is explored. This study examines a kinetic model featuring velocity-dependent collision frequency, evaluating its ability to replicate the impact of intermolecular potential on rarefied gas flows. The collision frequency is defined as proportional to the maximum of the inverse power-law potential, $C_n(r) \propto r^{-n}$, where $r$ represents the interparticle distance. Utilizing the Bhatnagar-Gross-Krook (BKG) collision operator, we derive the Knudsen layer oscillation and slip flow solutions for a hard sphere gas ($n=6$) and compare them against exact solutions. Furthermore, we analyze the slip length for a half-space wall potential, $U_{\rm wall}(r)$, which exhibits a minimum at a distance $r_{\rm min}$ from the surface. Our findings indicate that the proposed model successfully captures the effects of both gas-gas and gas-wall potentials. Specifically, the slip length is determined by the distance between the wall and the potential's minimum, as well as the magnitude of this minimum. Finally, we discuss the model's applicability to more sophisticated collision operators. We introduce a framework for semantic interpretation that relies on a single, untrained neural network to map between a latent space and the input space of a black-box system. This approach enables the efficient training of semantic models with minimal data, even when the black-box system lacks a trained component. By treating semantic interpretation as a black-box learning challenge, our method can be applied to a wide range of scenarios, including biological systems, legacy code, and other black-box models. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this technique facilitates the rapid discovery of new semantic models for both biological and software domains. The primary contributions of this work are the method itself, the insights gained from applying it, and the open-sourced code. The upcoming Electron-Ion Collider (EIC) will serve as a premier facility for investigating the internal structure of protons and nuclear protons, while also enabling a comprehensive examination of nucleon structure functions, parton distributions, and the dynamics of hadron formation. As a high-energy physics accelerator, the EIC will operate with proton beams ranging from 10 to 150 GeV and electron beams from 1.5 to 6 GeV. To achieve the necessary precision for these measurements, the Forward Silicon Tracker (FST) will deliver exceptional vertex and track resolution within a compact volume. This presentation will outline the design and development of the EIC's vertex tracking system, detailing the construction of the FST and the optimization of its readout and data processing systems. Furthermore, we will present initial test beam results from the EIC's R&D efforts. These results will demonstrate the tracker's performance in terms of spatial resolution, track reconstruction efficiency, and the accuracy of impact parameter and transverse impact parameter measurements. Additionally, we will showcase the development of a data visualization tool designed to facilitate the rapid analysis of track patterns and the identification of anomalies. Finally, we will present the outcomes of the EIC's first data-taking run at the Brookhaven National Laboratory (BNL) Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC). This will include an analysis of the track reconstruction efficiency and the quality of the achieved vertex and track resolution. Finally, we will discuss the ongoing work to integrate the EIC tracking system into the existing RHIC data acquisition infrastructure. This discussion will cover the development of a new data acquisition system tailored for the EIC, as well as the software and hardware upgrades required for the RHIC DAQ system. These upgrades are essential to support the EIC's high luminosity and the complex beam conditions inherent to a proton-proton collider. We will also present the results of the EIC's first data-taking run at RHIC. This will include an analysis of the track reconstruction efficiency and the quality of the achieved vertex and track resolution. Finally, we will discuss the ongoing work to integrate the EIC tracking system into the RHIC data acquisition infrastructure. This will cover the development of a new DAQ system for the EIC, as well as the software and hardware upgrades needed for the RHIC DAQ system. We report the discovery of a low-luminosity active galactic nucleus (AGN) in the nearby galaxy NGC 4490, identified through a significant luminosity fluctuation observed in the \ion{H}{i} 21-cm line. This AGN exhibits a nuclear velocity dispersion of $\sigma_{\rm nuc} = 100$ km s$^{-1}$ and a bolometric luminosity of $L_{\rm bol} = 10^{41.5}$ erg s$^{-1}$, derived from the average of optical and infrared continuum luminosities. The AGN's bolometric luminosity varied by a factor of 100 over a timescale of approximately 10 days, as evidenced by the $\sim$10-fold increase in \ion{H}{i} luminosity. This variation is comparable to the rapid brightening seen in the \ion{H}{i} lines of the nearby dwarf galaxy I Zw 18, which was previously attributed to a low-mass AGN eruption. We propose that the observed variability in NGC 4490 is also caused by an AGN eruption. The rapid rise and fall of the \ion{H}{i} line luminosity suggest that the eruption originates from the inner accretion disk, with a timescale of roughly 10 days. This finding supports the hypothesis that AGN eruptions can be detected in low-luminosity systems, potentially offering a method to identify a previously unknown population of low-mass AGN. Furthermore, the similarity in behavior between NGC 4490 and I Zw 18 implies that the physical mechanisms driving these eruptions are likely identical. Finally, the rapid variability in NGC 4490 may offer insights into the nature of the accretion process around low-mass AGN. The observed rise time of $\sim$10 days is consistent with the light-crossing time of the accretion disk, suggesting that the accretion disk in low-mass AGN may be geometrically thick. These results are based on data from the Green Bank Telescope, the Keck Observatory, and the Gemini Observatory. HD 58260 is a rapidly rotating, solar-type star known for hosting a large-scale magnetic field. This study presents spectropolarimetric observations of HD 58260 conducted at the Dunn Solar Telescope, utilizing emission lines of neutral helium and magnesium to measure the radial component of the magnetic field. These observations reveal a significant slope in the radial field profile, with the field strength increasing from the equator toward the pole. The data indicate a polar field strength of approximately 1.5 kG, which aligns with earlier measurements derived from absorption lines. Furthermore, the observed slope in the radial field profile is consistent with predictions from dynamo models. These findings offer the first direct confirmation of the poleward slope in the radial field profile of a solar-type star. Additionally, the results support the hypothesis that the large-scale magnetic field of HD 58260 is primarily generated by a dynamo mechanism similar to the Sun's. Finally, the observed slope in the radial field profile is comparable to that seen in the Sun, suggesting that the magnetic field structure of solar-type stars is likely governed by a universal set of physical laws. This conclusion is supported by the fact that all available measurements of magnetic field slopes in solar-type stars are consistent with a poleward slope. The paper concludes by discussing the implications of these results for the broader understanding of magnetic fields in solar-type stars. We present ALMA observations of the H30$\alpha$ recombination line in the low-metallicity starburst galaxy NGC 5253, which reveal a spatially resolved star formation rate surface density (SFR$_{\rm H30\alpha}$) that aligns well with the H$\alpha$-derived SFR surface density (SFR$_{\rm H\alpha}$) across the galaxy's central kiloparsec. This agreement indicates that H30$\alpha$ emission is a reliable star formation tracer in low-metallicity environments. Furthermore, we demonstrate that SFR surface density correlates with the ratio of H30$\alpha$ to H$\alpha$ flux, suggesting that H30$\alpha$ is particularly effective at tracing star formation in regions with high ionization. Finally, we find that SFR surface density scales with the square of the ionization parameter, a relationship consistent with findings from high-metallicity starbursts. These results suggest that H30$\alpha$ is an ideal probe for studying the connection between ionization parameters and star formation in both low- and high-ionization zones. Additionally, the data indicate that H30$\alpha$ emission is well-modeled by a single-temperature photoionization model, with a temperature of approximately 10,000 K, regardless of the ionization parameter. These findings support the hypothesis that H30$\alpha$ is a robust star formation indicator in low-metallicity galaxies. Our analysis also reveals that the H30$\alpha$/H$\alpha$ ratio is sensitive to the ionization parameter, making it a valuable tool for measuring this parameter in low-metallicity starbursts. Finally, we show that the H30$\alpha$/H$\alpha$ ratio can be used to distinguish between star-forming and post-starburst galaxies. Overall, these results underscore the utility of H30$\alpha$ as a powerful tool for investigating star formation in low-metallicity galaxies. We demonstrate that for any two continuous actions of a nontrivial finite cyclic group on a compact Hausdorff space $X$, if a third such action exists that is topologically conjugate to the first for every nontrivial group element but to the second for every $-1$-twist, then it is also conjugate to the second via a $\mathbb{Z}_2$-action. This result extends to $X$ being a compact Lie group, provided the acting groups act by continuous self-maps. Furthermore, assuming $X$ possesses a sufficiently rich structure, we establish that for any two actions of a nontrivial virtually cyclic group where each finite subgroup acts by homeomorphisms, conjugacy between the actions for every nontrivial element implies that the actions are conjugate by a virtually cyclic action. The latter finding also holds when $X$ is a compact Hausdorff space equipped with a free action of a nontrivial virtually abelian group. Additionally, we present examples illustrating that these results fail for the trivial action of a nontrivial virtually cyclic group on the one-point space. Finally, we propose several open questions regarding these phenomena. Notably, we prove that for any two actions of a finite cyclic group on a compact Lie group $X$ by Lie group automorphisms, if they are conjugate by an automorphism on every nontrivial element's action, they are conjugate by a virtually cyclic action. This extends to actions by continuous self-maps when $X$ is a compact Lie group possessing a faithful representation as a closed subgroup of the group of Lie group automorphisms. However, we also provide a counterexample for a compact Lie group $X$ with a free action by continuous self-maps, showing that the conclusion does not necessarily hold. These findings rely on the structure of the automorphism group of a compact Lie group, specifically the properties of its maximal tori and their centralizers. The paper concludes with a discussion of the broader implications of these results. This study introduces a nonparametric estimation framework for the conditional expectation operator (CEO), which maps a random variable to its conditional expectation given another. The proposed estimator relies on the empirical operator derived from finite samples and employs a data-driven bandwidth selection technique grounded in a novel nonparametric approximation of the operator's integrated mean squared error. We establish a data-dependent rate of convergence for this estimator and demonstrate its consistency. Furthermore, we develop a hypothesis testing procedure to evaluate whether the CEO is a bounded linear operator. Extensive Monte Carlo simulations assess the finite-sample performance of the proposed estimator and the resulting test, with results indicating promising empirical behavior. Finally, the methodology is applied to two real-world datasets: one analyzing the relationship between a firm's stock return and its market-to-book ratio, and another examining the link between a country's inflation rate and its output gap. In both applications, the CEO fails to qualify as a bounded linear operator. Additionally, we prove that the estimator is Hadamard differentiable and provide an implementation available on GitHub. Supplementary materials are accessible at https://www.econometricsociety.org/publications/quantitative-economics/2021-08-01/nonparametric-estimation-conditional-expectation/operators.shtml. To achieve this, we introduce a new observability concept for a broad category of nonlinear systems. We demonstrate that this concept ensures the existence of a unique continuous observer for any system within this category. Leveraging this theoretical framework, we develop a novel method to estimate both parameters and states in SIR and SEIR models. We validate the effectiveness of this approach through simulations. Furthermore, we apply the method to real-world data from the 2009 H1N1 influenza outbreak in France, utilizing hospitalization records and serological survey results. Our findings indicate that the proposed method yields more accurate estimates for both parameters and states compared to existing approaches. Additionally, we demonstrate that this method can effectively forecast the progression of the epidemic. Finally, we illustrate the method's potential to analyze the impact of non-pharmaceutical interventions on the epidemic's evolution. This is achieved by simulating various interventions, such as school closures, and analyzing their effects on the number of infections and the timing of the epidemic's peak. The results suggest that these interventions were effective in reducing the number of infections and delaying the onset of the epidemic. However, the analysis also reveals that these interventions had a limited effect on the epidemic's peak height. These findings are supported by data from the 2009 H1N1 outbreak in France and the 2020 COVID-19 outbreak in the United States. The proposed method is applicable to any SEIR or SIR model that incorporates a death compartment. This model can be utilized to estimate parameters and states, as well as to evaluate the impact of non-pharmaceutical interventions on the evolution of the epidemic. Temporal Knowledge Graphs (TKGs) extend traditional Knowledge Graphs by incorporating timestamps to capture dynamic events. While TKGs offer a more comprehensive representation of real-world data, current research primarily focuses on static models, leaving temporal information largely underutilized. This study investigates the effectiveness of static models in handling timestamps and demonstrates their viability for tedge. Our findings indicate that these static models achieve state-of-the-art performance across multiple benchmark datasets. Additionally, we show that specific data preprocessing techniques can enhance model performance, and we provide an in-depth analysis of the impact of various regularization strategies. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ashishkumar2001/teedge. This research was conducted as part of the tedge challenge. We hope these insights prove valuable for future TKG research. Ultrashort laser pulses are extensively utilized in science and technology, with Kerr-lens mode-locking (KLM) serving as a primary method for their generation. This review examines the stability and performance of ultrafast oscillators based on KLM by applying geometrical laser theory. The analysis covers both the conventional single-lens KLM model and an extended multi-lens model that incorporates the gain medium. The geometrical approach offers distinct benefits over the traditional paraxial theory, particularly in addressing non-paraxial effects and calculating the pulse's longitudinal position within the cavity. Furthermore, the study explores the potential of KLM oscillators for high-peak-power applications, specifically addressing the trade-off between pulse energy and the stability of the self-starting process. Finally, the paper presents a novel concept for high-energy KLM oscillators and outlines future research directions. This work serves as a resource for scientists and engineers developing KLM oscillators, aiming to enhance their performance and energy output. Additionally, it provides a pedagogical overview of laser theory, geometrical optics, and laser stability analysis, making it valuable for graduate students and researchers in physics and engineering. This paper introduces a novel Resource-Conscious Asynchronous Online Federated Learning (RC-AOL) framework designed for nonlinear regression. The core objective is to minimize the average squared error between predicted and actual outputs while simultaneously managing computational resources, specifically CPU usage, memory consumption, and communication costs. To achieve this, we propose a new asynchronous online learning algorithm that dynamically adjusts the learning rate and sampling probability for each participating agent. These adjustments are guided by a Q-learning-based model that continuously updates its policy to optimize resource efficiency. We provide a theoretical analysis demonstrating that the proposed method achieves a convergence rate of $O(1/T)$, where $T$ represents the total number of iterations. Furthermore, we validate the approach's effectiveness in nonlinear regression through extensive experiments conducted across varying numbers of agents and diverse computational resource constraints. The results indicate that our method outperforms existing asynchronous online learning approaches in terms of prediction accuracy and resource utilization. The source code is accessible at \url{https://github.com/ChenYi2000/RC-AOL}.

We introduce the concept of a high-dimensional cover, which includes hypergraphs that possess extender properties. Specifically, if the covering lines of a vertex set in such a cover correspond to extender spaces across all relevant cardinalities, then the cover itself functions as a high-dimensional extenders. Furthermore, we demonstrate that uniform covers constitute a subclass of high-dimensional extender spaces and provide a characterization of them using matrix theory. Finally, we outline several applications of these findings within finite geometry. A distinguishing feature of our approach is that it does not rely on vector spaces or fields, thereby enabling the construction of various geometric structures in prime characteristic that were previously unattainable. Additionally, our framework is applicable to high-dimensional extenders defined over other algebraic structures. The study investigates the magnetic properties of the centered honeycomb antiferromagnet GdInO$_3$, a material characterized by strong quasi-two-dimensionality. Using a combination of experimental data and theoretical modeling, we determined the magnetic structure and analyzed the temperature dependence of key parameters, including the Néel temperature ($T_N$), magnetic moment, and anisotropy. We demonstrate that the magnetic structure arises from the competition between two exchange interactions, $J_1$ and $J_2$, which are derived from the hopping integrals $t_1$ and $t_2$. Furthermore, we show that the hopping integral $t_2$ is highly sensitive to the ionic radius of the A-site ion, a factor that significantly influences the magnetic behavior. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for the broader class of centered honeycomb antiferromagnets. The experimental findings are supported by density functional theory calculations. We present a method for creating atomic vapor cells utilizing deep silicon etching and anisotropic etching techniques. These cells, which contain a single chip with etched channels, are designed for integration into compact optical setups. We demonstrate the fabrication of a cell with an internal volume of 1.5 cm³ that houses a 10 mm length silicon chip with an internal width of 1.5 mm. This design achieves a 90% transmission rate at a wavelength of 780 nm. We also outline a strategy for producing even smaller cells, with an internal volume of approximately 1 mm³, by employing a wafer-level bonding approach. Such miniaturized cells are ideal for integration into optical tables and for use in quantum optical experiments. We illustrate this potential by describing a setup for the quantum interference of single photons and atoms, which utilizes a cell volume of roughly 1.5 mm³. This configuration supports a maximum of 10 mW of 780 nm laser power and maintains a vapor density of approximately 10¹⁴ atoms/cm³. We anticipate that these small vapor cells will be integral to future quantum optical experiments. Additionally, we propose that these cells can be manufactured at a low cost using standard silicon foundry processes. This study introduces Deep Bellman Insurance (DBI), a novel deep learning framework designed to address the multi-period optimal reinsurance problem under the mean-variance criterion. The approach comprises two key components: the Deep Bellman Network (DBN) and the Deep Sampling Network (DSN). The DBN functions as a feed-forward artificial neural network that approximates the value function, whereas the DSN generates random samples from the action space to ensure sufficient exploration. By integrating these elements, the framework effectively circumvents the curse of dimensionality and learns an optimal reinsurance strategy without relying on predefined functional forms. Numerical experiments demonstrate that DBI successfully identifies optimal reinsurance policies and outperforms existing methods in both computational efficiency and solution quality. Furthermore, the framework's robustness is validated through sensitivity analyses. These findings indicate that DBI is highly effective for solving practical optimal reinsurance problems. Additionally, the framework is implemented in the R package `DeepInsurance`, which offers a user-friendly interface for applying the method. Sequential recommenders are widely used in industry to suggest the next item a user should engage with. However, these models often struggle to generalize to new users and fail to account for the purpose behind a user's sequence of interactions. To address these issues, we introduce a new framework that integrates latent user purpose into sequential recommenders. The reducible double confluent Heun equation (DCHE) is a second-order ordinary differential equation featuring three regular singularities and one irregular singularity of rank 1. It serves as a generalization of the confluent Heun equation (CHE) and arises in various physical contexts, including the quantum mechanical anharmonic oscillator, the Mathieu equation, and the Schrödinger equation for a charged particle in a uniform magnetic field subject to a specific potential. This paper demonstrates that the DCHE can be derived from the CHE through a specific symmetric unfolding of its source term. This unfolding is defined by a symmetric function $f(z)$ that possesses a zero at $z=0$ and two non-zero zeros, $\pm a$, where $a \in \mathbb{C} \setminus \{0\}$. The resulting DCHE is characterized by three finite exponents and one infinite exponent of order 1. We establish that the DCHE is reducible if and only if its exponents at the three regular singularities are either all zero or all unity. Furthermore, we show that the DCHE can be transformed into a form with a vanishing residue at the singularity $z=0$ through a specific gauge transformation. Finally, we derive the conditions under which the DCHE reduces to a Chebyshev-type equation. These findings are applicable to the double confluent form of the potential well introduced in [1]. Additionally, we provide a comprehensive set of reduction criteria for the DCHE, which are more stringent than those for the CHE. We also examine the conditions required for the DCHE to possess a single exponent at the singularity $z=0$ and for the singularity at infinity to be regular. Finally, we present a criterion for the reducibility of the DCHE based on the exponents at the three regular singularities. These results are also relevant to the double confluent form of the potential well discussed in [1].

Keywords: Double confluent Heun equation, reducibility, unfolding, symmetric unfolding, Chebyshev equation, exponents, gauge transformation, quantum mechanics, anharmonic oscillator, Mathieu equation, Schrödinger equation, potential well.

We introduce a topological model that lacks inherent symmetry, thereby challenging the conventional view that symmetry is essential for defining topological materials. This model is defined by a momentum-space Hamiltonian featuring a position-dependent mass term, which breaks translational symmetry. Despite this, the system maintains a robust topological characterization through the presence of a quantized Chern number. Furthermore, the model exhibits a momentum-dependent mass term that supports a momentum-space domain wall, resulting in the emergence of a zero-energy state at the K point within the Brillouin zone. This zero-energy state is protected by the system's topology and is identified as a momentum-space zero mode. Additionally, we demonstrate that the model can be derived from a position-space Hamiltonian that includes a gauge field. Finally, we show that this framework can be extended to a higher-dimensional system that displays a nontrivial $\mathbb{Z}_2$ topological invariant. These findings suggest that topological materials may exist without relying on symmetry, a hypothesis that could be tested through future experiments. Our results also provide a novel perspective on the relationship between position-space zero modes and momentum zero modes. Finally, we propose that this model could serve as a foundation for developing new topological materials. To facilitate this, we have included a proposal for a moiré heterostructure that can realize this model. We conclude by discussing the potential applications of this approach. This study introduces a design framework for multi-channel systems that enables decentralized control and operation. The proposed framework is inherently distributed, allowing each channel to be managed independently without requiring communication between channels. This approach is particularly advantageous for large-scale systems, such as multi-channel sensing networks, where integrating new channels is typically complex and demands significant human effort. We demonstrate that decentralized design and plug-and-play functionality can be achieved by appropriately selecting the channel input-output mapping. Our methodology involves first identifying the class of decentralized controllers capable of delivering desired performance, and subsequently designing the input-output mapping to facilitate such control. We illustrate the application of this method using linear time-invariant systems, specifically focusing on distributed $H_2$ performance. The resulting methodology is straightforward, requiring only the solution of linear matrix equations and the addition of feedforward terms. Furthermore, we provide a constructive proof of existence for the proposed controller and input-output mapping, accompanied by numerical examples that validate the approach. These examples highlight the method's ability to achieve distributed feedforward control, support plug-and-play operations, and deliver optimal performance. Finally, we extend this methodology to a broader context by applying it to the design of decentralized controllers for linear time-varying systems. In this extension, we utilize linear matrix inequalities to characterize the set of decentralized controllers that ensure specified performance levels. Our primary contribution lies in the development of this framework, which offers a systematic pathway for creating decentralized controllers and enables plug-and-play capabilities. The method is versatile and can be adapted to various performance criteria, including $H_2$, $H_\infty$, and robust stability. Additionally, the approach is applicable to decentralized control design in linear time-invariant systems, where it yields explicit parameterizations for dynamic controllers. The paper is structured as follows: Section II presents the problem formulation; Section III details the proposed methodology; Section IV applies the approach to decentralized control design; and Section V concludes with a summary and future research directions. Finally, Section VI offers concluding remarks.
